Ms STEPH COOKE ( Cootamundra ) ( 12:54 :53 ): My question is directed to the Minister for Local Government. What, if any, discussions did he have with the Minister for Lands and Property, or his chief of staff, regarding the Saravinovski NSW Civil and Administrative Tribunal [NCAT] proceedings at any time prior to Labor's preselection for Bayside Council?

Mr RON HOENIG ( Heffron — Minister for Local Government ) ( 12:55 :15 ): I told the other place during budget estimates hearings that as soon as proceedings were implemented in NCAT and were on a public list, I informed the local members as to the commencement of proceedings and I informed the New South Wales branch of the Labor Party. Shortly thereafter—at Mr Saravinovski's request, as I understand it—non-publication and non‑disclosure orders were made, so I was unable to have any further discussion in relation to the matter.

Ms DONNA DAVIS ( Parramatta ) ( 12:13 :59 ): My question is addressed to the Premier. Will the Premier please update the House on the Government's work to rebuild public education?

Mr CHRIS MINNS ( Kogarah — Premier ) ( 12:14 :10 ): I am happy to report that the Government is in the midst of building and upgrading 50 schools and public preschools across New South Wales. I note that the Coalition Government left New South Wales with fewer schools than when it started. Can you believe that? The Coalition Government oversaw a 35 per cent increase in demountable classrooms. It put out media releases claiming schools in Box Hill, Marsden Park, Gledswood Hills, Gregory Hills, Leppington, Schofields, Tallawong, Edmondson Park and Riverstone were completed when they had not even begun.

I am proud to report to the House that after turning the first sod 18 months ago, we have opened Darcy Road Public School, which has the capacity to grow four times larger than its original 255 students. It has two new multistorey buildings with 45 new classrooms. By the end of the year—this is the best bit—all demountable classrooms will be removed. This will open up 3,600 square metres of open playing surface for the kids. We have opened new schools in regional New South Wales at West Dapto, Flinders, Calderwood—the member for Kiama and the member for Shellharbour will be thrilled about that—and Medowie. Construction has finally begun at the Medowie High School. This new school was promised and planned in 1983. Medowie is one of the fastest growing suburbs in Port Stephens and one of the fastest growing communities in Australia. It needed a new school. It was neglected and forgotten by the previous Government. We are getting on with building it.

The good news is that the transformation of public education—an idea articulated and then executed by the Deputy Premier, and Minister for Education and Early Learning—has taken place in a short time. In 2½ years we have halved the number of cancelled and merged classes. Teacher resignations are at a four-year low for the first time in 13 years. In the 2025-26 budget, $9 billion will be allocated over four years—the largest number ever recorded—for new and upgraded schools. That money will go to the fastest growing communities, which is what taxpayers in New South Wales are demanding and expecting. There are, of course, alternative ideas and plans when it comes to new schools. [ Extension of time ]

I refer members to a headline in The Sydney Morning Herald on 20 October 2022 regarding the previous Government: "New Sydney public schools to share space with shops, apartments under radical proposal". The article stated that the Coalition Government was considering a radical plan to combine two new public schools with shops and high-rise apartments in the same development. A proposal for a new education campus at Macquarie Park with a capacity of 300 students was flagged as a way of partnering with private developers. What could go wrong?

The SPEAKER: Government members will come to order.

Mr CHRIS MINNS: The then New South Wales Minister, Sarah Mitchell, said the new primary school and high school were an opportunity to deliver the infrastructure to growing communities in an "innovative way". Members can imagine a student walking into science class past a Dan Murphy's on the ground floor. That would be a good idea. Imagine a student going to commerce class or the gym and waking past a new tobacconist on the ground floor. We could put a casino into Casino High School and save on signage. In that same article Stephen Earp, a planning adviser who works in development, said, "Mixed-use school developments are not the norm in New South Wales and need careful consideration." If you look closely, that is planning speak for "Are you crazy?" You might say, "What about a McDonald's in a public school?" It might seem insane, but I refer members to a budget estimates hearing in which the Hon. Sarah Mitchell was asked that exact question. I might be selectively quoting but not too badly. She said, "No decisions have been made yet. You are making an awful lot of assumptions in your question." There we have it: science, McDonald's, Dan Murphy's and tobacconists all in one place. Let us take the shadow Education portfolio off the National Party. [ Time expired. ]

Mrs SALLY QUINNELL ( Camden ) ( 12:23 :20 ): My question is addressed to the Minister for Roads. Following one of Sydney's wettest winters on record—including in my local community of Camden—will the Minister update the House on the Minns Labor Government's work to ensure faster repairs to our busiest corridors?

Ms JENNY AITCHISON ( Maitland — Minister for Regional Transport, and Minister for Roads ) ( 12:23 :37 ): I am pleased to be asked that question by the member for Camden. She has great interest in road safety and maintenance right across New South Wales and particularly in her electorate. A couple of weeks ago I was in the Camden electorate with the member, looking at those issues. I am pleased to report that we filled 84 potholes in the Camden council area. That pales into insignificance given we have filled more than 5,100 potholes in the past two months across the Greater Sydney road network, which is a good result because over the past 12 months we filled nearly 11,000.

The SPEAKER: Opposition members will come to order. There is too much audible conversation in the Chamber. The member for Kellyville will come to order. I direct the member for Kellyville to remove himself from the Chamber until the conclusion of the Minister's answer. The Minister has the call.

[ Pursuant to standing order the member for Kellyville left the Chamber at 12:24. ]

Ms JENNY AITCHISON: It has been distressing for the community, which is worried about the road conditions and the networks of potholes. The clowns on the other side just want to joke about it. They do not want to invest in maintenance.

Mr Dugald Saunders: We did!

Ms JENNY AITCHISON: No, you didn't.

The SPEAKER: The member for Dubbo will come to order.

Ms JENNY AITCHISON: At the last election, those opposite did not commit any extra money to invest in our roads. It was doughnuts.

Mr Alister Henskens: Point of order—

The SPEAKER: The Clerk will stop the clock. The Minister will resume her seat. The member for Wahroonga rises on a point of order.

Mr Alister Henskens: The Minister should address her comments through you, Mr Speaker, rather than directing them across the Chamber.

The SPEAKER: I uphold the point of order as a general admonishment to members. However, the Minister was directing most of her comments through the Chair.

Ms JENNY AITCHISON: I appreciate the ruling, Mr Speaker. New South Wales had its hottest wet weather in decades, and the Sydney metro road network in particular has struggled. We have brought forward spending $200 million. Those opposite are shy about their position, which I can understand because their position is to do nothing and let things happen. We have done more in the past two months than we did in the previous 12 months, and we will do more with this funding. What do those opposite have to say? They say, "We do not want to do that. You should not use that money." What is their plan? They have no plan. Those opposite took a commitment to the last election of exactly zero dollars for new roads. We have just announced an investment of $200 million on State roads in Greater Sydney. We have not forgotten the regions. At the Bush Summit, the Premier announced an investment of $155 million in regional State highways. A couple of weeks ago, I announced an investment of $46 million, so that is $201 million for the regions. [ Extension of time ]

The Government is spending more than $400 million this year to try to get on top of potholes on our roads. Those opposite said, "Why would you bring that money forward?"

The SPEAKER: The member for Oxley will come to order.

Ms JENNY AITCHISON: It is because the potholes get bigger, and they get more expensive, so we are doing what responsible governments do.

The SPEAKER: Order! I direct the member for Dubbo to remove himself from the Chamber under Standing Order 249A until the conclusion of the Minister's answer. If the member continues to have conversations on his way out, I will direct him to remove himself from the Chamber for the rest of the day.

[ Pursuant to standing order the member for Dubbo left the Chamber at 12:27 . ]

Ms JENNY AITCHISON: The member for Dubbo need not to worry; I will fix his roads too. This $400 million investment is on top of the $670 million that has gone to councils in regional New South Wales since 2023, the $220 million that went to Sydney councils for their roads in 2023, which we allowed them to spend over four years—they did not waste their time—plus another $1.024 billion that went towards disaster recovery last year. Those opposite could never get that money out the door because they do not care about their communities.

The SPEAKER: I call the member for Myall Lakes to order for the first time.

Ms JENNY AITCHISON: They did not understand how local government worked, so they expected councils to go out and get tenders to fix billions of dollars worth of road damage, without any certainty of funding. But we should not ask those opposite about local government; they do not know anything about it, as the member for Heffron would know.

The SPEAKER: I call the member for Myall Lakes to order for the second time.

Ms JENNY AITCHISON: We are working on fixing the backlog that those opposite left behind. When they were in government, they spent billions of dollars on Sydney megaprojects. They never invested in maintenance of the network.

The SPEAKER: I call the member for Coffs Harbour to order for the first time. I call the member for Albury to order for the first time.

Ms JENNY AITCHISON: There was $22 billion in cost blowouts and overspends on transport and roads projects that they could not keep under budget, while every single member in this Chamber and all of their communities have been riding on roughshod roads that were not maintained by those opposite. We are getting on with the job. It is a massive challenge, but I do not apologise for bringing forward maintenance to fix the mess left by those opposite. It is what we do every day in this Government.

tree_branches.text:
Ms JACQUI SCRUBY ( Pittwater ) ( 12:29 :35 ): My question is directed to the Minister for Health. Will the Minister confirm that, irrespective of ownership, Northern Beaches Hospital will continue to provide the same private hospital services under its new operating model?

Mr RYAN PARK ( Keira — Minister for Health, Minister for Regional Health, and Minister for the Illawarra and the South Coast ) ( 12:29 :55 ): I thank the member for Pittwater for her staunch advocacy on behalf of the people of the northern beaches, alongside the member for Wakehurst. This is arguably one of the most complex transactions this Government will undertake. It is certainly the most complex area of public administration that I have been involved in with the Treasurer. I am pleased that the member for Pittwater, who has been such a strong advocate, has been meeting with clinicians around this. I believe she recently held a round table with clinicians.

We understand the important role that the private sector plays in the delivery of health services right across New South Wales, particularly in relation to elective surgery. Similarly to education, where the system relies on private schools and Catholic schools, our health system relies on private hospitals to take the load off our very busy public hospitals. I am not in a position yet to outline to the House what that model will look like at Northern Beaches Hospital. But I assure both the member for Pittwater and the member for Wakehurst that not only are we engaging with clinicians—and I will be meeting with the staff medical council again very soon—but also the receiver and others around this. Once we have made a decision around the way forward on that hospital, we will also make it clear to the community, through the local members, and to this Parliament and the broader State of New South Wales.

To say it is complex is an understatement. This is a hospital that essentially has a long way to go yet on a private contractual arrangement. What we are attempting to do is bring that hospital back into public hands in a way that does not hurt taxpayers, ensures the continuity of care of services for the people of the northern beaches, and makes sure it plays a role across New South Wales in enhancing health services. All of that is extremely difficult and complex when there is not only a significant contract in place but we are now also dealing with the receivers. What it should highlight to this Parliament, and I hope to future parliaments, is that the privatisation of acute public health services is a stupid idea. Through this Government, this Parliament has passed legislation that will hopefully eliminate that bright-spark idea down the track and see it not taken any further. [ Extension of time ]

I wish I could highlight to the House the challenges that the member for Pittwater, the member for Wakehurst and their respective communities are now facing as a result of the privatisation of acute public health services. We made it clear at the time that it was the wrong move. At the time, there were going to be around five other hospitals under threat of this type of privatisation, including Shellharbour in my own region. That would have been absolutely disastrous. Given the challenges we are working through at the moment, to try and unpick five of these contracts would have been nearly impossible.

I update the member for Pittwater, the member for Wakehurst and the House on the transition team we have had at work over the last six or seven weeks. That team has had access to a very large number of documents, particularly in relation to the financial situation at the hospital, the staffing situation, the IT challenges and the broader operational challenges that we face as we move into this next phase. I acknowledge the work of the receiver and that of the taskforce, led by the chief operating officer of NSW Health, Alfa D'Amato, as well as NSW Treasury.

Yesterday the Treasurer and I once again met with Elouise and Danny Massa, the parents of Joe Massa, who were responsible for lighting the fire under this situation. We have been keeping them informed along the way. We will also ensure the local members for the electorates of Pittwater and Wakehurst remain informed so that they can keep their communities informed. This is a difficult and complex situation, but we are determined to get it resolved in the best interests of the people of the northern beaches as well as the broader New South Wales health system.

Mr JASON LI ( Strathfield ) ( 12:35 :07 ): My question is addressed to the Minister for Planning and Public Spaces. Will the Minister please update the House on the importance of reforming the existing planning system to address the State's housing crisis?

Mr PAUL SCULLY ( Wollongong — Minister for Planning and Public Spaces ) ( 12:35 :21 ): I thank the member for Strathfield for the question. He is determined and committed to making sure that we not only get a better deal on housing but also on jobs and the protection of the environment in New South Wales. I also acknowledge my new colleague in the Illawarra-South Coast region, the member for Kiama. I am glad her first question time has been a lively one. For decades, New South Wales has not been building enough housing. It has meant that young people have left the State and we have among the highest house prices in the world.

When we came to government in 2023, we started with a confused and confusing planning system that was in need of reform. House building had collapsed, with the forecast for a mere 180,000 homes over the next five years, less than half of that required under the housing accord target. Development application times averaged 116 days. Young people were giving up on New South Wales and Sydney, which is one of the least dense and most expensive cities on the planet. In fact, restrictions on the type of housing you could build in Sydney meant that we had less diversity in housing then than a century ago. That is how things had got. Permissibility of certain dwelling types had been removed. In areas that were zoned as medium density, one could not build a small apartment building. That is why we needed to get reform underway. At the same time, Sydney also had challenges with employment lands, with the amount of serviced and available industrial land plummeting under the previous Government.

In the decades since the Environmental Planning and Assessment Act was introduced, nearly 120 proposals to amend the Act have been before the Parliament, with mixed results. But that number of changes does not count the court decisions, the regulatory changes, the planning instruments, the practice notes and all the other things that govern the day-to-day interventions. Nor does it capture the ripple effect of other decisions in other areas of government on planning, or the decisions of the courts. Each change, perhaps logical in isolation, built up over time like cholesterol in an artery and blocked the system. That has made it harder to build a home. It has also made it harder to attract job-creating investments and get them going.

Reform is needed. Reform is overdue. In fact, reform is so overdue that some have even called for divine intervention to fix the New South Wales planning system. Priscilla Tran, the manager of urban renewal at Sydney Anglican Property, wrote recently in a LinkedIn post that she began praying for planning reforms last year. She applauded the New South Wales Government and urged the Opposition to get behind the current round of reforms. She stated:

Anyone that has ever had to interact with the system knows it often requires divine intervention to navigate the system let alone reform it!

That is not good enough in modern-day New South Wales. [ Extension of time ]

The Minns Government's planning reforms are part of a long-term framework to set up New South Wales for the next 20 years and beyond. It is a big but necessary set of reforms to the planning system to deliver homes, support and create jobs and protect and improve the environment. Alongside recent reforms like the Transport Oriented Development Program, our billion-dollar, world-leading Pre-sale Finance Guarantee and our Low and Mid-Rise Housing Policy, our legislative reforms are all aimed at clearing blockages and getting the planning system back on track so it can serve the people of New South Wales as intended.

Earlier reforms are starting to show results, with assessment times falling and proposals, constructions and completions rising. With around 90 per cent of development applications in the system worth $1 million or less, and when the median house price is over $1.5 million, we are sweating the small stuff and limiting our capacity to concentrate our resources on addressing the big issues. The Government's reforms reset the balance and re‑establish a planning system that delivers outcomes, not paperwork. It is a modern system that is faster and fairer. It also modernises the objectives of the Act. For the first time, the law explicitly recognises the need to build homes and respond to climate change. It embeds proportionality in decision-making, ensuring that effort matches risk.

It also expands complying developments, making sure that just because an applicant is not millimetre perfect does not mean they cannot get a clear and fast assessment. A new Development Coordination Authority will replace the confusing web of referrals to 22 different government agencies, saving time, reducing duplication and giving applicants one clear point of contact with the New South Wales Government. The new system also cements the role of the Housing Delivery Authority. These reforms are based on the Labor values of making it easier for someone to get a home and a job in a well‑connected community. They support the Government's housing agenda to help build a better New South Wales. These reforms deserve the support of all members of Parliament.

Dr MICHAEL HOLLAND ( Bega ) ( 12:43 :02 ): My question is addressed to the Minister for Health, Minister for Regional Health, and Minister for the Illawarra and the South Coast. Will the Minister update the House on the Minns Labor Government's work to deliver expanded health services to regional areas, including to my community across the Eurobodalla?

Mr RYAN PARK ( Keira — Minister for Health, Minister for Regional Health, and Minister for the Illawarra and the South Coast ) ( 12:43 :21 ): I thank the Parliamentary Secretary for Health for his fantastic question. It was great to join him recently, along with the Premier and the CEO of Southern NSW Local Health District, Margaret Bennett, for the topping out of Eurobodalla Regional Hospital. It seems incredible that only 15 or so months ago we were turning the sod on the hospital, and now its redevelopment is well underway. This $330 million hospital is an important piece of the health services puzzle on the far South Coast. An additional $70 million had to be allocated by the Government.

The delivery of world-class health services at the hospital will be groundbreaking for the people of the far South Coast. For the first time, the region will have a dedicated intensive care unit and MRI machine with better imaging. There will also be birthing and midwifery services, which I know the Parliamentary Secretary for Health is very keen to see. We are yet to meet a woman who delivered their baby south of Nowra, but I am sure we will meet one one day! This hospital is an important investment in health services by this Government for the far South Coast region, which plays an important role for the southern half of New South Wales.

People who know the area well will know that locals often travel significant distances to access care and ongoing treatment, as well as to work in its key hubs. The member for Bega has championed the hospital's redevelopment in this place from day one. Having seen it come out of the ground and then reach its highest point just last week, all members should be very proud of his record of advocating for his community. Well done to the member for Bega. This hospital is not just about building infrastructure. I have said from my first day as the Minister for Health that this Government's focus will be on service delivery and enhancing the number of staff providing those services.

Mr Mark Speakman: What about the Batemans Bay emergency department?

The SPEAKER: The Leader of the Opposition will come to order.

Mr RYAN PARK: I'll talk about Batemans Bay in a minute. My favourite schoolteacher, Clare McInerney, is here, so I won't be too disrespectful. Dapto High School is a very fine institution. [ Extension of time ]

This will be a level 4 hospital, so it will come with a significant increase in additional staff, more beds, more resources and more services for the far South Coast. The Government has also secured safe staffing ratios for South East Regional Hospital in Bega, something that the Opposition opposed.

Ms Yasmin Catley: They still do.

Mr RYAN PARK: They still do not support it. The Government has been able to secure the employment of the 1,112 additional nurses who were going to be removed. That is a fact.

The SPEAKER: The Leader of the Opposition will come to order.

Mr RYAN PARK: I think the Leader of the Opposition said something about Batemans Bay. Those who have a little understanding of health services will know that big emergency departments that are very close together in regional and rural areas essentially drain the workforce.

The SPEAKER: The member for Vaucluse will come to order.

Mr RYAN PARK: It would not be clinically safe and effective for patients to do that. Tragically for the Leader of the Opposition, he has not read the clinical services plan, which his former Government developed, in which it said that. I do not want to state the obvious, but I say to the member for Bega and to the House that the Government is determined to not only build the infrastructure the people of the far South Coast and New South Wales need, but also, importantly, staff and resource those health services for our communities. Regional, rural and remote health is near and dear to my heart. We need to continue to make sure we are investing outside of the greater metropolitan cities. With a strong advocate like the member for Bega, this Government will continue to do that for the people of the far South Coast.

tree_branches.text:
Dr MARJORIE O'NEILL ( Coogee ) ( 12:49 :27 ): My question is addressed to the Minister for Lands and Property, and Minister for Jobs and Tourism. Will the Minister update the House on the Minns Labor Government's progress to deliver the new Sydney Fish Market?

The SPEAKER: The member for Kogarah will come to order. The member for Canterbury will come to order.

Mr STEPHEN KAMPER ( Rockdale — Minister for Lands and Property, Minister for Multiculturalism, Minister for Sport, and Minister for Jobs and Tourism ) ( 12:49 :42 ): That is a proper question, and I thank the member for Coogee for it. It is going very well. I know that, just like me, the member cannot wait for the next icon of Sydney Harbour to open. It was promised over almost a decade by three Liberal governments; it will be delivered within one Labor Government.

The SPEAKER: I call the member for Oatley to order for the first time.

Mr STEPHEN KAMPER: He gets a bit edgy, Mr Speaker.

The SPEAKER: I call the member for Oatley to order for the second time. I call the member for Oatley to order for the third time.

Mr STEPHEN KAMPER: The member for Oatley is losing it. As we confirmed last week, the New South Wales Government will reach practical completion of the next iconic addition to Sydney Harbour in mid‑November. It has been a mammoth effort, and I thank everyone who has been involved in the construction of this fantastic masterpiece.

The SPEAKER: I call the member for Coffs Harbour to order for the second time.

Mr STEPHEN KAMPER: Here are some quick stats. The building includes 407 roof cassettes; 481 marine piles to support the building structure, wharfs and promenades; 594 glulam timber beams; 1,700 glass louvre panels used for facades; 6,000 tonnes of reinforcement from Active Steel; and 34,000 cubic metres of poured concrete, which is equivalent to nearly 14 Olympic swimming pools. The building will sit with the Harbour Bridge and the Sydney Opera House as a prominent Sydney landmark.

The SPEAKER: I call the member for Terrigal to order for the first time.

Mr STEPHEN KAMPER: Visitors, whether tourists or local, will be able to access the new markets however they please—by car, bus, light rail, metro or ferry. That is the full shebang! Those coming from the CBD will be able to enjoy an unbroken, continuous coastal walk all the way from Woolloomooloo to the new market.

The SPEAKER: The member for Bankstown will come to order.

Mr Jihad Dib: I was asking about jet skis.

Mr STEPHEN KAMPER: No jet skis. The new Sydney Fish Market will be the largest fish market in the Southern Hemisphere. It will not only highlight the world‑leading produce from our shores but also showcase Sydney's culinary excellence through a range of diverse dining and food options. Members know how much I love food; I have said that on many occasions. The market will include chefs like Luke Nguyen, Somer Sivrioglu and Junda Khoo, and the Trippas White Group along with local favourites such as Cow and the Moon gelateria and Touch_Wood. How good is that? It will have something for everyone. [ Extension of time ]

The new Sydney Fish Market is expected to draw in more than six million locals and tourists annually. It will become a leading tourist destination, especially for key markets such as Japan, South Korea, Singapore, Vietnam and China. We were proud to welcome some of their consular representatives last week. The new market will to be a fantastic addition to our harbour. It will be a tourist hotspot and a real focal point for the Bays area. I have been made aware by government agencies that members of this Parliament, especially the local members who make up Sydney Harbour and its waterways, have proposed other landmark buildings that they think would attract visitors to the harbour.

One of the most active local members is the Hon. Wes Fang, MLC, who has requested a Wagga Wagga museum in Drummoyne. I am not sure whether that has the support of the other local member, but Wes is definitely keen. Unsurprisingly, the member for Ryde was after a cat cafe. I understand that this has led to questions about food health and safety standards, but the member for Ryde has promised that the place will be spotless—licked clean. The member for Lane Cove did not want to build anything; he just wanted to let me know he is still here. It is good to see Robbo. He is an outstanding structure—formidable. Last, but not least, the member for Balmain was not sure what she wanted, but she was clear that it will only be delivered because of local Greens petitions.

tree_branches.text:
Dr DAVID SALIBA ( Fairfield ) ( 12:55 :58 ): My question is addressed to Minister for Police and Counter‑terrorism. Will the Minister update the House on how the NSW Police Force, through Taskforce Falcon, is tackling organised crime in our communities?

Ms YASMIN CATLEY ( Swansea — Minister for Police and Counter-terrorism, and Minister for the Hunter ) ( 12:56 :15 ): I thank the member for Fairfield for his question and for his ongoing support of his local police and the police of New South Wales. I acknowledge how shocking the recent violence on our streets has been. In fact, I am sickened—as are many members in this place—when I read reports of these senseless acts. Everyone deserves to feel safe, whether they are at home, at work or, indeed, walking down the road. The safety of our communities, especially in places where our children learn to play, is something that we take very seriously. I understand that the fact these attacks are targeted does nothing to dispel the fear and anxiety of people in our communities. Each act of violence creates the feeling that everyone is at risk. That violence cannot be tolerated, and New South Wales police are working tirelessly to come down hard on those who perpetrate this violence.

Members will recall that on 27 May I stood in this place and I advised the House that the police had established Taskforce Falcon, which brings together 13 different strike forces into one coordinated team. Taskforce Falcon is made up of 150 officers. It was set up with one objective: to bring to justice the criminal gangs who are responsible for these crimes, to end the violence and restore order in New South Wales. The taskforce is modelled on Taskforce Magnus, which, members will recall, was set up in response to the spate of public place shootings that we saw on our streets in 2023. Taskforce Magnus drew upon the experience of more than 50 detectives who made more than 160 arrests, laid more than 3,400 charges, and executed more than 300 firearms prohibition order searches and more than 160 search warrants. It does not stop there. They took more than 80 firearms off the streets and seized more than $5 million in prohibited drugs and almost $200 million in cash. That is extraordinary police work by the best in the business. As always, our police are working around the clock to keep our streets safe. I invite all members to join me in thanking them wholeheartedly. [ Extension of time ]

We know that their work is not only making a difference but also saving lives. On 1 October police charged a teenager over the death of Dawood Zakaria. He was murdered in an ambush in his car in Granville back in May. On 7 October police foiled what could have been an unspeakable act of violence intended to be committed in front of our most vulnerable in our community. Police swooped and arrested two men on their way to commit and live stream an execution outside a daycare centre, in front of young children.

Mr Ryan Park: Incredible policing.

Ms YASMIN CATLEY: I could not agree more with the Minister for Health. It is incredible policing. That happened again on 10 October, when police seized five so-called "kill cars" and arrested three men who were freelancing as criminal contractors. There are more than 280 stories like those in Taskforce Falcon. More than 280 arrests have been made and 650 charges have been laid. The message is simple: If people choose to participate in gangs and pick up guns or sell services to organised criminal networks, the police will find them and arrest them and they can expect to spend a long time in a small cell.

tree_branches.name: Reconciliation NSW
tree_branches.path: Legislative Assembly (2025-10-14) > Question Time > Reconciliation NSW
tree_branches.text:
Ms JENNY LEONG ( Newtown ) ( 13:01 :09 ): My question is directed to the Premier. During National Reconciliation Week, Reconciliation NSW was informed that, after nearly a decade, its core funding from the New South Wales Government would cease. Will the Minister explain why his Government has made the decision to stop ongoing core funding for Reconciliation NSW, potentially forcing it to close its doors and leaving us as the only State or Territory without a reconciliation council by the end of the year?

Mr CHRIS MINNS ( Kogarah — Premier ) ( 13:01 :42 ): I thank the member for her question. My understanding is that it was grant funding and not core funding, which is a distinction without a difference from Reconciliation NSW's point of view but an important one from an ongoing funding point of view. That $270,000 per year was granted by the department to Reconciliation NSW. I take the member's word for it that the funding had continued for 10 years. It has not been for the organisation's entire existence. My understanding is that the department for Aboriginal Affairs were told about or asked for an increase to $700,000. At that point, the leadership of the agency said, "This is not a government agency." Long-term funding needs to be slowly but surely acquired from other sources, whether it is philanthropic donations, other government agencies or core funding from the Commonwealth Government.

That does not mean that we are not spending any money on reconciliation, on progress towards a treaty for New South Wales or on Closing the Gap measures. In fact, New South Wales allocated $202 million in new funding for Closing the Gap initiatives in the 2025-26 budget for Aboriginal people. The truth of the matter is that, as good and as important as Reconciliation NSW is, it is not considered an Aboriginal community controlled organisation. That is an important distinction because the money that is applied from the department through the Minister goes towards Aboriginal controlled organisations. We regard that as important in a whole range of ways, for social, lobbying and community agencies as well as peak body initiatives. Our money is being directed towards Aboriginal controlled organisations. Reconciliation NSW is a good organisation. I am not downplaying its impact or importance. But I understand the reason for the funding and where it is being allocated. That is reasonable in the circumstances.

tree_branches.text:
Ms JULIA FINN ( Granville ) ( 13:04 :08 ): My question is addressed to the Minister for Industrial Relations, and Minister for Work Health and Safety. Will the Minister update the House on the Minns Labor Government's work to build a fairer system for workers across New South Wales?

Ms SOPHIE COTSIS ( Canterbury — Minister for Industrial Relations, and Minister for Work Health and Safety ) ( 13:04 :23 ): I acknowledge the wonderful member for Granville and Parliamentary Secretary to the Premier. She represents an important area of Western Sydney that is growing and is home to thousands of workers. Many people died from asbestos in factories and industrial estates in her area. The member has been advocating for solutions to those issues for a long time, particularly for dust diseases. The Minns Labor Government is committed to ensuring dignity, decent pay, fair conditions and, importantly, safe workplaces. We have delivered on our commitment to abolish the Opposition's draconian wages cap. We have re-established the Industrial Court and brought in a mutual gains bargaining system, with 91 per cent of State public sector workers covered by multi-year agreements. It is the first time in over 15 years that this has happened. That is a credit to the new bargaining system.

We have introduced historic laws to protect small business owner‑drivers. They have been advocating for that for a long time. Members on both sides of the House represent owner‑drivers and have been asking this Government and the former Government for solutions for a long time. We have also made changes to ensure protections for gig workers. We are currently in the process of ensuring that 250,000 community sector workers are being transferred into the portable long service leave scheme that we established. We want to keep workers in community sector organisations, like domestic violence workers or homelessness workers. That is why we established the portable long service leave scheme. We have also invested a historic $127 million into SafeWork NSW. That means 50 additional SafeWork inspectors, with 21 of those having a psychosocial background. We have a dedicated specialist team and an advisory service. Last week we announced a dedicated unit of the Office of the Director of Public Prosecutions. [ Extension of time ]

As we know, industrial manslaughter became an offence last year. We have established a new, dedicated unit for industrial manslaughter within the Office of the Director of Public Prosecutions. I acknowledge both the Premier and the Attorney General for that. Something important and historic happened yesterday: the proclamation of our new jurisdiction to combat bullying and harassment. The New South Wales Industrial Court has now established a bullying and harassment jurisdiction. That means that 50,000 local government workers and 430,000 public sector workers will have access. We have also introduced a gender equality object, which started yesterday. That is historic. I acknowledge everyone who has been involved in that.

I acknowledge that we have made changes to the Work Health and Safety Act. Those changes will protect workers across the public, private and community sectors. If workers are working in a tunnel, the Government has enabled permit holders to take photos and videos. There are privacy rules around that, but it means that we will have more evidence to prosecute where necessary. We still have a lot of work to do, particularly given those opposite did not do anything for 12 years. Our Government is making sure that working people across New South Wales have decent rights and decent conditions, and are working in safe workplaces. That is everything we are doing every day of this Government.

tree_branches.name: Retail Leases Amendment (Review) Bill 2025
tree_branches.path: Legislative Assembly (2025-10-14) > Bills > Retail Leases Amendment (Review) Bill 2025
tree_branches.text:
That this bill be now read a second time.

As Minister for Small Business, I am proud to introduce the Retail Leases Amendment (Review) Bill 2025, which delivers on our commitment to support small businesses across New South Wales by improving the fairness, clarity and efficiency of retail leasing arrangements. Retail leasing is a critical issue for small businesses. Whether a cafe in a suburban strip, a boutique in a regional town or a service provider in a shopping centre, thousands of businesses rely on fair and transparent leasing arrangements to operate and grow. The Retail Leases Act 1994 has long provided a framework to support good leasing practices, but it must evolve to meet the changing needs of our economy and our communities. The Government recognises that a well‑functioning leasing framework is essential to fostering commercial certainty, reducing disputes and supporting economic resilience.

Therefore, I am pleased to introduce the bill, particularly during Small Business Month, when we recognise the vital role that small businesses play in our communities and economy. I note that many members of this place have been out and about, recognising the wonderful small businesses across their electorates. The bill will amend the Retail Leases Act 1994 to improve the operation of the Act for lessors and lessees, including processes for entering into a lease and safeguards under the Act. This will strengthen the Act's primary policy objective of fostering good leasing practices between lessors and lessees. In 2023 the NSW Small Business Commission conducted a comprehensive statutory review of the Act, culminating in 32 recommendations aimed at improving clarity, consistency and outcomes for both lessors and lessees.

Following extensive consultation with industry stakeholders in late 2024 and early 2025, the Government has progressed a first tranche of reforms, reflected in the bill before the House today. This initial set of legislative reforms implements 13 of the review's 23 legislative recommendations. Stakeholders welcomed the phased approach, agreeing that the proposed initial reforms are more straightforward and that the remaining recommendations require further consideration and consultation due to their complexity and potential impacts on lessors and lessees.

I now turn to the detail of the bill. The bill introduces an objects provision, providing clear guidance on the purpose and scope of the Act. This will help lessors, lessees, legal practitioners and dispute resolution staff to understand how the Act is intended to operate and promote more consistent understanding of the roles and responsibilities of the leasing parties. The bill also provides for greater flexibility in how the Act applies, moving the list of excluded uses from the Act to the upcoming regulation. This change allows the framework to remain targeted and responsive to changing market conditions and tenancy models, while maintaining appropriate scrutiny through regulatory processes.

In addition, the bill clarifies that ancillary rights, such as car parking, signage and storage, are permitted as part of a retail lease, provided that the use of the premises is ancillary to the operation of the retail shop. This change resolves any ambiguity about the inclusion of such terms in retail lease agreements. The bill also improves the process for entering into retail lease arrangements, with a focus on flexibility, efficiency and informed decision-making. To consolidate references to disclosure statements, the bill updates terminology, ensuring consistency across the Act. "Disclosure statement" will now refer to both lessor and lessee disclosure statements, simplifying interpretation and application. The bill also allows the developing regulation to prescribe tailored disclosure statements for different types of retail leases: shopping centre leases and non-shopping-centre leases. This means the parties will receive information relevant to their circumstances and reduces the administrative burden of unnecessary information being required.

Currently a lessor is required to provide a disclosure statement at least seven days before a lease is entered into. The bill introduces an amendment to allow lessors and lessees to agree to a lesser period or waive this seven‑day period where both parties have received independent legal advice and consent in writing. This change maintains suitable safeguards while allowing parties to proceed more quickly where appropriate and agreed. The bill will also allow disclosure statements to be amended by mutual agreement, providing flexibility to correct or update information before or after the lease is entered into.

The bill provides the right to terminate a lease within six months if the lessor disclosure statement is not provided, is incomplete, or contains materially false or misleading information. Lessees may also recover reasonable costs incurred in connection with entering the lease. To further promote transparency, the bill provides for the developing regulations to prescribe documents such as fact sheets or guides to be provided to prospective lessees as soon as the prospective lessor enters into negotiations. Those documents will improve lessee understanding of key obligations and rights under the Act.

In response to practical challenges reported by lessors and lessees, the bill also introduces additional grounds to extend the three-month period for providing an executed lease and registering it. Those grounds may include situations where delays are caused by the lessee not providing insurance certificates, bank guarantees or other documents required under the lease, or where consent is needed from a head lessor or mortgagee and the lessor is actively seeking that consent. The bill also strengthens a number of key protections and processes under the Act. Currently a report on the outgoings statements for premises located outside shopping centres must be prepared by a registered company auditor. That can be unnecessarily burdensome. The bill will provide greater flexibility by allowing certified practising accountants to certify such statements, while retaining stronger arrangements for shopping centres due to their additional complexity.

The bill also clarifies that pharmacy-related sales are excluded from turnover rent, removing any ambiguity by aligning the Act with existing exemptions under other legislation and ensuring consistency across the sector. To improve certainty at the end of a lease, the bill clarifies the timing requirements for end-of-lease notifications. Where no further options to extend the lease exist, the lessor will be required to notify the lessee of their intentions between six and 12 months before the lease expires. Another important amendment in the bill removes the current restriction that prevents a lessor from recovering lease preparation expenses in circumstances where a lease could have been assigned but the parties instead agree to enter into a new lease.

That change reflects commercial reality and supports greater flexibility in contractual terms. In cases where a lessee is required to relocate to new premises, the bill prescribes commercial factors that must be considered when determining the rent payable under the new lease. Commercial factors include foot traffic, the surrounding retail mix, road frontage, and the shape, nature and configuration of each retail shop. That ensures that rent is determined fairly based on relevant circumstances. Finally, the bill repeals the redundant COVID-19 statutory powers that were introduced during the pandemic to respond to disruptions in retail trading and leasing. Those powers are no longer needed.

It is vital that the retail leasing framework in New South Wales remains fair, transparent and adaptable to the needs of modern businesses. The reforms are practical, balanced and responsive to the needs of the retail leasing sector. They will foster greater confidence in the retail leasing system from both landlords and tenants by improving clarity, streamlining processes and strengthening key safeguards. I am confident that the bill will support a more accessible and effective leasing environment for retailers across New South Wales. I acknowledge the presence in the Chamber of the member for Willoughby, the shadow Minister for Small Business. I commend the bill to the House.

Debate adjourned.

tree_branches.text: Ms JANELLE SAFFIN ( Lismore — Mini ster for Small Business, Minister for Recovery, and Minister for the North Coast ) —I wish to congratulate the team at Priceline Pharmacy in Lismore Square on an impressive list of state and national awards won recently. These include Store of the Year, State winner; Beauty Advisor of the Year Michelle Le Page, State and National winner; and Sisterhood Foundation Award, State and National winner. Being located so close to the Queensland border, Lismore is included in the Northern NSW/South East Queensland area of Priceline stores. Australia-wide, there are around 470 stores. Lismore Priceline Retail Manager Kristy Paterson told The Lismore App she was so proud of her team's achievements. Winning the Sisterhood Foundation Award was particularly special because the store raised over $30,000 for the eight Sisterhood Foundation charity partners – Jean Hailes for Women's Health, Smiling Mind, Her Herat, Share the Dignity, Fitted for Work, SisterWorks, Perinatal Anxiety and Depression Australia [PANDA] and Motherless Daughters. Kristy said this was achieved through in-store activities, like community days. "So we'll have face painting, nail painting and bake sales that we set up outside the store," Kristy said. Priceline staff bake cakes, biscuits and slices at home. Congratulations to all staff on their service and caring for community.
