tree_branches.name: Second Reading Debate
tree_branches.path: Legislative Assembly (2025-10-14) > Bills > Children (Education and Care Services National Law Application) Amendment Bill 2025 > Second Reading Debate
tree_branches.text:
Debate resumed from 10 September 2025.

Secondly, the bill creates new intervention powers. It empowers both the regulator and the Minister to intervene swiftly where there is an unacceptable risk to children. That includes issuing binding directions to providers, requiring immediate remedial action and acting decisively where waiting would place children at risk. The Opposition supports the intent. Child safety must always come first. But it is important to note that the bill contains significant new powers, particularly those vested in the Minister. The capacity for a Minister to issue binding directions to individual providers should not be taken lightly by the Parliament. While there may be circumstances that justify swift Executive action, such powers raise real questions about process, accountability, and checks and balances. Providers must have confidence that decisions will be exercised fairly, transparently and only in circumstances that genuinely warrant ministerial intervention. That is not to say that the powers are unwarranted, but they highlight the need for careful parliamentary scrutiny. When Parliament grants extraordinary powers to the Executive, it must also ensure that appropriate safeguards are in place.

Thirdly, the bill introduces transparency for families. It enables the regulator to publish more information about services considered high risk. Parents deserve access to that information so they can make informed choices about their children's care. Transparency builds trust, and the amendment in the bill rightly prioritises parents' right to know. Fourthly, the bill tightens requirements around staffing, including Working with Children Check clearances and prohibition orders. The provisions close loopholes that could otherwise allow unsuitable individuals to enter or remain in the sector. In a workforce that plays such a formative role in children's lives, it is only right that the highest standards of integrity and safety apply. Fifthly, the bill introduces provisions for the use of closed-circuit television in high-risk services. The intent is to deter misconduct and improve oversight where concerns have been identified. Caution is needed with CCTV, and the Parliament must remain vigilant about privacy, secure storage and the financial impact on smaller and community-based providers.

Finally, the bill establishes a Regulatory Authority Fund to ensure penalties and fees are reinvested directly into regulatory oversight. The public rightly expects that fines levied for failures in child safety are used to strengthen the system and prevent recurrence. The bill is not being introduced in a vacuum. New South Wales has the largest number of childcare facilities in the nation—around 34 per cent of all services in Australia. That brings both a responsibility to lead and a responsibility to ensure reforms are applied carefully and sustainably. Reviews of the sector have highlighted shortcomings in the regulatory framework and called for stronger tools for the regulator. The bill is one response, and its intent is clear: to put child safety above financial or commercial considerations. The Opposition agrees with that intent.

While we support the bill in principle, we also have a responsibility to consider its practical impact. On penalties, the increase is justified but they must act as a deterrent without creating unintended consequences such as discouraging services in communities that already face shortages of childcare places. On intervention powers, the ability to act quickly when children are at risk is essential, but ministerial directions, in particular, represent a very significant power. Parliament must be cautious about how such powers are framed and ensure that there are safeguards, transparency and accountability. On CCTV, while there are potential benefits, Parliament must address questions of privacy, data security and compliance costs. Compliance costs must not undermine the viability of community-run preschools in regional towns, which often operate on tight budgets. On national consistency, New South Wales is moving ahead of other jurisdictions in some areas. While this shows leadership, it risks creating inconsistencies within the national law framework. This is particularly relevant for providers operating across State borders, and for families in communities such as mine in Albury. Reforms aimed at strengthening safety must not inadvertently create unnecessary complexity.

For these reasons, the Opposition supported referral of this bill in the Legislative Council to a committee. That process provided an opportunity for stakeholders to be heard and for Parliament to test whether these new powers—especially ministerial directions—are framed appropriately, with the right balance of urgency, fairness and accountability. On a shortened timeframe, the inquiry established by Portfolio Committee No. 3 received nine submissions and heard from 15 witnesses during a public hearing on 26 September. I quote from the chair's foreword, which states:

During the inquiry, stakeholders raised a number of concerns about the drafting of the bill and the manner in which it was introduced. Some noted the significance of New South Wales seeking to deviate from the National Law and noted that the passing of the bill could undermine the ongoing process of states and territories working together to agree on changes to the National Law. Further, many stakeholders were concerned that they had not been consulted on a draft bill before it was introduced. Although many aspects of the bill were welcomed by stakeholders, issues were raised about a number of proposed provisions having unintended consequences and amendments to the bill were proposed and discussed.

Subsequent to that inquiry, the Opposition will seek to move amendments in the other House. I note the Minister's comments in this House during question time on 18 September criticising the referral to an inquiry, for which he should be roundly condemned. Inquiry was not about delay; it was about diligence. When dealing with laws that affect both child safety and the powers of the executive, Parliament has a responsibility to proceed cautiously, to listen carefully and to legislate responsibly. Stronger laws are only meaningful if they are implemented effectively. Oversight, resources for the regulator and support for providers to comply will all be essential.

In closing, I restate the Opposition's broad support for the bill. The reforms are important and respond to genuine concerns about safety and transparency in early education and care services. There are issues that warrant further consideration and that is why referral to a short inquiry in the other place was the right course. That process helped to ensure that the reforms are fair, proportionate and workable, and deliver stronger protections for children without unintended consequences for families or providers. Child safety is not negotiable. Parents deserve confidence, providers deserve clarity, and children deserve both safety and stability. Our responsibility is to ensure this legislation measures up to that promise. That is how we best serve children, families and communities across New South Wales. I support the bill.

The bill is the Government's decisive response. It raises the bar on child safety. It empowers our regulator with the tools it needs to act quickly and effectively. It delivers tougher penalties, stronger accountability, smarter monitoring and new nation-leading powers to prevent harm before it occurs. It restores trust and confidence in a sector that supports half a million children and their families in New South Wales every single day. New South Wales is home to the largest early childhood education and care sector in the nation. More than 6,000 services operate across our State in long day care, preschools, family day care, out-of-school hours care and mobile services. This is a critical part of our education system, but it is also vital social infrastructure that allows parents and carers to work and provide for their families.

The bill does three central things. First, it makes paramount the principle that the rights and best interests of children override all other interests. When conflicts arise—whether financial, operational or reputational—the safety of children will take precedence, full stop. This principle will be enshrined in law. Every provider, every director, every educator and the regulator itself will be bound by it. Second, the bill gives the regulator stronger enforcement powers. Maximum penalties are tripled. Penalties are scaled to the size of providers so that large operators face fines big enough to bite. More offences can now be dealt with through penalty notices rather than lengthy prosecutions, allowing faster and more certain consequences. Previous offences can be taken into account even if fines have been paid, closing a loophole that shielded repeat offenders.

Third, the bill provides new nation-leading powers to act swiftly when unacceptable risks to children emerge. Both the Minister and the regulator will be able to issue binding, unchallengeable directions to the sector. That could mean banning mobile devices in centres, mandating CCTV or requiring compulsory child safety training. It means that we no longer need to wait for tragedy to reveal gaps in the system. We will be able to act before harm occurs. The bill also strengthens whistleblower protections, tightens rules around re-applications for rejected providers, requires child-safe recruitment practices, expands information sharing with recruitment agencies and makes it an offence to provide unregulated home-based care.

Taken together, these reforms form the most significant overhaul of early childhood regulation in our State since the introduction of the national law in 2010. The overwhelming majority of educators and providers will welcome this bill. They do the right thing every day, and this bill protects their integrity as much as it protects children. It will draw a clear line between those who uphold the highest standards and those who do not deserve to operate. Unsafe services are no services at all. Families deserve better, and this bill delivers it. The Government is simultaneously investing in expanding preschool places, supporting Aboriginal Community Controlled Organisations to deliver more services, and ensuring that good providers can grow. But expansion without strong regulation is a false economy. Growth must be safe growth, and the bill ensures exactly that. In law, profit must never come before the protection of children.

This bill makes that principle ironclad. It strengthens penalties, enhances transparency, expands enforcement tools and creates the power to act quickly when risks emerge. It builds on the national framework but makes it fit for today's challenges. The safety of our children is not negotiable. Parents entrust us, the Government and this Parliament, with their most precious responsibility. That trust has been broken in the past. Today we take the steps to ensure that it is not broken again. I commend the bill to the House.

The review was led by former deputy NSW Ombudsman Mr Chris Wheeler. The Deputy Premier announced the intention to commission the review on 25 February 2025, with a clear brief: to examine whether our regulator is effective under the national law, and to recommend improvements to regulation, monitoring and support for services. Mr Wheeler delivered his final report on 31 May 2025. It analysed 34 serious matters and the compliance responses taken. The report also involved consultation with the sector. Mr Wheeler found that, within the constraints of the national law and available resources, the New South Wales regulatory authority has been effective but, concerningly, found that the regulator's performance is constrained by that national framework and that the regulator should be more transparent about compliance activities. Those findings go to the core of public trust. Parents want to know problems will be identified early, dealt with firmly and, critically, disclosed in ways that help them make informed choices.

The Wheeler review did not pull punches. It described the monetary penalties available as "paltry" and set out limitations in the infringement notice regime, noting that only a small subset of offences currently attract on‑the‑spot penalties—hardly conducive to swift, proportionate deterrence. These are not abstract critiques; they are practical barriers to protecting children. Mr Wheeler made 12 recommendations of systemic changes grounded in the casework. My colleagues will speak to other recommendations, such as reform of penalties and infringement notices, better whistleblower protections and targeted, risk-based use of CCTV as a regulatory condition in serious cases, balanced by privacy and due process. Today I will focus on the two recommendations that spoke of immediate change.

The first one is recommendation 6: Establish the regulatory authority as a separate agency, independent of the department's service delivery responsibilities. That goes to perceived and actual conflicts and strengthens accountability by ensuring the regulator's sole job is safeguarding children and enforcing the law. The second is recommendation 3: Mandate publication of meaningful compliance information, where services fail to meet standards so families can see not just the quality rating but the safety and performance record that sits behind it. The report also proposed practical communication steps, such as requiring services to display their compliance history or inform parents of their right to request.

On 26 June 2025 the Government announced a package to begin implementing the review. Firstly, it committed to establishing a new standalone, independent early childhood regulator, reporting directly to the Minister—exactly as the review recommended. Secondly, it strengthened the public's right to know, swiftly empowering the regulator to publish to the fullest extent allowed by the national law. Accordingly, the regulator has published 397 enforcement actions, including compliance notices and emergency action notices, from quarter 3; and compliance notices, emergency action notices, enforcement undertakings, cancellations and involuntary suspensions in quarter 4. Thirdly, it moved to amend the national law to increase penalties and to embed a "paramount consideration" of child safety, ensuring child safety is at the heart of early years learning. Fourthly, it enabled a risk-based CCTV trial. When safety concerns arise, the regulator may require cameras to assist timely, evidence-based investigations.

These immediate actions meet the moment. They put oxygen back into the system where it matters most: independent oversight, transparency, proportionate enforcement and practical tools for investigators. The bill before the House is the legislative expression of that approach. It updates our application Act to align New South Wales with the new expectations that the community—and, frankly, this Parliament—has of early childhood regulation. A key expectation is that we prioritise children's safety in decision-making. A "paramount consideration" obligation does not live on a poster or in a policy binder; it operates at the fulcrum of decisions where there are competing interests. When it is on the statute book, there is no ambiguity about what comes first. That is the case already in New South Wales, in the contexts covered by the Children and Young Persons (Care and Protection) Act 1998 and the Children's Guardian Act 2019. The bill extends the coverage to all children in education and care settings, and aligns our framework with that best practice.

Another expectation highlighted in the Wheeler review is that we must improve transparency so families can choose in the light, not in the dark. In line with the recommendations of Mr Wheeler and the expectations of the Deputy Premier, the New South Wales regulator has significantly expanded its publication of compliance and regulatory actions. However, the regulator is constrained from further publication by the national law. This bill works to push more information—important quality and safety information that is usable by parents and carers—into the public domain. It is a direct response to recommendation 3. Transparency is not a slogan; it is a set of practical choices. The bill will enable the New South Wales regulator, for the first time, to make sure that families are informed of any significant investigation of their child's centre.

At the moment, parents of children who may be victims are allowed to be told that an investigation is underway, but everyone else is kept in the dark. Any parent will say that is unacceptable. The bill means that when this happens in the future, the regulator has the power to suspend a service's rating—a clear signal for parents—and has the power to require the service to provide information about the investigation to all families. When enforcement action is taken, the regulator will have the power to publish information about that action so that parents will know, for example, that an educator has been suspended or that the service has been fined because it was not staffed appropriately.

The bill also empowers the regulator to require that services display their quality and compliance history. That means that parents will be able to see any and all of the issues the regulator has found with the service so choices they make about who to trust with their child's care are informed choices. Parents deserve to know about patterns of noncompliance and what is being done about them. Today's bill also supports independent regulation. The Wheeler review sets out the case plainly: When the regulator is embedded within a department that also runs preschools, conflicts of interest—perceived or real—can arise. A separate agency solves that problem at the root. It is a reform parents understand, and it gives our authorised officers the clarity and the backing they need to do a difficult job free from any perception of divided loyalties. The Government's immediate package commits to that path; today's bill is a key step in that journey.

The Wheeler review gives us a practical blueprint for a safer, more transparent and more trusted early childhood system. The community expects us to act, to put children's safety as the paramount consideration, to shine a light on performance, and to give our regulator the independence and tools to do its job. This bill is not the end of the journey; it is the essential first mile. It aligns New South Wales law with those expectations and with the Government's immediate package. It honours the work of the review and the voices of parents and educators who are rightly worried about the state of the sector. Most importantly, this bill does what the public rightly demands: it puts children first. I commend the bill to the House.

Parents trust childcare providers not merely to fill time but with their child's growth, their early learning, their friendships and their sense of belonging in the world. That trust is sacred, and when it is broken the consequences can be devastating. This bill is designed precisely to protect that trust. It creates a stronger, more transparent and more child-focused regulatory framework—one that reassures families that their children are safe, nurtured and thriving. Today I will outline in detail how the reforms contained in this bill will make a real and positive difference to the lives of families, and why parents across New South Wales can take confidence from the direction we are setting.

Above all else, this bill enshrines the principle that the rights and best interests of children are paramount. For parents, this is not just legal language. It is a promise. It means that every regulatory decision, every sanction and every intervention will be judged first and foremost by how it protects and promotes the wellbeing of children. When a parent or carer drops off their toddler each morning, they should know that every staff member is properly trained, that the service has been inspected and that safety protocols are not optional extras but legal requirements. When you leave your baby in the nursery room, you should be confident that supervision will never be left to chance.

The bill grants the regulator new powers to step in quickly where children's safety is compromised, for example, to impose safety measures such as banning mobile devices within services to minimise distractions and potential harm, and mandate the use of CCTV to enhance monitoring and accountability. It also strengthens mandatory training requirements for educators and staff, particularly focused on child protection and safety. For families, these provisions mean that risks to their children's safety will be managed proactively and effectively, with clear consequences for providers who fail to meet their obligations. This builds confidence that their children are in a secure environment where their wellbeing is the primary concern.

One of the hardest tasks for families is choosing a service. Parents often compare locations, fees, opening hours and learning programs, but too often the most important information has been hidden. This bill fixes that. From now on, services must publicly display their compliance history. Families will know at a glance whether a provider has been meeting standards or facing enforcement action. Services must disclose their ownership structure on signage and websites. Families will know whether the centre is locally run, part of a large chain or linked to complex corporate arrangements. The regulator will be able to publish information about high‑risk services and alert families if individuals have been excluded for safety reasons. This is about levelling the playing field for parents. Choosing a service should not be a gamble in the dark. With these reforms, families will have the knowledge they need to make informed choices. They will not have to rely on whispers in the playground or word-of-mouth warnings. They will have clear, reliable information directly from the regulator.

Families want to know that when rules are broken there are real consequences. For too long, penalties under the national law were too low to bite. Some providers treated them as just another overhead—a minor cost of doing business—while children and families carried the risk. This bill changes that. Penalties will triple across the board. A failure to supervise—one of the most serious offences—will now attract maximum fines of up to $34,000 for an individual, $172,000 for a provider and more than $500,000 for large corporate chains. Penalty infringement notices used for less serious but still significant lapses will also rise sharply. For families, these figures matter not because of their dollar value alone but because of what they signal: that Parliament recognises the gravity of the risks; that we are determined to deter corner-cutting, not tolerate it; and that safety is not negotiable.

The bill also introduces disciplinary notices, a new tool that fills the gap between a quiet word and a criminal sanction. These notices, with fines set at half the value of penalty infringement notices, allow the regulator to act swiftly when early intervention is needed. Parents will know that even lower level breaches will not be brushed aside but addressed transparently. At the upper end, the bill strengthens the option of disciplinary proceedings—faster and more efficient than a full court prosecution, but still capable of imposing strong penalties where breaches are serious. Taken together, this graduated regime means families can be confident that every breach, big or small, will be met with a proportionate response.

Trust between families and services depends on honest, timely communication. Too often in the past incidents were downplayed, delayed or hidden until rumours forced them into the open. This bill ensures that will no longer be acceptable. Families must be informed when a person is excluded from a service for safety reasons. They must be notified of key regulatory actions affecting their child's environment. For parents, this is about respect for their right to know what is happening in the place where their child spends much of their day and respect for their role as partners in protecting children's safety.

Parents are often the first to sense when something is not right: a rushed handover, a staff member stretched too thin, a child describing something that raises questions. Families need to know that if they raise these concerns, they will be taken seriously. This bill strengthens whistleblower protections for educators, staff and for parents too. It sends a clear signal that speaking up is not disloyal but is responsible. Raising concerns is not an act of hostility but an act of care. For families, this means confidence that the system wants to hear their voices and will protect those who come forward.

When we look at these reforms together, a clear picture emerges. This bill builds a regulatory system that families can truly trust, one that places children's safety at the centre of every decision, gives families clear, accessible and timely information, holds providers accountable with meaningful penalties, strengthens communication and transparency and encourages vigilance and openness through whistleblower protections. This bill is about making sure that every parent who kisses their child goodbye at the service door can walk away knowing that their child is safe, cared for and learning in a place that meets the highest standards. It is about showing families that their voices matter, their concerns are heard and their children's wellbeing is non-negotiable. For all these reasons, I commend the bill to the House.

The bill is the New South Wales Government's first legislative response to the systemic issues laid bare by the work that The Greens have been doing investigating the early childhood education and care sector that were publicised by several journalists, including most notably Adele Ferguson with her Four Corners exposé earlier in the year. The bill seeks to implement some of the recommendations of the Wheeler review, which was commissioned by the New South Wales Government just ahead of the first Education portfolio budget estimates hearing, when the Standing Order 52 documents were first used for questioning by The Greens; some of the agreements reached at a national level that are intended to make their way into the national law, initiated through the Victorian Parliament and then to be adopted in other States and Territories; and New South Wales' conclusions from Operation Tenterfield, the New South Wales, Queensland and Commonwealth investigations in response to the horrific child sexual abuse perpetrated against hundreds of children in multiple centres across New South Wales and Queensland, which also affected families in my electorate of Balmain.

On this point, the law in its current form inadvertently incentivises early childhood education and care operators to keep quiet about serious incidents that they may become aware of. Because of the limitation period for the commencement of these offence proceedings, they can avoid repercussions for failing to disclose matters to the regulator in a timely way. While they may be banned from running a centre in the future, operators cannot be held accountable for any conduct that they have failed to disclose if they can see out the brief two-year period before the regulator becomes aware that an offence has been committed. The Greens will be moving an amendment to close this unfortunate loophole, about which I will have more to say later. I commend the Minister's office for being so collaborative and helpful on this front.

The bill seeks to provide that the protection of the rights and best interests of children is paramount in the provision and regulation of early childhood education and care, including a legislative attempt to override a for‑profit company's statutory purposes under Commonwealth law; add a number of additional offences and disciplinary provisions; markedly increase the fines applicable to offences and prescribe a number of offences to be now PIN-able, which means they are subject to penalty infringement notices and the regulator can more easily issue on-the-spot fines to service providers; standardise more information being readily accessible to families regarding the performance of their early learning centre; and provide the Minister with broad powers to issue directions to the regulator and the sector.

The Greens welcome the Government's action in response to the issues that we have been raising in the early childhood education and care sector this year. However, this hurriedly produced bill includes several provisions that seek to implement reforms that have not been well consulted on. There are obvious typos in some of those provisions, so it is clear that the drafting requires more work. Again, I acknowledge my Greens colleague Ms Abigail Boyd for her important work on these matters. The opportunity for stakeholders to ventilate their views through the parliamentary inquiry that she chaired for just a few short weeks will ensure that the bill is fit for purpose. Several organisations raised serious concerns during the inquiry, arguing that its rushed process, lack of consultation and unclear interaction with existing regulatory systems risk undermining, rather than improving, child safety. It is critical that these concerns are taken seriously.

The Office of the Children's Guardian cautioned that the bill overlaps with its existing responsibilities under the Children's Guardian Act 2019, potentially creating confusion and duplication between agencies. It also warned that without further legislative clarity, operational difficulties could prevent regulators from achieving their child protection aims. Community Early Learning Australia supported the stronger penalties, but warned that linking fines to a new compliance fund could create a perverse financial incentive for over-enforcement. It also noted that increased personal liability could deter volunteers from serving at community-run centres.

The Independent Education Union described the bill's penalties as disproportionate, particularly for low‑paid educators and nominated supervisors who may lack control over staffing or resourcing. It argued that the bill's focus on punishment rather than prevention risks worsening workforce stresses and shortages. Finally, a joint submission from major non-profits questioned why New South Wales is proceeding ahead of national reforms without more consultation, warning that this fragmented approach risks inconsistency and confusion across jurisdictions. We now have the opportunity to resolve those issues and concerns through amendments, and The Greens will have more to say on that when the matter progresses to the other place.

The bill represents an important and overdue reform to the way that New South Wales protects children in early childhood education and care. It places the rights and best interests of children at the centre of the law, where they always should have been. The Greens welcome the introduction of a paramount consideration clause under new section 3A of the Children (Education and Care Services National Law Application) Act 2010. This reform establishes a statutory obligation that the protection of the rights and best interests of each child must be the paramount consideration in giving effect to the law. Until now, under the National Quality Framework the rights and best interests of children have been treated as merely one of six guiding principles.

This change gives that principle proper legal weight. It also ensures that every regulatory decision, approval, sanction or enforcement action must be made through the lens of what best serves the child. This is not a symbolic statement; it provides a clear legal foundation for decision-making and removes any ambiguity about competing obligations. It also ensures that providers cannot justify unsafe practices or cost-cutting measures on the grounds of profitability or convenience and embeds child safety and wellbeing as the organising value of the entire regulatory framework. Importantly, the bill also begins the process of establishing a standalone Early Childhood Education and Care Regulatory Authority separate from the Department of Education.

The independent Wheeler review made clear that the existing arrangement, where the secretary of the department is both the funder and the regulator of early childhood services, is a structural conflict of duties. The secretary serves two masters, as both a provider of government preschools and the regulator of the whole sector. The Greens share the view that regulation must be independent, transparent and free from such conflicts. Therefore, we support the creation of a separate regulatory authority, and we call on the Government to ensure that it is properly resourced. We will monitor its establishment closely to ensure that it has both the independence and the capacity to use the stronger enforcement powers provided under this bill.

The bill also addresses one of the most troubling gaps in the current system: the complex and fragmented process for mandatory reporting in the early childhood sector. At present, workers and managers face overlapping and often confusing obligations under different pieces of legislation. In practice, that has led to under-reporting of serious incidents, delayed responses and, at times, complete inaction. The Royal Commission into Institutional Responses to Child Sexual Abuse made it clear that these ambiguous reporting pathways put children at risk. The Wheeler review reached the same conclusion, describing the current framework as unrealistic for more than 6,000 early childhood services across New South Wales. By creating a single point of contact within the new regulator for the reporting of all non-police related safety concerns, this reform will simplify obligations and strengthen accountability. It will make it easier for workers to do the right thing and much harder for services to look the other way.

These changes also give meaningful effect to Australia's commitments under the United Nations Convention on the Rights of the Child, which enshrines every child's right to safety, dignity and participation. Together, the primacy of children's interests, an independent regulator and clear mandatory reporting pathways will help to build a system more worthy of the trust placed in it by families across the State. For too long, child safety in early education has relied on goodwill and guidance, but this bill will finally make it the law. There have been some horrendous things going on in childcare centres, places where we drop our children every day and in which we put so much trust. Our children are our most precious things. When we leave them there, we expect and hope that they will be cared for properly, respected and treated well.

As this process has been worked through, I have heard some of the things that families have been through. Listening to the stories of the people in my electorate who have been affected by some of the most abhorrent behaviour within the childcare sector has been shocking and horrifying, so it will be good to see the law strengthened. I encourage members to support The Greens' amendment. I commend the bill to the House.

The bill raises the floor on child safety. It brings stronger enforcement, clearer accountability and smarter monitoring. It draws on the lessons of the Wheeler review, the tragic failings exposed by Operation Tenterfield and the National Child Safety Review. The reforms make one thing absolutely clear: children are not just a consideration; they are the paramount consideration. For the first time, the law will explicitly require that the rights and best interests of children prevail over competing interests, whether those are commercial, administrative or corporate. The new statutory requirement sets a clear expectation that every decision, every action, every policy in the early education sector must begin and end with one question: What is best for the child? No more excuses. No more grey areas. Paramountcy is the foundation of the entire reform package.

I highlight the changes under the bill. Firstly, there will be stronger penalties and a smarter compliance regime. The bill triples every maximum penalty, and for large providers—those with more than 25 services—the fines will be nine times higher than before. It introduces disciplinary action tools so the regulator can issue proportionate responses, from guidance and improvement plans through to disciplinary notices and fines. The new offence of inappropriate conduct fills a dangerous gap. It allows regulators to act when behaviour risks a child's emotional, psychological or physical safety, before it escalates into serious harm. Secondly, there is the change that increases transparency and information sharing. The bill removes the barriers that stop the regulator from publishing vital information. Families will finally have access to clear, timely information about compliance and enforcement actions. Services will have to publish their full compliance histories, and regulators will be able to alert all parents—not just those directly affected—when a serious investigation is underway.

Thirdly, there are new and improved levers for the regulator and Minister. Both will have the power to issue directions to act swiftly where risks arise. That could mean mandating child safety training across the sector or swiftly implementing a mobile device ban in services where it is needed. Those powers ensure that government can act decisively and transparently to protect children. Finally, the bill brings better oversight and quality improvement. The regulator can now suspend or revoke a service's quality rating while investigations are ongoing. A service under scrutiny cannot continue displaying a sign saying "exceeding" at the front gate when there are serious questions inside. Together, these measures build a more responsive, transparent and accountable system.

Some will say these reforms are tough. But unsafe supply is no supply at all. A system that tolerates risk to children is not one that parents can trust. Others will ask why now? Why not wait for national agreement? The truth is that New South Wales cannot and should not wait. The reforms align with the national child safety agenda, but they go further because the risks we face are real and immediate. While the powers arising from the bill are strong, they are balanced. Review rights remain for most regulatory decisions, except where there is an unacceptable risk to children. Judicial review will still be available. That balance protects both fairness and safety. Paramountcy does not mean uniformity. It means recognising that every child—whether they live with a disability, whether their parents speak English at home or another language, or whether they are growing up in Strathfield or in Bourke—deserves to be safe, supported and included.

Early education is not babysitting; it is nation building. It shapes who our children become and who we are as a community. But families will only participate if they trust the system. A recent survey found that around 10 per cent of children have been withdrawn from early education because parents were worried about safety. There is a crisis of confidence, and the bill is how we fix it. By acting now, New South Wales leads the nation. We restore trust, protect children and ensure that every parent can again feel safe leaving their child in the care of others. The bill delivers what parents, educators and children have been asking for—clarity, accountability and courage. We are setting a higher standard for safety, quality and trust in early education; we are doing it in law. This is about more than regulation. It is about values and about what we, as a Parliament and as a society, choose to stand for. I commend the bill to the House.

New South Wales has led the national conversation, informed by the Wheeler review, which the Deputy Premier commissioned to examine our regulatory authority with clear eyes and a child-first lens. The review recommended stronger transparency, modernised enforcement and the creation of an independent, child safety focused regulator. On 25 June the New South Wales Government announced the immediate actions of stronger laws, higher fines, greater publication of safety and performance information, and a pathway to a standalone regulator. We shared the Wheeler report with other jurisdictions to help shape the national agenda, which is now reflected in the EMM package.

Importantly, the independent Weatherill-White review in Victoria, released on 15 August, validated the recommendations of Mr Wheeler. Across different systems and experiences, both reviews converged on the same reforms that the nation is now pursuing. They called out the need to put children first in the law—a paramount consideration that rules when interests collide—to improve transparency for families so they see not only ratings but also the compliance and enforcement history; to let families know when services have been "working towards" for too long so that underperformance cannot hide in plain sight; for a trial of the use of CCTV that is evidence led and privacy aware to aid investigations and deter misconduct; to strengthen enforcement settings with practical, proportionate tools and penalties that deter; and to improve child-safe recruitment, including having registers and stronger information sharing.

Those are not slogans; they are specific and appropriate measures. The national package now reflects them. But while these positions have been broadly agreed nationally, we know that there will be a period before they are fully implemented in the national law. A long wait is not acceptable to New South Wales families, who expect action now. The bill is how we improve safety for children in New South Wales immediately and how we continue to lead and advocate for national improvements. I home in on one element where parents rightly expect clarity: CCTV. Nationally, Ministers agreed to a CCTV assessment in up to 300 services, guided by experts including the Australian Centre for Child Protection, with participation payments for small and medium services.

Work begins immediately. The assessment starts in the fourth quarter of 2025. We will provide advice on best-practice use including on privacy, storage and operational frameworks. New South Wales will participate. We will bring our own trial cohort into the mix, including a targeted mandatory participation component so that the assessment has the reach and diversity it needs to produce reliable evidence. CCTV has many considerations, not least the privacy and dignity of children. That is precisely why we will trial it. The purpose is to robustly road‑test different models and safeguards to protect privacy, to produce usable evidence for investigators and to deter misconduct. The national assessment and our New South Wales participation will be designed with those aims in mind.

The bill empowers the Minister or the regulator to require participation in the trial in defined circumstances—through conditions on provider or service approvals or by specific direction—ensuring that New South Wales can meet its obligations as part of the national assessment and gather high-quality, representative evidence. In future, depending on the results, those same levers could be used carefully and proportionately to widen uptake of CCTV. In short, we are equipping New South Wales to follow the evidence. As I mentioned, CCTV was a recommendation of the New South Wales Wheeler review as well as the Victorian Weatherill and White review. While the Weatherill and White review validated the Wheeler positions, it also in some ways went further.

New South Wales asked Mr Wheeler to consider the regulatory context, but the Victorian brief was wider and considered not just the regulatory context but the whole of the inputs to the sector. Weatherill and White recommended that the Commonwealth lead a re-think of the whole of the education and care services system, calling for a fundamental reset of the design and oversight of the system, including reliance of the market. In principle, the New South Wales Government supports that outlook. It is critical that, as a nation, we elevate safety and quality in the system settings and across governance, incentives and information sharing. We will advocate for those issues at the national table. In the meantime, we will not wait to use the levers we already have the power to improve. That is the purpose of the bill.

I turn to the workforce. In the press conference after EMM, every Minister began by recognising educators as the best asset we have. The vast majority of people working in early childhood settings are there for the right reasons, and work hard every day to ensure our littlest learners are safe and supported. Many have been deeply shaken by the recent sickening reports. The national package invests in mandatory training, developed by the Australian Centre for Child Protection, so that all educators in the sector understand their obligations and can spot warning signs. New South Wales additional resourcing ensures that our officers can guide, support and, where needed, enforce. This is not about regulation versus workforce; it is regulation with workforce. We know that the regulator cannot be in all services all day every day. We need a confident and responsive workforce that is aligned to the mission to keep children safe in high-quality education and care so that good practice is the norm and poor practice is corrected quickly. Leadership is about doing the right thing before it becomes the only thing.

On 25 June New South Wales put forward a plan to the nation's education Minister for stronger laws, higher fines, real transparency and an independent regulator shaped by the Wheeler review. On 15 August Victoria's Weatherill and White review landed with strikingly similar conclusions. On 22 August Ministers adopted those core ideas nationally. The bill ensures that New South Wales does not just keep up with that momentum but keeps setting it. Practically, this is what that means in the coming months: New South Wales embeds children-first decision-making now, making good the national paramountcy commitment; New South Wales aligns our publication settings with the national transparency push and goes further so that families see conditions, visits, breaches and enforcement outcomes clearly and promptly; and New South Wales uses conditions on approvals to support the national CCTV assessment, including targeted mandatory participation for selected services and, if the evidence shows benefits, to expand use with strong privacy guardrails.

The Wheeler and the Weatherill and White reviews validate the route. The bill is about how we take the next steps in New South Wales: clear paramountcy in practice, stronger transparency for families, modern enforcement with real teeth; and the legal levers to support and—if the evidence supports it—scale targeted CCTV. All that parents and carers want in New South Wales is to know that their children are protected and looked after, and that there is no risk of what has happened in the past occurring again. Any parent in New South Wales will emphasise that they want their children to be safe. I commend the bill to the House.

Everyone deserves to be safe and everyone deserves a happy childhood. Unfortunately, that is not the case for everyone in New South Wales. That is what the bill is about. For parents, carers and the broader family, trust in our childcare system is important. Parents go to work and leave their precious kids in childcare facilities. We must ensure that robust systems are in place to ensure that trust is maintained. The bill is about child safety as well as three underlying elements. The first is accountability, the second is monitoring and the third is enforcement. It also uses robust processes to prevent bad acts from happening.

Many members have spoken about the content of the bill, including the Minister in his second reading speech. A key item that I bring to the attention of the House is the increase in whistleblower protections. Detection and prevention often come about through whistleblowers. We must ensure that they are protected and feel that they can come forward and speak up without fear, so that the system is robust. The new nation-leading power for the Minister and regulator to make time-limited, specific, unchallengeable directions to the sector where there is an unacceptable risk to child safety and/or consideration of child safety being of paramount concern is important. Decisions sometimes need to be made quickly. That includes matters such as the banning of mobile devices, the use of CCTV and further child safety training. It is important to make those decisions. The Minister will act on that primary value of protection for children. I agree with that, irrespective of other concerns.

The regulator is to publish more information about high-risk services, including current investigations. That is an important transparency aspect attached to the sector. There is a lot of community anxiety—especially over the media reports from the past couple of months—about the protection of children. It is important that transparency is reinforced. The bill clarifies that sexual offences or sexual misconduct triggers a serious incident reporting requirement, and that when there is a serious incident the provider must give evidence that it notified the child's parents. Again, it is about transparency. This is serious. We must make sure that occurs. Finally, the bill introduces requirements for child safe recruitment practices, including checking whether current and prospective staff have been prohibited. That vetting process is critical. We must vet everything that we do. We must make sure that we have robust measures to vet and protect our most precious resource—our kids. Safety is important. I reiterate that we need to strive for zero failures. Every kid is precious. Every family is of paramount importance. I commend the bill to the House.

I will start by responding to the comments made by the Legislation Review Committee. I acknowledge the important work that the committee does and the role that it plays. In regard to the regulation powers proposed in new section 301A, I note that the power is not arbitrary; it is a deliberate and proportionate response to the gaps identified by the Wheeler review and by troubling cases in the early childhood education and care sector. A modern regulator must be able to respond flexibly and quickly, especially a regulator whose purpose is to protect children. Waiting years for reform cycles when new risks emerge is unacceptable. New section 301A creates the necessary responsiveness. It allows regulations to be made where new risks are identified across services, for example, for emerging compliance failures or new business models that threaten children's safety and wellbeing.

Importantly, it is not a blank cheque. Regulations made under new section 301A must be consistent with the national law and the paramountcy principle. They must be tabled in Parliament and subject to disallowance, and operate within the scope of the enabling Act, which remains focused on child safety and quality of care. The powers reflect the current approach to regulation‑making powers under the national law and so would position any New South Wales regulations made in reliance on this power to strengthen protections to be adopted nationally.

Additional checks and balances have been imported from the Subordinate Legislation Act 1989. They include the requirement for an opinion from the Parliamentary Counsel or Attorney General endorsing the lawfulness of any proposed regulation before it can be made, and a requirement for New South Wales Governor approval. Those are real, practical safeguards. They mean Ministers and the regulator cannot just make up new offences or requirements at a whim; they must operate transparently under parliamentary oversight and within the legislative purpose. New section 301A is not about unchecked power; it is about ensuring the law keeps pace with the risks children face. It is about striking the right balance between flexibility, accountability and, above all, the safety of children in education and care services.

The treatment of guidelines in the bill is not a case of Executive overreach; it is a case of clear and helpful guidance to ensure consistency, fairness and proportionality in how the law is applied. Authorised officers are making compliance and disciplinary decisions that directly affect services and individuals. That requires professional judgement and training to ensure that they are consistent in their decision‑making. Clear guidance helps to ensure that decisions do not vary based on the officer, region or even personal interpretation. That is fair for providers, educators and families.

Guidelines strengthen, rather than undermine, the rights of individuals because they make enforcement more predictable and consistent. In addition, guidelines cannot override the Act or regulations; they must remain within the statutory framework Parliament sets. They are not intended to set additional binding requirements. The section that refers to guidelines is drafted broadly, but breadth is necessary because the guidelines must be able to address the full range of matters that can arise under the national law, from quality standards to disciplinary provisions. Narrowing that power risks leaving dangerous gaps where inconsistent practices can persist.

As I and Government members have said, the bill is nation leading, imperative and deliberately reformist. The Government's changes to early childhood education and care regulation are leading nationally because they directly respond to the findings of an independent review into early childhood education and care regulation in New South Wales, commissioned by the Deputy Premier and published earlier this year. The review, conducted by former Deputy Ombudsman Chris Wheeler, found that the New South Wales regulator was significantly constrained by the national law—the law we seek to amend—as it applies to New South Wales today. Mr Wheeler found that the national law hampered in a number of respects the regulator's efforts to address operators that either were not up to scratch or were not fully committed to the provision of quality education and care.

Mr Wheeler found that the regulator needs to be strengthened and empowered to protect children by reforming the national law. The New South Wales Government is responding accordingly, both in terms of establishing it as an independent entity and bolstering its ranks with an initial $55 million investment into more boots on the ground. This bill gives it the powers needed to fulfil its critical mission. For children and families, the reforms deliver stronger protections, greater transparency and far-reaching oversight of services. Parents and families can be confident that the care their children receive meets the highest standards of safety and quality.

The shadow Minister expressed concerns about the nation‑leading regulation and ministerial direction power. That is a powerful, well-designed tool that gives the Government the power to move quickly and decisively. It futureproofs the bill. Where a new risk or threat emerges, it allows it to swiftly issue a legally binding direction to the sector. It also includes clear safeguards, as directions can only be made when necessary to prevent unacceptable risk to the safety of a child or children, and the Minister can only make a direction after receiving advice from the regulator.

I also acknowledge contributions from members who raised questions about how the reforms will change the way the sector is regulated. Let me be clear: We are giving the regulator stronger enforcement powers, independent oversight and risk-based monitoring. More ability to enforce compliance through graduated and responsive regulatory action, tripling maximum penalties, ensuring the rights and interests of children in early childhood education and care prevail over competing private interests, eliminating existing barriers that impede the regulator to publish public information, and new powers that allow targeted and responsive action are all practical, targeted measures that ensure the regulator can act swiftly when children are at risk. The regulation will work in practice, not just on paper.

There were concerns expressed about the consultation during the development of the bill. I acknowledge those. It should be noted, though, that the bill has been a long time coming. We have had many reviews and those reviews have included significant consultation. There are also many national initiatives and agreed positions included in the bill. In fact, the detailed consultation and consideration of items from the national decision regulation impact statement—the DRIS—has strengthened our confidence in those changes for New South Wales. These are things that the whole country agrees should change. Of course, we are working, and we will continue to work, with services and peak bodies on the sequencing so that it is practical and responsive to need, and we will issue a plain English guidance and support where it is required. Where it is needed, we will include transitional arrangements so services can comply without disruption.

There have been a number of concerns raised that the reforms might place pressure on services. To be clear, the purpose of the legislation is not to close services; it is to ensure that every service—whether public, community or private—meets the highest standards of child safety and quality. If any service cannot comply, it is because it is failing the children in its care and the community rightly expects action. We will support providers through guidance, compliance frameworks and phased implementation to minimise disruption. The reforms are about raising the bar, not restricting choice. If any provider cannot meet those standards, the protection of children must always come first.

While indicating support for the bill, the member for Balmain raised issues with New South Wales going it alone. The reforms align with the National Quality Framework while addressing the unique scale and complexity of the New South Wales sector, the largest in the country. We are setting up a system that is nationally consistent but tailored to New South Wales. Frankly, we think it is a benchmark the rest of the nation will need to follow. I trust that, in time, other jurisdictions will do that so that all children in early childhood education and care can enjoy the protections we are legislating today. I would certainly like to see similar legislation in Victoria, where I have a granddaughter in early childhood care. All of us have interests in this sector and want to ensure it is the absolute best it can be.

It is not uncommon for State and Territories to apply local requirements despite national schemes. The national law already contains multiple State-based carve-outs and exceptions. While a number of changes in the bill have already been agreed in principle at the national level, going from in-principle agreement to law in the national system is a very long process that requires unanimous agreement from all jurisdictions, and we are not prepared to wait. The system needs improvement now, and children deserve protection now. The solid reforms like whistleblower protections and those called for by Chris Wheeler in his independent review are in this bill. Again, given of the pace of national change, New South Wales has made the other jurisdictions aware, but they are not even at the in‑principle agreement stage in the national conversations. Those positions should become national positions in time, but that could take a while. This reform bill proposes making those protections available to children and families in New South Wales now.

The member for Balmain highlighted concerns that were raised at the upper House committee inquiry about disproportionate penalties for workers. Our main concern is for families who are scared by the headlines about children being harmed in early education and care services. The sector is under pressure, but that cannot be an excuse for failing to act. As I have made clear, the vast majority of people who work in the sector do a fantastic job, and all members who have contributed to debate have said that. This bill protects children and families but, in doing so, eventually it will also protect the reputation and integrity of the vast majority of workers and providers who do the right thing by our children.

These reforms ensure that the bad actors do not tarnish the good, and that the community can continue to place their trust in a sector that is so vital to our children and State. Concerns were raised about the burden on providers, but the Government believes the real burden is the one that families carry when children are harmed because the regulations were too weak. We are asking more of providers because parents, carers and families expect nothing less than the highest standards of safety. For the vast majority of providers who already do the right thing, these reforms will mean business as usual. For those who do not do the right thing, the days of cutting corners are over. Stronger rules do not hurt the sector; they protect its reputation, level the playing field and restore the confidence of families who entrust their children to it every day.

The impact on community providers was also raised. The Government acknowledges the great work of community providers. As a result of the bill, community-based and not-for-profit providers will not be punished for doing the right thing. It is quite the opposite. A stronger system protects their reputation by ensuring that the bad behaviour of a few operators does not tarnish the whole sector. It is important to consider that while some parts of the sector may be considered lower risk in general, children in every part of the sector should be protected. If a small community-run centre does the wrong thing and does not take child safety seriously, the regulator is empowered to deal with that, just as it is empowered to deal with the big corporate entities. The paramount concern must always be the safety and wellbeing of the child.

Families and communities have rightly demanded action on this matter. The Government is listening and acting decisively. Children and families deserve nothing less than a system that is safe, accountable and trusted. That is exactly what the bill delivers. I note The Greens will move an amendment at the consideration in detail stage, and I can confirm the Government will support that amendment. I appreciate the contribution from the member for Balmain, who spoke about the constructive working relationship between The Greens and the Minister's office during this process, which has been very helpful. I acknowledge also the role played by Ms Abigail Boyd in raising a lot of community concerns. I saw those reports and, like many of us, was extremely disturbed.

I particularly acknowledge the role played by Deputy Premier Prue Car. She set a lot of this work in motion and I am sure she would have loved to introduce the bill to the House. The Deputy Premier deserves huge credit for the pace of change we have been able to produce in New South Wales and for taking such decisive action in this field. I give her great credit for that. I thank also the Hon. Courtney Houssos, who has taken responsibility for this process. I thank the office of the Deputy Premier and the Department of Education for their great work on the bill and for speaking to Opposition and crossbench members about amendments to it. I foreshadow that the Government will move an amendment to the bill in the upper House. I commend the bill to the House.

TEMPORARY SPEAKER ( Mr Clayton Barr ): The question is that this bill be now read a second time.

Motion agreed to.

Consideration in detail requested by Ms Kobi Shetty.

tree_branches.name: Mr EDMOND ATALLA
tree_branches.path: Legislative Assembly (2025-10-14) > Bills > Children (Education and Care Services National Law Application) Amendment Bill 2025 > Second Reading Debate > Mr EDMOND ATALLA
tree_branches.text:
Mr EDMOND ATALLA ( Mount Druitt ) ( 16:18 :48 ): I support the Local Court and Bail Legislation Amendment Bill 2025. The bill makes two key reforms to strengthen and modernise our justice system in New South Wales. First, the bill changes the title of judicial officers presiding in the Local Court from magistrate to judge, and makes equivalent changes to associated titles, such as Chief Magistrate, Deputy Chief Magistrate, Children's Magistrate, Chief Industrial Magistrate and others. Second, the bill makes technical but significant amendments to the Bail Act 2013 and 13 other Acts to ensure consistency and clarity following the commencement of section 70A of the Bail Act earlier this year. Together the reforms modernise the way we recognise judicial officers in the Local Court and provide clarity on bail decision-making, ensuring the highest standards of fairness and public confidence.

The New South Wales Local Court is the busiest court in Australia. Judicial officers in that jurisdiction make more than 90 per cent of all judicial decisions in our State. In 2024 alone, nearly 389,000 criminal matters were commenced in the Local Court, alongside over 67,000 civil matters. Those figures show an increase of more than 30 per cent in the last decade in both jurisdictions. The matters coming before the Local Court are increasingly serious and complex. Following the 2018 table offences reform, the Local Court now deals with serious offences such as robbery and drug supply. Local Court judicial officers can impose sentences of up to two years imprisonment for a single offence or up to five years in aggregate for multiple offences. Those are serious judicial functions, and they require clarity, authority and public respect. Yet the title of magistrate does not properly reflect either the role or the responsibilities carried out by those officers. In some international jurisdictions, the term refers to lay officers, administrative officials or people without legal training. The bill corrects that.

By conferring the title of judge on judicial officers of the Local Court, we recognise their qualifications, authority and central role in our justice system. The bill will bring New South Wales into line with the Northern Territory and the Commonwealth, which have already made the change. Importantly, I note that the reform does not alter powers, functions, protections, remuneration or conditions of office. Local Court judicial officers will continue to be appointed by the Governor and their remuneration will continue to be assessed by the Statutory and Other Offices Remuneration Tribunal. The changes are not about hierarchy; they are about clarity, consistency and respect.

The second part of the bill deals with the important issue of bail. In June 2024 the House passed the Bail and Other Legislation Amendment (Domestic Violence) Bill. That bill introduced section 70A of the Bail Act 2013, which commenced on 14 March this year. That section makes clear that registrars and other authorised justices can no longer make bail decisions. The intention is simple and sound. The decision as to whether an accused person should be released from custody pending trial is a matter of great significance that is properly reserved for judicial officers and police in the first instance. Since 14 March, that has been the law in practice. Registrars are no longer making bail determinations, but a technical review of the Bail Act and related legislation revealed numerous outdated references to registrars, authorised justices and other officers. Those provisions are now inconsistent with section 70A and have the potential to create confusion. The bill fixes that problem.

Schedule 3 amends the Bail Act and 13 other Acts to remove references to registrars and other officers as bail decision-makers, ensuring clarity for practitioners, courts and the public. Those changes are precise, technical and essential. The bill is carefully drafted to ensure continuity. Savings and transitional provisions mean that existing decisions remain valid and no proceedings will be disrupted. Current office holders in the Local Court, the Children's Court and the industrial jurisdiction will seamlessly transition to their new judicial titles without requiring new commissions or oaths. Protections of independence and integrity that currently apply to magistrates will continue to apply to judges of the Local Court. Oversight arrangements, including the important work of the Judicial Commission of New South Wales, will remain unchanged.

The Local Court is the people's court. It is the first point of contact for most New South Wales citizens who encounter our justice system, whether in criminal, civil, family or other matters. It is right and proper that the judicial officers presiding in that court are recognised with the title of judge. That change acknowledges the seriousness of their role, enhances public confidence and brings New South Wales into alignment with best practice across Australia. The bill is about respect, clarity and modernisation. It respects the work of Local Court judicial officers, clarifies the law of bail and modernises our justice system for the benefit of the people of New South Wales. I commend the bill to the House.

tree_branches.name: Dr MICHAEL HOLLAND

Dr MICHAEL HOLLAND ( Bega ) ( 18:22 :43 ): On Monday 15 September, I was pleased to attend the sod turning event for the new Moruya High School support unit. Construction has begun on the new $7 million support unit, while another $13 million in upgrades is on the way for the school as part of the Minns Labor Government's work to rebuild public education and ensure students in regional New South Wales have access to every opportunity to achieve their full potential. The new support unit will contain seven permanent support classrooms with practical activities areas, breakout spaces, an outdoor play area, a covered outdoor learning area, accessible toilets and change rooms, laundry, kitchen, staff room and a new access road with undercover drop-off area and car-parking facilities. The project is due for completion by term 2, 2026, replacing five ageing demountables which were a legacy of the former Liberal-Nationals Government.

The new support unit will better support students with disabilities, ensuring all students have access to the same educational opportunities. This will provide students with the safe and supportive environment they deserve. This support unit will not only enhance learning but also ensure that families in Moruya and across the region know their children are being given the best chance to thrive. Moruya High School is also one of the 33 schools across New South Wales to receive a share of a $100 million investment from the New South Wales Government as part of the High Potential and Gifted Education [HPGE] partner schools program.

Moruya High School will receive facility upgrades to accommodate increased enrolments, broaden educational opportunities and facilitate the delivery of tailored HPGE course offerings. These opportunities include activities such as class-level acceleration programs, inter-school competitions and tournaments, and other statewide opportunities. The works will include upgrades to science, technology, engineering and mathematics classrooms, technology and applied studies classrooms, and the music room, performance area and sound studio. Works will also include upgrading the sports court, which will include a new court surface, fencing and line marking; updating the science lab, library and administration buildings; installing air conditioning across the school; improving senior lockers; a new covered walkway; and an automated front gate.

Staff at these schools will work with HPGE experts to deliver more opportunities that challenge and extend students to reach their potential. Teachers will receive dedicated professional learning to assist with identifying and rolling out more High Potential and Gifted Education opportunities for their students. Broader professional learning will also be provided to teachers in all New South Wales public schools as part of the Minns Labor Government's commitment to expanding access to High Potential and Gifted Education opportunities across the system.

Families in the Eurobodalla can also look forward to improved public schools under the Minns Labor Government, including High Potential and Gifted Education upgrades at Batemans Bay High School as well as a new school hall for Mogo Public School. The Batemans Bay High School development includes upgrades to the food technology and vocational education and training kitchen; to five science laboratories, including three prep rooms; and to two woodwork rooms, two metal work rooms and storage space. These works are part of the Minns Labor Government's plan to rebuild public education with a record $2.1 billion in the 2025-26 budget for new and upgraded schools across regional New South Wales.

A new hall and learning space will be constructed at Mogo Public School thanks to the latest round of funding under the Albanese Federal Government's schools upgrade fund. Mogo Public School has been granted $1.7 million under round two of the fund, which aims to assist public schools with the greatest need, including schools with high numbers of students from low-socio economic backgrounds, First Nations students and students with disability. The Minns Labor Government is making sure that time spent in the classroom is well spent. Under the previous Liberal Government, teachers were leaving the profession in droves resulting in 10,000 merged or cancelled classes each day. Under a Minns Labor Government, teacher vacancy rates have dropped.

Since coming to government, we have reduced the number of vacancies by 76 per cent in the Bega electorate. That means that our kids are spending more time learning in class and receiving more attention from their teachers. Our students have regained approximately half a million hours of lost learning as a result. In contrast to the former Liberal-Nationals Government, the Minns Labor Government is making teachers permanent. We are investing in public education, making over 16,000 temporary teachers and support staff permanent and increasing teachers' pay to attract and retain our best and brightest. This is part of a record investment in school infrastructure under the 2025-26 New South Wales budget, ensuring every student, regardless of postcode, can reach their full potential.
