tree_branches.text:
Ms KOBI SHETTY ( Balmain ) ( 16:05 :00 ): I move The Greens amendment No. 1 on sheet c2025-223A:

No. 1 When proceedings may be brought

Page 37, Schedule 1 [8], proposed Schedule 1 [36]–[38], lines 1–16. Omit all words on the lines. Insert instead—

[36] Section 284

Omit the section. Insert instead—

284 When proceedings may be brought [NSW]

(1) Subject to section 181 (6) and subsection (2), proceedings for an offence under this Law must be commenced within two years after the later of the following—

(a) the Regulatory Authority becoming aware of the alleged offence;

(b) the commencement of this section.

(2) If the Regulatory Authority is required to suspend taking action in relation to the alleged offence under this Law because of a concurrent investigation or proceedings in relation to or involving matters connected with or incidental to the same conduct under another Act, proceedings for the offence under this Law must be commenced within two years after any proceedings in relation to the conduct under the other Act have been finalised.

Note— This section is a substituted NSW provision.

The current loophole that lets early childhood education operators avoid accountability for serious incidents if they remain silent during the two-year limitation period will not be fully addressed by the bill. This amendment will properly close that loophole by allowing retrospective regulatory action in a limited way. That should be reserved for particularly egregious offences, and it is with this intention that I move the amendment. The law in its current form incentivises centre operators to keep quiet about serious incidents they may become aware of. Because of the limitation period, they can avoid some repercussions by failing to disclose matters to the regulator in a timely way, for whatever reason.

While they may be banned from running a centre in the future, operators cannot be held accountable for some of the conduct they have failed to disclose if they can see out the brief two-year period before the regulator becomes aware that an offence has been committed. The bill remedies that issue by amending section 284 of the Act to allow regulatory action up to two years after becoming aware of the offence, rather than two years after the date of an offence being committed. However, it does not address the issue retrospectively, and some former operators who may have presided over terrible incidents of abuse will remain capable of avoiding appropriate regulatory action. While some providers might have simply not paid attention to what happened on their watch, others at the very worst end of the scale may have covered up something altogether, so the impacts of the loophole are significant.

When members debate legislation in this place, we can be fairly abstract, but the action that needs to be taken to fix this problem will have tangible and lasting impacts for those who rely on us to change our laws for the better. I have supported a couple of local families who discovered that their children were caught up in the horrors uncovered by Operation Tenterfield. I put on record the words of one particular parent:

On the 17th of January 2023, mid morning, my life changed. Two detectives came to my house to tell me that 7 years ago, a predator had repeatedly sexually assaulted my child at her childcare.

My beautiful, smart, funny, kind baby girl, had been assaulted by this disgusting man repeatedly. She was a baby. I know this because she was only 2 when I removed her from that childcare.

These last few years have been awful—

there were a few swear words that I modified, but they are completely reasonable given the circumstances—

If you haven't lived it, you can't understand it.

I am lucky. I know what happened to my daughter. I can make sure she is supported and cared for.

I am lucky. I am not confused by her anxiety.

I am lucky. The man who assaulted my daughter is in prison. Not for what he did to my daughter, but for what he did to other little girls. But that is ok for now.

However, on that day our world changed. I lied to my child for the first time. I lied about who had come to our house that day when I had made her go out.

I've had to continue lying about why I don't sleep, why I am very quick to react, why I go from zero to furious in seconds, why I am sad. All the time.

But I am lucky.

I am also angry. So angry that I have no words to describe it - it's primitive.

He was able to hurt children because the people who were meant to be watching were not. They worked with this man, every day, for years. They socialised with him, trained with him, but they did not pay attention to what he was actually doing.

It was not a one off, an accident, a slip, a misunderstanding. He sexually assaulted 23 little girls that they were responsible for. Over and over and over.

The operators said that there was nothing they could do. They said it was not their fault.

They have walked away, knowing that the time has passed for them to be held accountable. They can tell themselves it was out of their control, they could not know. They have gone back to their before lives.

I can't go to my before life.

I have had to leave my job, my daughter and I both see psychologists, I'm medicated to just sleep a few hours in a row. I know that I have lied to my daughter and one day she will hate me for that.

We live with this every day.

Those are the words of this incredible woman who has been through absolute hell. This amendment will allow proceedings to commence within two years of the commencement of the legislation, which will capture those older incidents, particularly those that are so serious. I again thank the Minister's staff, particularly Jo, who has been incredible through this entire process, being always willing to pick up the phone. I thank the Government, the crossbench members and the Opposition for their engagement. I urge members to support this amendment so that we can deal with this in a proper way.

tree_branches.text: Mr JASON LI ( Strathfield ) ( 18:1 4 :35 ): I acknowledge the outstanding and brave work of officers from the Burwood Police Area Command and Auburn Police Area Command, led by Superintendent Christine McDonald and Superintendent Robert Toynton respectively, who responded to two serious incidents in our community last week. On 5 October, officers from Burwood Police Area Command led a major operation in Croydon Park after a public-place shooting. With support from specialist units, they entered a dangerous situation, arrested a man and restored safety to the area. Their courage and professionalism protected lives. In Strathfield, another distressing incident left many in our community shaken. I extend my thoughts to the victim, her family and the child who had to witness such trauma. Officers from Auburn Police Area Command acted swiftly and compassionately, arresting the alleged offender. I thank all the officers and first responders involved. Their bravery, care and commitment keep our community safe. Strathfield remains one of the safest and most inclusive places in Australia, and we each share a responsibility to keep it that way.

tree_branches.name: Ms ANNA WATSON
tree_branches.path: Legislative Assembly (2025-10-14) > Bills > Children (Education and Care Services National Law Application) Amendment Bill 2025 > Second Reading Debate > Ms ANNA WATSON
tree_branches.text: Ms ANNA WATSON ( Shellharbour ) —I would like to acknowledge and congratulate Amanda Kowalczyk from Koonawarra Public School on receiving the Secretary's Award for Excellent Service. Amanda's tireless dedication and outstanding contributions to her school community have made a lasting impact on students, staff, and families alike. Her professionalism, compassion, and unwavering commitment to public education are truly commendable. This award is a reflection of her leadership and the care she brings to her role each day. On behalf of the Shellharbour electorate, I would congratulate Amanda on her amazing work and for being awarded the Secretary's Award for Excellent Service. The recognition is so well deserved, and I know the entire electorate joins me in celebrating her success.

tree_branches.name: Dr DAVID SALIBA
tree_branches.path: Legislative Assembly (2025-10-14) > Bills > Children (Education and Care Services National Law Application) Amendment Bill 2025 > Second Reading Debate > Dr DAVID SALIBA
tree_branches.text:
Dr DAVID SALIBA ( Fairfield ) ( 16:52 :35 ): I speak in support of the Local Court and Bail Legislation Amendment Bill 2025, and I commend the Attorney General for not only for his work on this but also his work since coming to government. I note the bill also deals with matters pertaining to domestic violence, and I commend the Attorney General for his legislative approach to that as well. The bill predominantly relates to a name change to "judge" for magistrates or judicial officers of the Local Court. I have a deep appreciation for the judicial officers of the Local Court. As a law student back in the day, one of my first interactions with the system was going to Liverpool Local Court. It was an eye-opening experience in terms of the scale of work. I note the member for Orange, who is in the Chamber, has probably done a lot of work in Cabramatta and Liverpool in his capacity as a police officer.

It was an eye-opening experience for me to see the administration of justice and the work of magistrates and support staff. They deal with a large volume of matters, and they require great intellect to absorb so much information in a short period. Adjudicating and making critical decisions that have lifelong impacts on people requires significant intellect, and I have a deep appreciation for that. To see the administration of justice in action inspired me in my law degree and during my career in policing as well. I commend magistrates for the work they do, and recognising them through a proposed name change is important. It is also important from a recruitment and retention perspective. As law graduates become solicitors and barristers, there will be a correlation with people wanting to be judges of the Local Court. It is a career that makes a big difference and is critical within the Fairfield community, for example.

I want to encourage legal practitioners and children at school to become judges of the Local Court. I cannot wait to see more people from Western Sydney become judges, including children from migrant families who are the first in their families to go to university, the first to be admitted as lawyers and the first to go on the bench. It would be amazing to see it in rural areas and other areas across New South Wales as well. The bill also makes consequential amendments to section 70A of the Bail Act, and I welcome that. I thank everyone who works in the Local Court system. I commend the bill to the House.

tree_branches.name: Mr STEVE WHAN
tree_branches.path: Legislative Assembly (2025-10-14) > Bills > Children (Education and Care Services National Law Application) Amendment Bill 2025 > Second Reading Debate > Mr STEVE WHAN
tree_branches.text: Mr STEVE WHAN ( Monaro — Minister for Skills, TAFE and Tertiary Education ) —At the end of this week on Saturday the 18th, Queanbeyan is holding its annual Diwali-Mela lantern festival, and it's set to be the biggest one yet. I've spoken about this festival before, but I believe it's worth reiterating: our diversity is one of our great strengths as a community, and as a country. Coming together to celebrate the triumph of light over dark, and good over evil is a wonderfully fitting way to celebrate this strength. Thanks to a successful grant application, Queanbeyan-Palerang Council were awarded nearly $54,000 to put towards making this festival of light even brighter. I wouldn't dare miss it and I can't wait to see everyone there.

It will do that by allowing the regulator to consider cases which have already timed out, for two years from the commencement of the section. This is a reasonable amendment that allows major historic cases to be addressed, while acknowledging that it is not practical or possible to prosecute all historic cases. That is why we support it. I certainly acknowledge the family's trauma that the member for Balmain has outlined. It is awful to even think about that happening, let alone to experience it. We support the amendment.

TEMPORARY SPEAKER ( Mr Clayton Barr ): The question is that The Greens amendment No. 1 on sheet c2025-223A be agreed to.

Amendment agreed to.

TEMPORARY SPEAKER ( Mr Clayton Barr ): The question is that clauses 1 and 2 and schedules 1 and 2 as amended be agreed to.

Clauses 1 and 2 and schedules 1 and 2 as amended agreed to.

tree_branches.name: Ms KOBI SHETTY
tree_branches.path: Legislative Assembly (2025-10-14) > Bills > Children (Education and Care Services National Law Application) Amendment Bill 2025 > Consideration In Detail > Ms KOBI SHETTY
tree_branches.text:
Ms KOBI SHETTY ( Balmain ) ( 16:05 :00 ): I move The Greens amendment No. 1 on sheet c2025-223A:

No. 1 When proceedings may be brought

Page 37, Schedule 1 [8], proposed Schedule 1 [36]–[38], lines 1–16. Omit all words on the lines. Insert instead—

[36] Section 284

Omit the section. Insert instead—

284 When proceedings may be brought [NSW]

(1) Subject to section 181 (6) and subsection (2), proceedings for an offence under this Law must be commenced within two years after the later of the following—

(a) the Regulatory Authority becoming aware of the alleged offence;

(b) the commencement of this section.

(2) If the Regulatory Authority is required to suspend taking action in relation to the alleged offence under this Law because of a concurrent investigation or proceedings in relation to or involving matters connected with or incidental to the same conduct under another Act, proceedings for the offence under this Law must be commenced within two years after any proceedings in relation to the conduct under the other Act have been finalised.

Note— This section is a substituted NSW provision.

The current loophole that lets early childhood education operators avoid accountability for serious incidents if they remain silent during the two-year limitation period will not be fully addressed by the bill. This amendment will properly close that loophole by allowing retrospective regulatory action in a limited way. That should be reserved for particularly egregious offences, and it is with this intention that I move the amendment. The law in its current form incentivises centre operators to keep quiet about serious incidents they may become aware of. Because of the limitation period, they can avoid some repercussions by failing to disclose matters to the regulator in a timely way, for whatever reason.

While they may be banned from running a centre in the future, operators cannot be held accountable for some of the conduct they have failed to disclose if they can see out the brief two-year period before the regulator becomes aware that an offence has been committed. The bill remedies that issue by amending section 284 of the Act to allow regulatory action up to two years after becoming aware of the offence, rather than two years after the date of an offence being committed. However, it does not address the issue retrospectively, and some former operators who may have presided over terrible incidents of abuse will remain capable of avoiding appropriate regulatory action. While some providers might have simply not paid attention to what happened on their watch, others at the very worst end of the scale may have covered up something altogether, so the impacts of the loophole are significant.

When members debate legislation in this place, we can be fairly abstract, but the action that needs to be taken to fix this problem will have tangible and lasting impacts for those who rely on us to change our laws for the better. I have supported a couple of local families who discovered that their children were caught up in the horrors uncovered by Operation Tenterfield. I put on record the words of one particular parent:

On the 17th of January 2023, mid morning, my life changed. Two detectives came to my house to tell me that 7 years ago, a predator had repeatedly sexually assaulted my child at her childcare.

My beautiful, smart, funny, kind baby girl, had been assaulted by this disgusting man repeatedly. She was a baby. I know this because she was only 2 when I removed her from that childcare.

These last few years have been awful—

there were a few swear words that I modified, but they are completely reasonable given the circumstances—

If you haven't lived it, you can't understand it.

I am lucky. I know what happened to my daughter. I can make sure she is supported and cared for.

I am lucky. I am not confused by her anxiety.

I am lucky. The man who assaulted my daughter is in prison. Not for what he did to my daughter, but for what he did to other little girls. But that is ok for now.

However, on that day our world changed. I lied to my child for the first time. I lied about who had come to our house that day when I had made her go out.

I've had to continue lying about why I don't sleep, why I am very quick to react, why I go from zero to furious in seconds, why I am sad. All the time.

But I am lucky.

I am also angry. So angry that I have no words to describe it - it's primitive.

He was able to hurt children because the people who were meant to be watching were not. They worked with this man, every day, for years. They socialised with him, trained with him, but they did not pay attention to what he was actually doing.

It was not a one off, an accident, a slip, a misunderstanding. He sexually assaulted 23 little girls that they were responsible for. Over and over and over.

The operators said that there was nothing they could do. They said it was not their fault.

They have walked away, knowing that the time has passed for them to be held accountable. They can tell themselves it was out of their control, they could not know. They have gone back to their before lives.

I can't go to my before life.

I have had to leave my job, my daughter and I both see psychologists, I'm medicated to just sleep a few hours in a row. I know that I have lied to my daughter and one day she will hate me for that.

We live with this every day.

Those are the words of this incredible woman who has been through absolute hell. This amendment will allow proceedings to commence within two years of the commencement of the legislation, which will capture those older incidents, particularly those that are so serious. I again thank the Minister's staff, particularly Jo, who has been incredible through this entire process, being always willing to pick up the phone. I thank the Government, the crossbench members and the Opposition for their engagement. I urge members to support this amendment so that we can deal with this in a proper way.

tree_branches.name: Local Court and Bail Legislation Amendment Bill 2025
tree_branches.path: Legislative Assembly (2025-10-14) > Bills > Local Court and Bail Legislation Amendment Bill 2025
tree_branches.text:
Debate resumed from 17 September 2025.

The second matter the bill deals with is thoroughly cosmetic: It changes the title of judicial officers in the Local Court from "magistrate" to "judge". That takes the overwhelming majority of the 56 pages of the bill. We have a youth crime crisis in New South Wales, but there have been no legislative provisions, other than a bail provision some time ago, to deal with it. We brought forward a private member's bill to deal with aspects of the youth crime crisis in New South Wales by, for example, expanding the offences that would constitute repeat offences for the purposes of a more difficult bail test, introducing a range of measures for the revocation of bail resulting from recalcitrant behaviour of young people charged with serious offences while on bail, and bringing New South Wales into conformity with other States where there is electronic monitoring of young people on bail. All of those provisions were rejected by the Government, and nothing constructive was put up in their place. Yet a 56-page bill is presented to this place to make cosmetic changes to the titles of the judicial officers who preside in the Local Court.

We think it is regrettable that the priorities of this Government are cosmetic matters of this kind, rather than substantive matters. Of course, in saying that I mean no disrespect to the judicial officers of the Local Court. I have appeared in the Local Court many times and, frankly, am in awe of the work our magistrates do. The variety and volume of matters dealt with by a judicial officer of the Local Court make the role incredibly challenging and difficult. It is a role that so many judicial officers of the Local Court perform with great skill, expertise and diligence. As a group, they are to be commended. But it is regrettable that there is not a more substantive bill coming before this Parliament to deal with the many law-and-order and other issues confronting the legal profession and the judiciary. We support the bill—we would not want to be seen to not be supporting the judiciary of the Local Court—but we exhibit our concern about this Government's priorities.

The New South Wales Local Court is the busiest court in Australia. Judicial officers in that jurisdiction make more than 90 per cent of all judicial decisions in our State. In 2024 alone, nearly 389,000 criminal matters were commenced in the Local Court, alongside over 67,000 civil matters. Those figures show an increase of more than 30 per cent in the last decade in both jurisdictions. The matters coming before the Local Court are increasingly serious and complex. Following the 2018 table offences reform, the Local Court now deals with serious offences such as robbery and drug supply. Local Court judicial officers can impose sentences of up to two years imprisonment for a single offence or up to five years in aggregate for multiple offences. Those are serious judicial functions, and they require clarity, authority and public respect. Yet the title of magistrate does not properly reflect either the role or the responsibilities carried out by those officers. In some international jurisdictions, the term refers to lay officers, administrative officials or people without legal training. The bill corrects that.

By conferring the title of judge on judicial officers of the Local Court, we recognise their qualifications, authority and central role in our justice system. The bill will bring New South Wales into line with the Northern Territory and the Commonwealth, which have already made the change. Importantly, I note that the reform does not alter powers, functions, protections, remuneration or conditions of office. Local Court judicial officers will continue to be appointed by the Governor and their remuneration will continue to be assessed by the Statutory and Other Offices Remuneration Tribunal. The changes are not about hierarchy; they are about clarity, consistency and respect.

The second part of the bill deals with the important issue of bail. In June 2024 the House passed the Bail and Other Legislation Amendment (Domestic Violence) Bill. That bill introduced section 70A of the Bail Act 2013, which commenced on 14 March this year. That section makes clear that registrars and other authorised justices can no longer make bail decisions. The intention is simple and sound. The decision as to whether an accused person should be released from custody pending trial is a matter of great significance that is properly reserved for judicial officers and police in the first instance. Since 14 March, that has been the law in practice. Registrars are no longer making bail determinations, but a technical review of the Bail Act and related legislation revealed numerous outdated references to registrars, authorised justices and other officers. Those provisions are now inconsistent with section 70A and have the potential to create confusion. The bill fixes that problem.

Schedule 3 amends the Bail Act and 13 other Acts to remove references to registrars and other officers as bail decision-makers, ensuring clarity for practitioners, courts and the public. Those changes are precise, technical and essential. The bill is carefully drafted to ensure continuity. Savings and transitional provisions mean that existing decisions remain valid and no proceedings will be disrupted. Current office holders in the Local Court, the Children's Court and the industrial jurisdiction will seamlessly transition to their new judicial titles without requiring new commissions or oaths. Protections of independence and integrity that currently apply to magistrates will continue to apply to judges of the Local Court. Oversight arrangements, including the important work of the Judicial Commission of New South Wales, will remain unchanged.

The Local Court is the people's court. It is the first point of contact for most New South Wales citizens who encounter our justice system, whether in criminal, civil, family or other matters. It is right and proper that the judicial officers presiding in that court are recognised with the title of judge. That change acknowledges the seriousness of their role, enhances public confidence and brings New South Wales into alignment with best practice across Australia. The bill is about respect, clarity and modernisation. It respects the work of Local Court judicial officers, clarifies the law of bail and modernises our justice system for the benefit of the people of New South Wales. I commend the bill to the House.

In my electorate of Lane Cove and across the State, people are deeply concerned about community safety. They are frustrated by the growing problem of youth crime and crime generally. They see victims waiting months, sometimes years, for their matters to be heard in all levels of courts across New South Wales. They hear about overflowing court lists, overworked court staff, and judges and magistrates trying to do more with less. Under those conditions, mistakes will be made and I fear that things may well be overlooked. People who should not slip through the cracks will do so, not because those in the system do not care but because the system is stretched beyond its limits. Those are the pressures that deserve the Parliament's attention and the issues that demand reform.

Changing a title from magistrate to judge will not reduce delays, will not help police and the courts who are dealing with repeat youth offenders, and will not ease the frustration of victims who see offenders walk free because the system is stretched beyond capacity. The community expects more from the Parliament than symbolic gestures. We should be talking about how to reduce the crushing workload in our local courts, how to better resource the justice system and how to ensure that when a person walks into a courtroom, they have confidence that their matter will be heard promptly and fairly. The bill was an opportunity to confront those challenges and to show that the Parliament understands the pressures faced by our courts and is prepared to do something about them. Instead we have a change of titles that will not make a difference to the people who depend on the courts every day.

I make the point clearly that I have great respect for those who sit on the bench of the Local Court. They deal with difficult, sometimes distressing matters daily. They deserve the unwavering support of Parliament and the community and not just symbolic recognition. Our focus should be on ensuring that justice in New South Wales is not delayed, that communities are safe and that the system commands the trust of those it serves. Titles are secondary; outcomes are what count. The people of Lane Cove and communities across the State want a justice system that works and not one that simply looks like it does. For that reason, while I support the passage of the bill, I do so in the hope that the Government will soon turn its attention to the real issues of delays, resourcing and the growing challenges that are eroding confidence in our justice system. Justice must not only be done; it must be seen to be done—and it must be done without delay. That is what the people of New South Wales deserve.

The main amendment proposed by schedules 1 and 2 to the bill amends the Local Court Act 2007 and various other Acts to replace the term "magistrate" with the term "judge" or "judges", as the case may be. The bill is important because it recognises in law what has long been true in practice for decades—that magistrates are now judges in all but name. I am extremely pleased to stand in this historic chamber and recognise the importance of the role of magistrates in our society. I am pleased that on the passing of this bill, and its subsequent commencement, magistrates will be known as judges.

The office of magistrate has a history that goes back not just decades, but centuries. The office of magistrate finds its origin in the ancient office of justice of the peace in England. In 1344, Edward III provided by statute that "Two or three persons of the best reputation in the counties should be assigned by the King's commission as keepers of the peace and they, with others learned in law, should hear and determine charges of felonies and trespasses against the peace." That moment was a turning point in our legal history. It marked the transformation of the keeper of the peace—formerly a more ad hoc and informal local position—into a judicial officer empowered to hear and determine criminal matters. From that time onward, the justice of the peace—or "magistrate" as they came to be known—held both executive and judicial functions. While their roles waned and waxed over the years, they were the face of law and order in local communities through the centuries.

When the first fleet arrived in 1788, the English office of justice of the peace was transplanted to New South Wales. Governor Phillip himself was commissioned as a justice of the peace, and he appointed others from amongst the small number of officers in the colony to assist him. These early magistrates exercised extraordinary powers. They were responsible not only for summary criminal jurisdiction, but also for administering the convict system itself. In many respects, they were administrators, judges and law enforcers rolled into one. As the colony matured, so too did the office of magistrate. In the nineteenth century stipendiary magistrates were appointed—legally trained professionals who took on what had previously been the preserve of lay justices. By the turn of the twentieth century, the magistracy in New South Wales was effectively a branch of the public service. But it is from the late twentieth century that we can trace the emergence of the modern magistracy as we know it today.

As the Magistrates Court continued to expand its exercise of judicial power, a tension emerged: How can the Magistrate's Court maintain the principal of judicial independence when its officers serve at the pleasure of Executive Government? With the passage of the Local Courts Act 1982, magistrates were finally severed from the public service, achieving structural independence. Four years later, the Judicial Officers Act 1986 secured their tenure by ensuring that magistrates, like judges of the higher courts, could only be removed by Parliament. From that point on, magistrates were no longer hybrid administrators; they were fully independent judicial officers. The former Chief Magistrate, Mr Ian Pike, and Magistrate Arthur Reidel—two magistrates I have appeared before—captured this transformation perfectly in the epilogue they wrote for Hilary Golder's High and Responsible Office: A History of the NSW Magistracy . They wrote:

In just under 200 years the lay justice, creature of Edward III, in New South Wales became a judge in all but name, possessing professional qualifications, judicial independence and tenure.

That sentence is exactly the nub of this bill. The legislation is not about creating a new judicial office. It is about aligning the name of the office with the reality of what magistrates already do—they are judges.

Names and symbols matter. In a society governed by the rule of law, the justice system depends upon public confidence and respect. The overwhelming majority of interactions that people in New South Wales have with the judicial system occur in the Local Court. It is where bail is determined, pleas are entered, sentences are imposed, protection orders are made and civil disputes are heard. For the most part, the Local Court is the only place where the people of New South Wales experience our judicial system. It is therefore essential that the public understand that these judicial officers are not bureaucrats and not mere functionaries. They are, in real terms, judges. Their title should reflect the dignity and the judicial power that they exercise every day. As the Attorney General has pointed out, changing the title will also bring New South Wales into line with the Northern Territory and the Commonwealth, which both changed the name of "magistrate" to "judge".

I also acknowledge the continuing role of justices of the peace, who were the origin of this office. They remain an important part of the legal landscape, providing accessible services in communities across New South Wales. The history of our magistracy and the role of justices of the peace are deeply intertwined. While the two paths have diverged, the wisdom of our forebears who established the local justices of the peace and enabled that office to flourish remains apparent all these centuries later. The dignity and professionalism of the modern Local Court—and indeed our entire legal system—rests on those historical foundations. As we have heard, the bill amends the Bail Act 2013 as well as 13 other Acts to make it clear that registrars are not authorised to make a bail decision. The amendment follows on from debate on the Bail and Other Legislation Amendment (Domestic Violence) Bill 2024, which took place in this House on 5 June 2024. Sixteen months later, we are making further amendments to tidy up the work done on that day.

I thank the Attorney General for making further amendments to the Bail Act 2013 and to 13 other Acts to make it clear to the community and the courts that registrars may not make a bail decision. The heart of this bill, however, lies in recognising the value to our legal system of the work undertaken by magistrates. The change of title recognises the true value of the work of magistrates in our State. Changing the title so that magistrates will be known as judges strengthens public confidence in the work carried out within the Local Court. I commend the bill to the House.

The bill will introduce two major reforms: first, changing the title of "magistrate" to that of "judge"; and, secondly, removing the power of registrars to make decisions regarding bail of an accused person. I will address the key amendments. The bill will amend the Local Court Act 2007 to change the title of judicial officers presiding in the Local Court of New South Wales from "magistrate" to "judge" and will make similar changes to other titles of judicial officers within the Local Court framework. It is important to note that the bill will not alter the existing powers of these new judges or the functions, protections, remuneration or conditions of judicial officers presiding in the Local Court.

Schedule 1, items [1] to [19] will amend the Local Court Act 2007 to implement the change of title, with schedule 1 [20] inserting provisions to ensure continuity and clarity during this transition. Upon commencement, those provisions will abolish the offices of Chief Magistrate, Deputy Chief Magistrate and magistrate. Individuals holding those offices immediately before the abolition will be appointed as Chief Judge of the Local Court, Deputy Chief Judge of the Local Court and a judge of the Local Court. Importantly, the provisions in schedule 1 will confirm that a person appointed or acting in a new office will be subject to the same terms and conditions that applied to the corresponding former office immediately before commencement.

In effect, schedule 1 also ensures that any person appointed to act as a judge of the Local Court will continue in that role for the remainder of the term for which they were originally appointed; confirms that a person appointed to a new office in accordance with the amendments in this bill does not require a new commission to be issued under the public seal of the State of New South Wales; and ensures that the abolition of the former offices does not affect ongoing or pending proceedings. Schedule 1 will prevent delays in proceedings by ensuring a person appointed to a new office may continue to hear and determine matters that were before them immediately prior.

Finally, the amendments within schedule 1 also provide continuity by deeming that any act done by a person while holding a former office immediately before commencement will continue to have effect, as if made under their corresponding new office. Schedule 2 to the bill makes consequential amendments to a range of Acts across the Local Court framework, effecting the change of title reform. For example, schedule 2 [11] and [52] will amend legislation governing judicial officers within the Local Court framework—namely, the Children's Court Act 1987 and the Industrial Relations Act 1996. It establishes new judicial offices of Children's Judge, Chief Industrial Local Court Judge and Industrial Local Court Judge.

I will now address the amendments regarding bail proposed in schedule 3 to the bill. The bill makes technical amendments to the Bail Act 2013, clarifying the application of section 70A to ensure that only judicial officers and police can make bail decisions. Section 70A was originally inserted as a standalone amendment to the Bail Act 2013 during parliamentary debate on the Bail and Other Legislation Amendment (Domestic Violence) Bill 2024 in this House in June 2024, as part of the New South Wales Government's suite of measures to combat domestic and family violence. Section 70A prohibits registrars from making bail decisions. It commenced on 14 March 2025, and it has been fully operationalised across New South Wales since that time. However, the Bail Act 2013 itself and 13 other Acts still contain provisions referring to people other than judicial officers and police making bail decisions. Those provisions are no longer in use by registrars, having been legally superseded by section 70A.

Amendments are required to formally update the provisions to ensure consistency across legislation and to provide clarity for practitioners, courts and the public. Accordingly, schedule 3 [1] amends the Bail Act, as the primary instrument governing bail, to remove the term "authorised justice" from the definition of "bail authority" in section 4 of the Act. The role of a modern magistrate originates from a tradition that has evolved over time. Deputy Chief Magistrate Theo Tsavdaridis wrote a fantastic summary in relation to this, entitled From Whence We Came: Justices of the Peace and the Birth of the Magistracy . Historically, the terms "justice of the peace" and "magistrate" were used interchangeably. During the colonial governance of New South Wales, the function of a magistrate was largely administrative in nature, and their powers for punishment of offenders were not defined by legislation. In fact, the original colonial magistrates were not paid a salary but were compensated by other means, such as access to convict labour. It was a very different role compared with the modern magistrate we know today.

In 1881 the Metropolitan Magistrates Act 1881 was passed, establishing "skilled and trained" magistrates to serve the Sydney district. Those magistrates were granted exclusive jurisdiction over criminal summary offences, reflecting the increasing complexity and need for a more specialised approach to justice. For a period of time, magistrates served a function as public servants, accountable to the Executive arm of government. However, with the introduction of the Local Courts Act 1982, that accountability to the Executive was phased out. Through the Judicial Officers Act 1986, magistrates were redefined as independent judicial officers, on the same terms as judges of the District and Supreme courts. Magistrates became independent from the Executive and were able to make decisions free from political interference. From 1955 up until today, there have been no appointments of lay—or non-legally trained—magistrates. The role of a magistrate is integral, and their title should reflect that importance. They make decisions that affect individuals' lives and the safety of our community in New South Wales.

The Local Court is a foundation of our justice system. It provides a fair forum to consider and resolve legal disputes, and to determine the application and validity of both common law and statute. The Local Court is the engine room of our State's justice system. The Local Court is where almost all domestic and family violence matters are heard and where all criminal proceedings commence and, in fact, where most finish. Local Court judicial officers determine more than 90 per cent of all judicial matters in New South Wales, with demand growing both in volume and complexity. In 2024 alone, some 388,000 general crime matters were commenced in the Local Court. That is a 34 per cent increase over the past decade. In the civil jurisdiction, over 67,000 matters commenced in 2024 in what is a 31 per cent increase from 2022. The demand on judicial officers in the Local Court cannot be overstated. [ Extension of time ]

Turning to the bail decision-making process in New South Wales, section 70A of the Bail Act was introduced in the Government's suite of measures to combat the unacceptable rates of domestic and family violence across the State. This bill seeks to give further effect to and clarify the integral provision to ensure bail determinations are only made by judges or the police. This is a crucial measure to ensure community safety. Members would know how our community was shattered last year when we lost a vibrant young soul, Molly Ticehurst. She was a loving daughter, a dog mum and a committed early childhood educator, and we lost her to domestic violence. The Government's proposed changes to our bail laws last year and today are in memory of Molly. Molly was a victim of intimate partner violence by a man who was on bail for some very serious offences. Her former partner was charged with breaching an apprehended violence order, assault, stalking, and causing damage to property and harm to her family pet. He was then released on bail and charged with her murder. Molly's future was taken—stolen—by an ex-partner. The reforms in this bill aim to strengthen the important amendment of section 70A, to prevent further loss and tragedy in our community.

Registrars play an important role in the administration of justice in our courts, but our magistrates are best placed to make those difficult decisions. The prohibition on bail decision-making in section 70A was just one part of a multi-faceted response by the Minns Labour Government to improve our response to domestic, family and sexual violence. The Bail and Other Legislation Amendment (Domestic Violence) Act 2024 passed Parliament in June 2024, and also strengthened the unacceptable risk and show cause tests for bail, required electronic monitoring of people charged with certain serious domestic violence offences against intimate partners, and introduced new measures to make it easier for police to prosecute perpetrators who use tracking devices in a domestic violence context.

In conclusion, I thank the dedicated judicial officers who preside over the Local Court for their commitment to our community. Local Court judicial officers are the front line, ensuring access to justice and community safety. I commend Chief Magistrate His Honour Judge Michael Allen and Deputy Chief Magistrate His Honour Theo Tsavdaridis for driving this important reform. This reform is not just about changing a name or a title. It is about ensuring that the skill, service and integrity of judicial officers in the Local Court are properly recognised and appreciated. It also ensures that the decisions that matter most for our community sit with judicial officers. I commend the bill to the House.

We have a chronic shortage of magistrates in regional New South Wales. For example, an average list day in Moree is in excess of 200 or 250 cases. We have one list day a week in Moree and then we roll into hearing days. Once the magistrate has finished two or three days, depending on the week, he or she has to drive 150 kilometres across to Inverell to deal with at least 200 matters on that list. They then have a full day of hearings. That magistrate may, if he or she is lucky, be on the road by six o'clock on Friday night to drive home. The Government needs to look at the workload that our magistrates are undertaking and urgently appoint more of them, particularly in regional areas. We also need better facilities in our local courts.

I have courtrooms in my electorate at Glen Innes and Walcha that still do not have audiovisual link facilities. That means that practitioners cannot run a domestic violence hearing in either Glen Innes or Walcha, and the parties involved in that proceeding have to travel 100 kilometres down the road to Armidale. That is difficult for victims of domestic violence. It is also difficult for offenders. It is difficult for the legal profession because it means additional costs. The majority of domestic violence cases in New South Wales involve Legal Aid. Lawyers do not want to take on those cases because they are not funded for travel, and the situation snowballs. Whilst this bill is well intentioned and it is great to be able to call a magistrate a judge, we have missed an opportunity. The bill is window-dressing, and I urge the Government to look at the fundamental issues in our Local Court system: overworked and under-resourced magistrates, and poor facilities. If we looked at all of those issues, I am sure the bill would receive a lot of bipartisanship support and we could work together to try to address those things.

It was an eye-opening experience for me to see the administration of justice and the work of magistrates and support staff. They deal with a large volume of matters, and they require great intellect to absorb so much information in a short period. Adjudicating and making critical decisions that have lifelong impacts on people requires significant intellect, and I have a deep appreciation for that. To see the administration of justice in action inspired me in my law degree and during my career in policing as well. I commend magistrates for the work they do, and recognising them through a proposed name change is important. It is also important from a recruitment and retention perspective. As law graduates become solicitors and barristers, there will be a correlation with people wanting to be judges of the Local Court. It is a career that makes a big difference and is critical within the Fairfield community, for example.

I want to encourage legal practitioners and children at school to become judges of the Local Court. I cannot wait to see more people from Western Sydney become judges, including children from migrant families who are the first in their families to go to university, the first to be admitted as lawyers and the first to go on the bench. It would be amazing to see it in rural areas and other areas across New South Wales as well. The bill also makes consequential amendments to section 70A of the Bail Act, and I welcome that. I thank everyone who works in the Local Court system. I commend the bill to the House.

I welcome this announcement. The Local Court now deals with cases that are more complex than we have ever seen before. The number of table 1 offences being dealt with to finality in the Local Court has increased significantly over the years. The court is getting through a significant volume of work, and it can impose sentences of imprisonment for more than one offence. If the court were to cumulate sentences for two or more offences, it could be looking at issuing a period of up to five years imprisonment. The role of the magistrate these days has well and truly evolved, and I think it makes perfect sense that a name change is part of the legislation. I heard the member for Northern Tablelands speak earlier. I think all the magistrates I know would love an associate. Judges get associates in the District Court and elsewhere. Being a Local Court magistrate is a very hard job. Magistrates deal with a large volume of cases on a daily basis, often on a country circuit travelling hundreds of kilometres, but they do not have the luxury of an associate, unlike District Court judges. I think they would appreciate that. I will pass it on to the Attorney General's office for consideration.

The part of the bill relating to certain judicial officers making bail decisions arose in relation to the tragic murder of Molly Ticehurst, a young woman who lived in Forbes in my electorate. Her perpetrator is sitting in a prison cell at the moment awaiting finality. That saw a movement across not only New South Wales but also Australia for domestic violence reform. I pay tribute to Molly Ticehurst and her family. I know they would be keen to see this legislation passed to tidy up the approval of bail applications by judicial officers. As the member for Fairfield indicated, I also pass on my appreciation to all magistrates. Chief Magistrate—soon to be Chief Judge—Michael Allen, who many years ago was a barrister in Orange, has done a magnificent job since taking over as the head of the Local Court of New South Wales. With that, I commend the bill to the House.

The ASSISTANT SPEAKER ( Mr Jason Li ): It being 5.00 p.m., pursuant to standing and sessional orders, debate is interrupted for the public interest debate. I set down resumption of the debate as an order of the day for a later hour.
