tree_branches.text:
Debate resumed from 17 September 2025.

The second matter the bill deals with is thoroughly cosmetic: It changes the title of judicial officers in the Local Court from "magistrate" to "judge". That takes the overwhelming majority of the 56 pages of the bill. We have a youth crime crisis in New South Wales, but there have been no legislative provisions, other than a bail provision some time ago, to deal with it. We brought forward a private member's bill to deal with aspects of the youth crime crisis in New South Wales by, for example, expanding the offences that would constitute repeat offences for the purposes of a more difficult bail test, introducing a range of measures for the revocation of bail resulting from recalcitrant behaviour of young people charged with serious offences while on bail, and bringing New South Wales into conformity with other States where there is electronic monitoring of young people on bail. All of those provisions were rejected by the Government, and nothing constructive was put up in their place. Yet a 56-page bill is presented to this place to make cosmetic changes to the titles of the judicial officers who preside in the Local Court.

We think it is regrettable that the priorities of this Government are cosmetic matters of this kind, rather than substantive matters. Of course, in saying that I mean no disrespect to the judicial officers of the Local Court. I have appeared in the Local Court many times and, frankly, am in awe of the work our magistrates do. The variety and volume of matters dealt with by a judicial officer of the Local Court make the role incredibly challenging and difficult. It is a role that so many judicial officers of the Local Court perform with great skill, expertise and diligence. As a group, they are to be commended. But it is regrettable that there is not a more substantive bill coming before this Parliament to deal with the many law-and-order and other issues confronting the legal profession and the judiciary. We support the bill—we would not want to be seen to not be supporting the judiciary of the Local Court—but we exhibit our concern about this Government's priorities.

The New South Wales Local Court is the busiest court in Australia. Judicial officers in that jurisdiction make more than 90 per cent of all judicial decisions in our State. In 2024 alone, nearly 389,000 criminal matters were commenced in the Local Court, alongside over 67,000 civil matters. Those figures show an increase of more than 30 per cent in the last decade in both jurisdictions. The matters coming before the Local Court are increasingly serious and complex. Following the 2018 table offences reform, the Local Court now deals with serious offences such as robbery and drug supply. Local Court judicial officers can impose sentences of up to two years imprisonment for a single offence or up to five years in aggregate for multiple offences. Those are serious judicial functions, and they require clarity, authority and public respect. Yet the title of magistrate does not properly reflect either the role or the responsibilities carried out by those officers. In some international jurisdictions, the term refers to lay officers, administrative officials or people without legal training. The bill corrects that.

By conferring the title of judge on judicial officers of the Local Court, we recognise their qualifications, authority and central role in our justice system. The bill will bring New South Wales into line with the Northern Territory and the Commonwealth, which have already made the change. Importantly, I note that the reform does not alter powers, functions, protections, remuneration or conditions of office. Local Court judicial officers will continue to be appointed by the Governor and their remuneration will continue to be assessed by the Statutory and Other Offices Remuneration Tribunal. The changes are not about hierarchy; they are about clarity, consistency and respect.

The second part of the bill deals with the important issue of bail. In June 2024 the House passed the Bail and Other Legislation Amendment (Domestic Violence) Bill. That bill introduced section 70A of the Bail Act 2013, which commenced on 14 March this year. That section makes clear that registrars and other authorised justices can no longer make bail decisions. The intention is simple and sound. The decision as to whether an accused person should be released from custody pending trial is a matter of great significance that is properly reserved for judicial officers and police in the first instance. Since 14 March, that has been the law in practice. Registrars are no longer making bail determinations, but a technical review of the Bail Act and related legislation revealed numerous outdated references to registrars, authorised justices and other officers. Those provisions are now inconsistent with section 70A and have the potential to create confusion. The bill fixes that problem.

Schedule 3 amends the Bail Act and 13 other Acts to remove references to registrars and other officers as bail decision-makers, ensuring clarity for practitioners, courts and the public. Those changes are precise, technical and essential. The bill is carefully drafted to ensure continuity. Savings and transitional provisions mean that existing decisions remain valid and no proceedings will be disrupted. Current office holders in the Local Court, the Children's Court and the industrial jurisdiction will seamlessly transition to their new judicial titles without requiring new commissions or oaths. Protections of independence and integrity that currently apply to magistrates will continue to apply to judges of the Local Court. Oversight arrangements, including the important work of the Judicial Commission of New South Wales, will remain unchanged.

The Local Court is the people's court. It is the first point of contact for most New South Wales citizens who encounter our justice system, whether in criminal, civil, family or other matters. It is right and proper that the judicial officers presiding in that court are recognised with the title of judge. That change acknowledges the seriousness of their role, enhances public confidence and brings New South Wales into alignment with best practice across Australia. The bill is about respect, clarity and modernisation. It respects the work of Local Court judicial officers, clarifies the law of bail and modernises our justice system for the benefit of the people of New South Wales. I commend the bill to the House.

In my electorate of Lane Cove and across the State, people are deeply concerned about community safety. They are frustrated by the growing problem of youth crime and crime generally. They see victims waiting months, sometimes years, for their matters to be heard in all levels of courts across New South Wales. They hear about overflowing court lists, overworked court staff, and judges and magistrates trying to do more with less. Under those conditions, mistakes will be made and I fear that things may well be overlooked. People who should not slip through the cracks will do so, not because those in the system do not care but because the system is stretched beyond its limits. Those are the pressures that deserve the Parliament's attention and the issues that demand reform.

Changing a title from magistrate to judge will not reduce delays, will not help police and the courts who are dealing with repeat youth offenders, and will not ease the frustration of victims who see offenders walk free because the system is stretched beyond capacity. The community expects more from the Parliament than symbolic gestures. We should be talking about how to reduce the crushing workload in our local courts, how to better resource the justice system and how to ensure that when a person walks into a courtroom, they have confidence that their matter will be heard promptly and fairly. The bill was an opportunity to confront those challenges and to show that the Parliament understands the pressures faced by our courts and is prepared to do something about them. Instead we have a change of titles that will not make a difference to the people who depend on the courts every day.

I make the point clearly that I have great respect for those who sit on the bench of the Local Court. They deal with difficult, sometimes distressing matters daily. They deserve the unwavering support of Parliament and the community and not just symbolic recognition. Our focus should be on ensuring that justice in New South Wales is not delayed, that communities are safe and that the system commands the trust of those it serves. Titles are secondary; outcomes are what count. The people of Lane Cove and communities across the State want a justice system that works and not one that simply looks like it does. For that reason, while I support the passage of the bill, I do so in the hope that the Government will soon turn its attention to the real issues of delays, resourcing and the growing challenges that are eroding confidence in our justice system. Justice must not only be done; it must be seen to be done—and it must be done without delay. That is what the people of New South Wales deserve.

The main amendment proposed by schedules 1 and 2 to the bill amends the Local Court Act 2007 and various other Acts to replace the term "magistrate" with the term "judge" or "judges", as the case may be. The bill is important because it recognises in law what has long been true in practice for decades—that magistrates are now judges in all but name. I am extremely pleased to stand in this historic chamber and recognise the importance of the role of magistrates in our society. I am pleased that on the passing of this bill, and its subsequent commencement, magistrates will be known as judges.

The office of magistrate has a history that goes back not just decades, but centuries. The office of magistrate finds its origin in the ancient office of justice of the peace in England. In 1344, Edward III provided by statute that "Two or three persons of the best reputation in the counties should be assigned by the King's commission as keepers of the peace and they, with others learned in law, should hear and determine charges of felonies and trespasses against the peace." That moment was a turning point in our legal history. It marked the transformation of the keeper of the peace—formerly a more ad hoc and informal local position—into a judicial officer empowered to hear and determine criminal matters. From that time onward, the justice of the peace—or "magistrate" as they came to be known—held both executive and judicial functions. While their roles waned and waxed over the years, they were the face of law and order in local communities through the centuries.

When the first fleet arrived in 1788, the English office of justice of the peace was transplanted to New South Wales. Governor Phillip himself was commissioned as a justice of the peace, and he appointed others from amongst the small number of officers in the colony to assist him. These early magistrates exercised extraordinary powers. They were responsible not only for summary criminal jurisdiction, but also for administering the convict system itself. In many respects, they were administrators, judges and law enforcers rolled into one. As the colony matured, so too did the office of magistrate. In the nineteenth century stipendiary magistrates were appointed—legally trained professionals who took on what had previously been the preserve of lay justices. By the turn of the twentieth century, the magistracy in New South Wales was effectively a branch of the public service. But it is from the late twentieth century that we can trace the emergence of the modern magistracy as we know it today.

As the Magistrates Court continued to expand its exercise of judicial power, a tension emerged: How can the Magistrate's Court maintain the principal of judicial independence when its officers serve at the pleasure of Executive Government? With the passage of the Local Courts Act 1982, magistrates were finally severed from the public service, achieving structural independence. Four years later, the Judicial Officers Act 1986 secured their tenure by ensuring that magistrates, like judges of the higher courts, could only be removed by Parliament. From that point on, magistrates were no longer hybrid administrators; they were fully independent judicial officers. The former Chief Magistrate, Mr Ian Pike, and Magistrate Arthur Reidel—two magistrates I have appeared before—captured this transformation perfectly in the epilogue they wrote for Hilary Golder's High and Responsible Office: A History of the NSW Magistracy . They wrote:

In just under 200 years the lay justice, creature of Edward III, in New South Wales became a judge in all but name, possessing professional qualifications, judicial independence and tenure.

That sentence is exactly the nub of this bill. The legislation is not about creating a new judicial office. It is about aligning the name of the office with the reality of what magistrates already do—they are judges.

Names and symbols matter. In a society governed by the rule of law, the justice system depends upon public confidence and respect. The overwhelming majority of interactions that people in New South Wales have with the judicial system occur in the Local Court. It is where bail is determined, pleas are entered, sentences are imposed, protection orders are made and civil disputes are heard. For the most part, the Local Court is the only place where the people of New South Wales experience our judicial system. It is therefore essential that the public understand that these judicial officers are not bureaucrats and not mere functionaries. They are, in real terms, judges. Their title should reflect the dignity and the judicial power that they exercise every day. As the Attorney General has pointed out, changing the title will also bring New South Wales into line with the Northern Territory and the Commonwealth, which both changed the name of "magistrate" to "judge".

I also acknowledge the continuing role of justices of the peace, who were the origin of this office. They remain an important part of the legal landscape, providing accessible services in communities across New South Wales. The history of our magistracy and the role of justices of the peace are deeply intertwined. While the two paths have diverged, the wisdom of our forebears who established the local justices of the peace and enabled that office to flourish remains apparent all these centuries later. The dignity and professionalism of the modern Local Court—and indeed our entire legal system—rests on those historical foundations. As we have heard, the bill amends the Bail Act 2013 as well as 13 other Acts to make it clear that registrars are not authorised to make a bail decision. The amendment follows on from debate on the Bail and Other Legislation Amendment (Domestic Violence) Bill 2024, which took place in this House on 5 June 2024. Sixteen months later, we are making further amendments to tidy up the work done on that day.

I thank the Attorney General for making further amendments to the Bail Act 2013 and to 13 other Acts to make it clear to the community and the courts that registrars may not make a bail decision. The heart of this bill, however, lies in recognising the value to our legal system of the work undertaken by magistrates. The change of title recognises the true value of the work of magistrates in our State. Changing the title so that magistrates will be known as judges strengthens public confidence in the work carried out within the Local Court. I commend the bill to the House.

The bill will introduce two major reforms: first, changing the title of "magistrate" to that of "judge"; and, secondly, removing the power of registrars to make decisions regarding bail of an accused person. I will address the key amendments. The bill will amend the Local Court Act 2007 to change the title of judicial officers presiding in the Local Court of New South Wales from "magistrate" to "judge" and will make similar changes to other titles of judicial officers within the Local Court framework. It is important to note that the bill will not alter the existing powers of these new judges or the functions, protections, remuneration or conditions of judicial officers presiding in the Local Court.

Schedule 1, items [1] to [19] will amend the Local Court Act 2007 to implement the change of title, with schedule 1 [20] inserting provisions to ensure continuity and clarity during this transition. Upon commencement, those provisions will abolish the offices of Chief Magistrate, Deputy Chief Magistrate and magistrate. Individuals holding those offices immediately before the abolition will be appointed as Chief Judge of the Local Court, Deputy Chief Judge of the Local Court and a judge of the Local Court. Importantly, the provisions in schedule 1 will confirm that a person appointed or acting in a new office will be subject to the same terms and conditions that applied to the corresponding former office immediately before commencement.

In effect, schedule 1 also ensures that any person appointed to act as a judge of the Local Court will continue in that role for the remainder of the term for which they were originally appointed; confirms that a person appointed to a new office in accordance with the amendments in this bill does not require a new commission to be issued under the public seal of the State of New South Wales; and ensures that the abolition of the former offices does not affect ongoing or pending proceedings. Schedule 1 will prevent delays in proceedings by ensuring a person appointed to a new office may continue to hear and determine matters that were before them immediately prior.

Finally, the amendments within schedule 1 also provide continuity by deeming that any act done by a person while holding a former office immediately before commencement will continue to have effect, as if made under their corresponding new office. Schedule 2 to the bill makes consequential amendments to a range of Acts across the Local Court framework, effecting the change of title reform. For example, schedule 2 [11] and [52] will amend legislation governing judicial officers within the Local Court framework—namely, the Children's Court Act 1987 and the Industrial Relations Act 1996. It establishes new judicial offices of Children's Judge, Chief Industrial Local Court Judge and Industrial Local Court Judge.

I will now address the amendments regarding bail proposed in schedule 3 to the bill. The bill makes technical amendments to the Bail Act 2013, clarifying the application of section 70A to ensure that only judicial officers and police can make bail decisions. Section 70A was originally inserted as a standalone amendment to the Bail Act 2013 during parliamentary debate on the Bail and Other Legislation Amendment (Domestic Violence) Bill 2024 in this House in June 2024, as part of the New South Wales Government's suite of measures to combat domestic and family violence. Section 70A prohibits registrars from making bail decisions. It commenced on 14 March 2025, and it has been fully operationalised across New South Wales since that time. However, the Bail Act 2013 itself and 13 other Acts still contain provisions referring to people other than judicial officers and police making bail decisions. Those provisions are no longer in use by registrars, having been legally superseded by section 70A.

Amendments are required to formally update the provisions to ensure consistency across legislation and to provide clarity for practitioners, courts and the public. Accordingly, schedule 3 [1] amends the Bail Act, as the primary instrument governing bail, to remove the term "authorised justice" from the definition of "bail authority" in section 4 of the Act. The role of a modern magistrate originates from a tradition that has evolved over time. Deputy Chief Magistrate Theo Tsavdaridis wrote a fantastic summary in relation to this, entitled From Whence We Came: Justices of the Peace and the Birth of the Magistracy . Historically, the terms "justice of the peace" and "magistrate" were used interchangeably. During the colonial governance of New South Wales, the function of a magistrate was largely administrative in nature, and their powers for punishment of offenders were not defined by legislation. In fact, the original colonial magistrates were not paid a salary but were compensated by other means, such as access to convict labour. It was a very different role compared with the modern magistrate we know today.

In 1881 the Metropolitan Magistrates Act 1881 was passed, establishing "skilled and trained" magistrates to serve the Sydney district. Those magistrates were granted exclusive jurisdiction over criminal summary offences, reflecting the increasing complexity and need for a more specialised approach to justice. For a period of time, magistrates served a function as public servants, accountable to the Executive arm of government. However, with the introduction of the Local Courts Act 1982, that accountability to the Executive was phased out. Through the Judicial Officers Act 1986, magistrates were redefined as independent judicial officers, on the same terms as judges of the District and Supreme courts. Magistrates became independent from the Executive and were able to make decisions free from political interference. From 1955 up until today, there have been no appointments of lay—or non-legally trained—magistrates. The role of a magistrate is integral, and their title should reflect that importance. They make decisions that affect individuals' lives and the safety of our community in New South Wales.

The Local Court is a foundation of our justice system. It provides a fair forum to consider and resolve legal disputes, and to determine the application and validity of both common law and statute. The Local Court is the engine room of our State's justice system. The Local Court is where almost all domestic and family violence matters are heard and where all criminal proceedings commence and, in fact, where most finish. Local Court judicial officers determine more than 90 per cent of all judicial matters in New South Wales, with demand growing both in volume and complexity. In 2024 alone, some 388,000 general crime matters were commenced in the Local Court. That is a 34 per cent increase over the past decade. In the civil jurisdiction, over 67,000 matters commenced in 2024 in what is a 31 per cent increase from 2022. The demand on judicial officers in the Local Court cannot be overstated. [ Extension of time ]

Turning to the bail decision-making process in New South Wales, section 70A of the Bail Act was introduced in the Government's suite of measures to combat the unacceptable rates of domestic and family violence across the State. This bill seeks to give further effect to and clarify the integral provision to ensure bail determinations are only made by judges or the police. This is a crucial measure to ensure community safety. Members would know how our community was shattered last year when we lost a vibrant young soul, Molly Ticehurst. She was a loving daughter, a dog mum and a committed early childhood educator, and we lost her to domestic violence. The Government's proposed changes to our bail laws last year and today are in memory of Molly. Molly was a victim of intimate partner violence by a man who was on bail for some very serious offences. Her former partner was charged with breaching an apprehended violence order, assault, stalking, and causing damage to property and harm to her family pet. He was then released on bail and charged with her murder. Molly's future was taken—stolen—by an ex-partner. The reforms in this bill aim to strengthen the important amendment of section 70A, to prevent further loss and tragedy in our community.

Registrars play an important role in the administration of justice in our courts, but our magistrates are best placed to make those difficult decisions. The prohibition on bail decision-making in section 70A was just one part of a multi-faceted response by the Minns Labour Government to improve our response to domestic, family and sexual violence. The Bail and Other Legislation Amendment (Domestic Violence) Act 2024 passed Parliament in June 2024, and also strengthened the unacceptable risk and show cause tests for bail, required electronic monitoring of people charged with certain serious domestic violence offences against intimate partners, and introduced new measures to make it easier for police to prosecute perpetrators who use tracking devices in a domestic violence context.

In conclusion, I thank the dedicated judicial officers who preside over the Local Court for their commitment to our community. Local Court judicial officers are the front line, ensuring access to justice and community safety. I commend Chief Magistrate His Honour Judge Michael Allen and Deputy Chief Magistrate His Honour Theo Tsavdaridis for driving this important reform. This reform is not just about changing a name or a title. It is about ensuring that the skill, service and integrity of judicial officers in the Local Court are properly recognised and appreciated. It also ensures that the decisions that matter most for our community sit with judicial officers. I commend the bill to the House.

We have a chronic shortage of magistrates in regional New South Wales. For example, an average list day in Moree is in excess of 200 or 250 cases. We have one list day a week in Moree and then we roll into hearing days. Once the magistrate has finished two or three days, depending on the week, he or she has to drive 150 kilometres across to Inverell to deal with at least 200 matters on that list. They then have a full day of hearings. That magistrate may, if he or she is lucky, be on the road by six o'clock on Friday night to drive home. The Government needs to look at the workload that our magistrates are undertaking and urgently appoint more of them, particularly in regional areas. We also need better facilities in our local courts.

I have courtrooms in my electorate at Glen Innes and Walcha that still do not have audiovisual link facilities. That means that practitioners cannot run a domestic violence hearing in either Glen Innes or Walcha, and the parties involved in that proceeding have to travel 100 kilometres down the road to Armidale. That is difficult for victims of domestic violence. It is also difficult for offenders. It is difficult for the legal profession because it means additional costs. The majority of domestic violence cases in New South Wales involve Legal Aid. Lawyers do not want to take on those cases because they are not funded for travel, and the situation snowballs. Whilst this bill is well intentioned and it is great to be able to call a magistrate a judge, we have missed an opportunity. The bill is window-dressing, and I urge the Government to look at the fundamental issues in our Local Court system: overworked and under-resourced magistrates, and poor facilities. If we looked at all of those issues, I am sure the bill would receive a lot of bipartisanship support and we could work together to try to address those things.

It was an eye-opening experience for me to see the administration of justice and the work of magistrates and support staff. They deal with a large volume of matters, and they require great intellect to absorb so much information in a short period. Adjudicating and making critical decisions that have lifelong impacts on people requires significant intellect, and I have a deep appreciation for that. To see the administration of justice in action inspired me in my law degree and during my career in policing as well. I commend magistrates for the work they do, and recognising them through a proposed name change is important. It is also important from a recruitment and retention perspective. As law graduates become solicitors and barristers, there will be a correlation with people wanting to be judges of the Local Court. It is a career that makes a big difference and is critical within the Fairfield community, for example.

I want to encourage legal practitioners and children at school to become judges of the Local Court. I cannot wait to see more people from Western Sydney become judges, including children from migrant families who are the first in their families to go to university, the first to be admitted as lawyers and the first to go on the bench. It would be amazing to see it in rural areas and other areas across New South Wales as well. The bill also makes consequential amendments to section 70A of the Bail Act, and I welcome that. I thank everyone who works in the Local Court system. I commend the bill to the House.

I welcome this announcement. The Local Court now deals with cases that are more complex than we have ever seen before. The number of table 1 offences being dealt with to finality in the Local Court has increased significantly over the years. The court is getting through a significant volume of work, and it can impose sentences of imprisonment for more than one offence. If the court were to cumulate sentences for two or more offences, it could be looking at issuing a period of up to five years imprisonment. The role of the magistrate these days has well and truly evolved, and I think it makes perfect sense that a name change is part of the legislation. I heard the member for Northern Tablelands speak earlier. I think all the magistrates I know would love an associate. Judges get associates in the District Court and elsewhere. Being a Local Court magistrate is a very hard job. Magistrates deal with a large volume of cases on a daily basis, often on a country circuit travelling hundreds of kilometres, but they do not have the luxury of an associate, unlike District Court judges. I think they would appreciate that. I will pass it on to the Attorney General's office for consideration.

The part of the bill relating to certain judicial officers making bail decisions arose in relation to the tragic murder of Molly Ticehurst, a young woman who lived in Forbes in my electorate. Her perpetrator is sitting in a prison cell at the moment awaiting finality. That saw a movement across not only New South Wales but also Australia for domestic violence reform. I pay tribute to Molly Ticehurst and her family. I know they would be keen to see this legislation passed to tidy up the approval of bail applications by judicial officers. As the member for Fairfield indicated, I also pass on my appreciation to all magistrates. With that, I commend the bill to the House.

Mr ALISTER HENSKENS ( Wahroonga ) ( 18:27 :25 ): A highlight of each year for me is when I host two high school leaders from each secondary school in the Wahroonga electorate for a tour and special dinner in the President's Dining Room at Parliament House here in Macquarie Street. This annual tradition—commenced by my predecessor, as member for Ku-ring-gai—has now survived a redistribution and provides these remarkable young people with an opportunity to understand some of our State's democratic history, to witness its democratic processes in action and to better understand how decisions made in this place affect lives and communities. It also provides me with a valuable opportunity to hear directly from our young people about their perspectives on various issues.

Every year, without exception, I am deeply impressed by the confidence, curiosity and engagement of our young leaders. Their level of maturity and insight reflects the strong values instilled in them by their families, schools and teachers. The students in attendance this year were Jazarah Tambyrajah and Nell Owen from Abbotsleigh, Huntley Stace and Bea Meyer from Barker College, Ruby Young and Helen Bui from Hornsby Girls High School, Arjun Vishnu and Chester Swaffer from Knox Grammar School, Keenor Sabaa and Lucy McKenna from Loreto Normanhurst, Ashwyn Tyagi and Ashton Huynh from Normanhurst Boys High School, Abigail Chapman and Thomas Passe-de Silva from Pennant Hills High School, Ang-Ya Koo and Emily Abadee from Pymble Ladies' College, Maya Manjah and Eliza Waugh from St Leo's Catholic College, Sophie Robinson and Angus Lloyd from Turramurra High School, and Audrey Kennedy and Toby Pope from Wahroonga Adventist School. These young leaders are aspirational, intelligent and forward-thinking.

During our conversations, many shared their ambitions for the future, expressing a strong desire to contribute meaningfully to society. They spoke about pursuing varied careers in areas such as law, engineering, science and even actuarial studies, showing a passion about learning more about our world and building our future communities. A number of students also shared their interest in healthcare professions such as physiotherapy and medicine, motivated by a desire to help others and improve quality of life. It was clear that these students possess both ambition and compassion—qualities that will undoubtedly serve them and our State well in the future.

We also spoke about their broader hopes for the future, from attending university and studying abroad, to travelling and experiencing life beyond their local communities. Their eagerness to learn and to explore the world reminded me of the importance of nurturing curiosity and global awareness in our young people. When I finished high school, I too had the opportunity to travel, spending several months backpacking through Europe. It remains one of the most rewarding experiences of my life. I was able to visit family in the Netherlands, immerse myself in different cultures and see firsthand the diversity and richness of the world beyond Australia. That experience broadened my perspectives and deepened my appreciation for the opportunities we have here at home.

As these students approach such a significant milestone, I encouraged them to maintain a sense of balance and wellbeing. It is important that they do not become overwhelmed by pressure or lose sight of what brings them happiness. Making time for friends, family and the activities they enjoy is essential for making it through the end of school. Those moments of connection and rest are not distractions; they are what sustain us through the most challenging periods of our lives. This week, many year 12 students will commence their HSC exams—the culmination of 13 years of schooling, effort and dedication. I wish all the students across New South Wales who are sitting their HSC exams this year the very best and congratulate them on completing high school. The Wahroonga electorate is an educational powerhouse, with the most HSC students each year in our State. I had the opportunity to attend the graduation ceremonies of those high schools during the last week of term 3. Those ceremonies were an important time to celebrate all that the year 12 students had achieved and to recognise the high achievers of each school before they undertake their final exams.

Finally, I remind students that while academic results are important, they do not define a person's worth or future potential. Success takes many forms, and often life provides unexpected opportunities. Even if the first pathway does not unfold exactly as they had planned, they will have countless ways to reach their goals. With determination, curiosity and persistence, they can achieve whatever they set their mind to. I genuinely believe that success is 10 per cent inspiration and 90 per cent perspiration. I encourage every student to stick out whatever they wish to do. Go well, and congratulations on completing high school.

tree_branches.name: Mr EDMOND ATALLA
tree_branches.path: Legislative Assembly (2025-10-14) > Bills > Local Court and Bail Legislation Amendment Bill 2025 > Second Reading Debate > Mr EDMOND ATALLA
tree_branches.text:
Mr EDMOND ATALLA ( Mount Druitt ) ( 16:18 :48 ): I support the Local Court and Bail Legislation Amendment Bill 2025. The bill makes two key reforms to strengthen and modernise our justice system in New South Wales. First, the bill changes the title of judicial officers presiding in the Local Court from magistrate to judge, and makes equivalent changes to associated titles, such as Chief Magistrate, Deputy Chief Magistrate, Children's Magistrate, Chief Industrial Magistrate and others. Second, the bill makes technical but significant amendments to the Bail Act 2013 and 13 other Acts to ensure consistency and clarity following the commencement of section 70A of the Bail Act earlier this year. Together the reforms modernise the way we recognise judicial officers in the Local Court and provide clarity on bail decision-making, ensuring the highest standards of fairness and public confidence.

The New South Wales Local Court is the busiest court in Australia. Judicial officers in that jurisdiction make more than 90 per cent of all judicial decisions in our State. In 2024 alone, nearly 389,000 criminal matters were commenced in the Local Court, alongside over 67,000 civil matters. Those figures show an increase of more than 30 per cent in the last decade in both jurisdictions. The matters coming before the Local Court are increasingly serious and complex. Following the 2018 table offences reform, the Local Court now deals with serious offences such as robbery and drug supply. Local Court judicial officers can impose sentences of up to two years imprisonment for a single offence or up to five years in aggregate for multiple offences. Those are serious judicial functions, and they require clarity, authority and public respect. Yet the title of magistrate does not properly reflect either the role or the responsibilities carried out by those officers. In some international jurisdictions, the term refers to lay officers, administrative officials or people without legal training. The bill corrects that.

By conferring the title of judge on judicial officers of the Local Court, we recognise their qualifications, authority and central role in our justice system. The bill will bring New South Wales into line with the Northern Territory and the Commonwealth, which have already made the change. Importantly, I note that the reform does not alter powers, functions, protections, remuneration or conditions of office. Local Court judicial officers will continue to be appointed by the Governor and their remuneration will continue to be assessed by the Statutory and Other Offices Remuneration Tribunal. The changes are not about hierarchy; they are about clarity, consistency and respect.

The second part of the bill deals with the important issue of bail. In June 2024 the House passed the Bail and Other Legislation Amendment (Domestic Violence) Bill. That bill introduced section 70A of the Bail Act 2013, which commenced on 14 March this year. That section makes clear that registrars and other authorised justices can no longer make bail decisions. The intention is simple and sound. The decision as to whether an accused person should be released from custody pending trial is a matter of great significance that is properly reserved for judicial officers and police in the first instance. Since 14 March, that has been the law in practice. Registrars are no longer making bail determinations, but a technical review of the Bail Act and related legislation revealed numerous outdated references to registrars, authorised justices and other officers. Those provisions are now inconsistent with section 70A and have the potential to create confusion. The bill fixes that problem.

Schedule 3 amends the Bail Act and 13 other Acts to remove references to registrars and other officers as bail decision-makers, ensuring clarity for practitioners, courts and the public. Those changes are precise, technical and essential. The bill is carefully drafted to ensure continuity. Savings and transitional provisions mean that existing decisions remain valid and no proceedings will be disrupted. Current office holders in the Local Court, the Children's Court and the industrial jurisdiction will seamlessly transition to their new judicial titles without requiring new commissions or oaths. Protections of independence and integrity that currently apply to magistrates will continue to apply to judges of the Local Court. Oversight arrangements, including the important work of the Judicial Commission of New South Wales, will remain unchanged.

The Local Court is the people's court. It is the first point of contact for most New South Wales citizens who encounter our justice system, whether in criminal, civil, family or other matters. It is right and proper that the judicial officers presiding in that court are recognised with the title of judge. That change acknowledges the seriousness of their role, enhances public confidence and brings New South Wales into alignment with best practice across Australia. The bill is about respect, clarity and modernisation. It respects the work of Local Court judicial officers, clarifies the law of bail and modernises our justice system for the benefit of the people of New South Wales. I commend the bill to the House.

tree_branches.text: Dr HUGH McDERMOTT ( Prospect ) —On Sunday 28th September, I was delighted to meet with volunteers and parishioners from Wentworthville Anglican Church and present them with a Community Building Partnership grant. Established more than a century ago in 1919, Wenty Anglican is an historic faith-based community located in the heart of our local Prospect Electorate. Today, the Church conducts English and Tamil language church services on Sundays and operate numerous community-focused services, including language classes for new migrants. Their community garden caters especially to refugees with a history of trauma and marginalised individuals from culturally diverse and disadvantaged backgrounds. This year, Wenty Anglican successfully applied for a Community Building Partnership grant of $42,562 to supply and install reverse cycle air conditioning units for their main auditorium. This grant will ensure that parishioners attending church services and community functions can operate comfortably through the colder and the warmer months. On the day, I joined the Wenty Anglican family during their Sunday service, to pray together and to connect afterwards for morning tea. Thank you David Misztal, Pastor, and all parishioners and volunteers at Wentworthville Anglican Church for your continued service and amazing community spirit.

tree_branches.name: Dr DAVID SALIBA
tree_branches.path: Legislative Assembly (2025-10-14) > Bills > Local Court and Bail Legislation Amendment Bill 2025 > Second Reading Debate > Dr DAVID SALIBA
tree_branches.text:
Dr DAVID SALIBA ( Fairfield ) ( 16:52 :35 ): I speak in support of the Local Court and Bail Legislation Amendment Bill 2025, and I commend the Attorney General for not only for his work on this but also his work since coming to government. I note the bill also deals with matters pertaining to domestic violence, and I commend the Attorney General for his legislative approach to that as well. The bill predominantly relates to a name change to "judge" for magistrates or judicial officers of the Local Court. I have a deep appreciation for the judicial officers of the Local Court. As a law student back in the day, one of my first interactions with the system was going to Liverpool Local Court. It was an eye-opening experience in terms of the scale of work. I note the member for Orange, who is in the Chamber, has probably done a lot of work in Cabramatta and Liverpool in his capacity as a police officer.

It was an eye-opening experience for me to see the administration of justice and the work of magistrates and support staff. They deal with a large volume of matters, and they require great intellect to absorb so much information in a short period. Adjudicating and making critical decisions that have lifelong impacts on people requires significant intellect, and I have a deep appreciation for that. To see the administration of justice in action inspired me in my law degree and during my career in policing as well. I commend magistrates for the work they do, and recognising them through a proposed name change is important. It is also important from a recruitment and retention perspective. As law graduates become solicitors and barristers, there will be a correlation with people wanting to be judges of the Local Court. It is a career that makes a big difference and is critical within the Fairfield community, for example.

I want to encourage legal practitioners and children at school to become judges of the Local Court. I cannot wait to see more people from Western Sydney become judges, including children from migrant families who are the first in their families to go to university, the first to be admitted as lawyers and the first to go on the bench. It would be amazing to see it in rural areas and other areas across New South Wales as well. The bill also makes consequential amendments to section 70A of the Bail Act, and I welcome that. I thank everyone who works in the Local Court system. I commend the bill to the House.

tree_branches.text: Mr PHILIP DONATO ( Orange ) —Mr Speaker, I would like to acknowledge the wonderful achievement of Olsen Kennedy, who was awarded the Duke of Endinburgh's Gold award this year, the highest offered after securing the program's silver and bronze medals. Olsen took up the challenge in year nine and has been working steadily towards completion with an hour's work in each category a week. Olsen's gold medal achievement was highlighted by a trip to New Zealand on cricket tour while he has camped and hiked in a number of national parks in the region. He has learned the flute, worked with Stannies' St Vincent De Paul committee, played rugby, and assisted with college masses. I congratulate Olsen on his commitment to completing this arduous yet extremely worthwhile scheme. His dedication to its principles of personal growth will serve him well.

tree_branches.name: Public Interest Debate
tree_branches.path: Legislative Assembly (2025-10-14) > Public Interest Debate
tree_branches.text:
That this House:

(1) Notes that the New South Wales Labor Government inherited a teacher shortage crisis from the former Liberal-Nationals Coalition, which saw up to 3,311 teacher vacancies in November 2022 and 10,000 merged and cancelled classes every day.

(2) Supports the removal of the wages cap, which allowed for an historic pay deal for teachers and has resulted in a 61 per cent drop in teacher vacancies from last year to this year in addition to halving the number of merged and cancelled classes.

(3) Supports the building of new and upgraded schools in fast-growing communities, including Emerald Hills, Grantham Farm, West Dapto, Wilton, Tallawong, Wentworthville, Calderwood, Jordan Springs and Leppington, after a decade of neglect by the former Liberal-Nationals Government, which left New South Wales with fewer schools than it started with.

Former Prime Minister Bob Hawke said:

The importance of education and the creation of equality of opportunity in education. These are, to me, the most fundamental things about a decent society.

Education is the great constant. It is where children build friendships, find purpose and begin to understand who they are as a person. As they grow, it becomes the foundation for the adults they will become, shaping how they think, contribute and engage with the wider world. I am a living example of what a strong public education system can do. My dad left school at 14 to become an apprentice carpet layer and help raise his siblings, while my mum left school at 15. In many parts of the world that would have been my path too, whether I liked it or not. But because I had access to a strong public education system, I had the chance to apply myself, go to university and eventually stand in this place.

This is a story shared by several generations across the State and the nation, where education has given families like mine the opportunity to build something better for future generations. However, under the previous Government, that opportunity became harder to reach. On any given day, public schools in this State were short by around 3,000 casual teachers, forcing thousands of classes to be merged, cancelled or left with minimal supervision. Nearly nine in 10 schools reported daily staff shortages, with principals pulled from their offices just to keep classrooms running. Public education funding was slashed, including a $148 million cut that left schools scrambling to meet basic needs; TAFE was gutted and hollowed out by a $196 million shortfall; and campuses were sold off, with hundreds of staff gone. The Liberals even closed schools. There were more public schools in New South Wales when they came to government than when they left. They walked away from their responsibility to provide every community with access to quality public education.

Those were not isolated incidents; they were deliberate choices to underfund, cut and walk away from public education. In doing so, too many students found it harder to access the one thing that could change their lives: a fair go in the classroom. The Minns Labor Government is rebuilding education from the ground up. We abolished the wages cap and delivered the biggest teacher pay rise in a generation, restoring respect, fairness and stability to the profession. We reduced teacher vacancies by 61 per cent, down from 2,460 under the previous Government to just 962 today. We halved the number of merged and cancelled classes, and teacher resignations are now at their lowest level in 13 years. The Government has also invested a record $9 billion in new and upgraded schools—more than at any time in the State's history—with 50 major projects already underway. We are also delivering 100 new public preschools, the biggest expansion of early learning this State has ever seen. The Liberals did not build a single public preschool in their 12 years in government.

I spoke about the number of schools that went down under the previous Government, but it gets worse. Two sites were earmarked as public schools in my electorate of Leppington, but both were relinquished by the former Government. In their place—surprise, surprise—three private schools have purchased those sites. So education will be provided there, but it will not be public education—because we know what the Opposition thinks about that. In 2024 the Government released the NSW Enrolment Growth Audit, which found that the Leppington‑Catherine Field area in my electorate ranked ninth in the entire State for student growth, with enrolments rising by 173 per cent between 2018 and 2023—which is 942 additional students in just five years—far outpacing the population forecasts. The same audit found that dwelling growth was up 98 per cent, nearly doubling from around 3,700 to 7,300. Those numbers tell a pretty obvious story to anyone who cares about public education: Rapid development and swelling enrolments meant that there was a clear need for more schools.

The previous Government failed to act, but this Government is getting on with the job. In Leppington, teacher vacancies are down by more than 55 per cent and six new public preschools are being built, at Eschol Park, Kearns, Robert Townson, Greenway Park, Leppington and Emerald Hills. The Government is also building the first public school for Austral, Leppington and Denham Court, where much of the growth in my electorate has been and at which I was very excited to recently do the sod turn. Thousands of houses have been built in that area over the past decade, and this Government is building its first high school. The Government is also investing in the existing public schools at Leppington, Austral, Greenway Park and Dalmeny as part of a broader statewide effort to match infrastructure with population growth.

I know that is a novel idea to those opposite, but it is something Labor members believe in. We know that education is not just a line item in a budget or a bunch of numbers in a spreadsheet. It is the foundation of opportunity, equality and growth. It lifts families, strengthens communities and builds a fairer State for everybody. Education changed my life, and I want it to change the lives of every child growing up in Leppington and across this great State. This Government is delivering on its mission to provide a stronger, fairer, better-resourced public education system for New South Wales.

Ms Liza Butler: What did you build?

Mr JUSTIN CLANCY: I am going to talk about that. In fact, let me go straight to it. Let us go to Labor's 2023-24 budget papers. This week the Government was out spruiking Western Sydney, where Labor claims to be delivering major projects for schools in Carlingford West, Cumberland High, Darcy Road, Girraween, Melrose Park, Parramatta East, Rydalmere, Telopea and Wentworth Point.

Mr Matt Cross: What does the budget say?

Mr JUSTIN CLANCY: This Government's first budget states, "Ongoing works—new and upgraded schools". Hang on a moment. Those were Coalition schools, weren't they? Some 106 of them were handed on to this Government. Labor members talk about rebuilding and fixing, but all they are good at is cutting the ribbons on projects already funded by the Coalition. They rebrand teacher initiatives as their own and pretend that the system is suddenly working better when they turn up for the photo. The Liberal-Nationals Government invested more than any government in New South Wales history, with a $17.7 billion pipeline, 213 new and upgraded schools delivered and, as I mentioned—as is in the Government's budget papers—106 were in progress when we left office. The Labor budget papers makes for great reading. They also say things like taxation revenue is up 26 per cent in the first two years of this Government; its deficit is up. These are great budget papers to read through in that regard.

This year Labor announced only 15 new or upgraded schools, while our last budget had 23. In our last budget, capital expenditure in education increased by 29 per cent; under Labor that is just 6.7 per cent, a fraction of what is needed to keep pace with enrolment growth. The Premier turned up to open Darcy Road Public School, which is another one in this budget paper listed under "Ongoing works—new and upgraded schools". That is a project entirely funded by the Liberal-Nationals Government, and it was claimed as a Labor success. All Labor members had to do was cut the ribbon. Having said that, there are schools like those in my own community—again announced in 2022, listed in the Labor budget papers—that are yet to see a shovel in the ground. That is again deeply concerning for my community and for a lot of communities across our State. We hear the talk, but we are yet to see the action.

I am pleased that the member for Leppington mentioned Bob Hawke when he talked about teachers. I mention another great Labor colleague in the Federal Government, Minister Jason Clare. As I have said before in this Chamber, he spoke about the post-COVID issue with teachers as being a nationwide crisis. Let us not pretend that it is unique to New South Wales; it is a national—in Victoria and Western Australia—and an international issue. Also, the issue is not just about wages. It is also about retention, workload, behaviour management and support. Our teachers in our electorates are telling us that. Remuneration matters. In fact, the Liberal-Nationals Government went to the last election with $152,000 salary for senior high-end teachers. Members can check this. As of August 2025, the website of those opposite says that same teacher can at the moment expect to be paid $144,000. Labor's problem is that they look for a headline, not a plan. I focus on something important in that regard. The member for Leppington touched on TAFE. I bring it back to early childhood. I ask the member, what is his Government doing for our community preschools?

Mr Warren Kirby: Public preschools in schools.

Mr JUSTIN CLANCY: Even when it is spoken about in the Chamber, those opposite do not hear it. They do not listen. They do not open their ears to the impact on community preschools.

Mr Warren Kirby: One hundred public preschools.

Mr JUSTIN CLANCY: I am happy for the member for Riverstone to talk about public preschools, because he continues to miss the point. He forgets about community preschools, and that is the problem we face. Those opposite sit there and forget everything about community preschools. The ones that are asked to do the heavy lifting should be supported. They are experiencing the pay gap and should be helped along. I move amendments, and I table those amendments— [ Time expired. ]

Looking at the population of The Ponds High School, this year it has 2,207 students enrolled. This year it has 330 students sitting for the HSC; next year that is expected to reach about 400. The neighbouring suburb on the other side of that area is Stanhope Gardens. Again, there was a proposed high school for Stanhope Gardens. Members would think that the previous Government would perhaps build a high school there to alleviate some of the pressure off The Ponds High School. But no, instead, again it relinquished that high school site and sold it off, again resulting in more houses.

It goes on and on with the previous Government. In the list of "Top 20 student enrolment growth areas in New South Wales government schools: 2018-2023", in terms of estimation compared with actual enrolments, Schofields - East was number one and Marsden Park was number two. A public school was opened in Marsden Park in 2021, with capacity for 1,000. But, of course, the school reached student enrolments of 2,000 by 2024. This Government built Melonba Public School and Melonba High School to meet the demand of an area that ranks second highest in New South Wales for student growth, which had increased by almost 1,000 per cent. In 2018 the Marsden Park area had 236 student enrolments. That number had ballooned to 2,493 by 2023, which is the year that those opposite left government.

This story goes on and on in north-west Sydney. Number six in the list was Box Hill-Nelson. The enrolments there had grown from 119 in 2018 to 1,445 in 2023. That is an increase of over 1,100 per cent. What did communities in that area get? They got zero schools. Not a single school was built. It is astonishing that members of the former Government are now running a campaign talking about how under-resourced that area is by our Government. But it was not our Government that let down the good people of Box Hill; it was the former Government and the council that runs that area. Over and over again, the record of the previous Government is deplorable. It can only be put into two baskets: either wilful neglect or gross mismanagement. Take your pick on those.

By contrast, this Government has built or is building nine new schools across north-west Sydney, across those three regions that I mentioned. A public primary school, with a co-located preschool, is almost completed at Nirimba Fields. A primary school in Tallawong is well and truly underway. We have a contract signed for Tallawong high school; that is soon to be built. Box Hill High School will open. In the case of Box Hill Public School, the situation was so acute that we had to build a temporary school to take care of the students while the permanent school is being built. Schools are being built in Marsden Park.

Grantham Farm is another area in the Riverstone electorate that has been exploding in population. Oddly enough, when the announcement was made for the new public school at Grantham Farm—one of my team managed to pull up a news article from 2017 when I was working in the business chamber—that site was also proposed to be sold off by the previous Government. Instead of building new schools, it was adamant that it would sell off the sites that were proposed for schools in the fastest growing area in New South Wales, with tens of thousands of young families moving there. Over and over again, those school sites were sold off. This Government is getting on with doing the job. But we are not just building schools. We have increased wages and given teacher numbers a massive boost in New South Wales. That is as a direct result of policies that we put in place.

Mr Nathan Hagarty: Point of order: I know those opposite had a problem delivering projects on time, but it appears they cannot deliver amendments on time as well. Can I have some clarity on whether the amendments of the member for Albury have been accepted?

Mr Ra y Williams: Just calm down, it's all right. There are two other speakers to come.

Mr Nathan Hagarty: He is the Assistant Speaker. I am seeking clarification as to whether the tabled amendments were accepted.

The ASSISTANT SPEAKER ( Mr Jason Li ): The amendments have not been moved yet.

Mr Nathan Hagarty: Thank you for the clarification. Two more strikes; I reckon those opposite can do it. All the best!

That the motion be amended by omitting all words after "House" and inserting instead:

(1) Notes the former Coalition Government delivered 213 new and upgraded schools between 2011 and 2023, with a further 106 planned for 2023-2027.

(2) Notes the Minns Labor Government's approach to education investment is to take credit for schools funded and approved by the Coalition, such as Darcy Road Public School, Carlingford West, Cumberland, Girraween, Melrose Park, Parramatta East, Rydalmere, Telopea, Wentworth Point and Westmead.

The one thing that members cannot question is what is in the budgets—current and previous. Budgets tell the tale of the legacy left by the Liberal-Nationals Government between 2011 and 2023. It will come as no surprise to most people across New South Wales that we made a multibillion investment in the upgrading or building of 213 schools. Fifty of those schools were built at a cost of $2 billion in Western Sydney. A $17 billion capital expenditure pipeline was increased by 30 per cent in the 2022-23 Liberal-Nationals budget. That is in contrast to the current 2025-26 budget, with capital expenditure by the Minns Labor Government at a mere 6 per cent. In the years to come there will be a rapid decline once schools are completed and the ribbons are cut on projects that we planned, funded and commenced construction on.

I put on record a few of those 50 schools. Nangamay Public School was completed in March 2023, Nepean Creative and Performing Arts High School was completed in October 2022, Mainsbridge School was completed in October 2022, Jamison High School was completed in April 2022, Greystanes Public School was upgraded and completed in March 2022, Glenmore Park High School was completed in October 2022, and Croydon Public School was upgraded and completed in January 2022. Cranebrook High School was completed in August 2022, Parramatta West Public School was completed in August 2021, Kingswood High School was completed in October 2021, William Stimson Public School was completed in February 2020, Westfields Sports High School—a wonderful school—was completed in August 2020, Pendle Hill Public School was completed in April 2020 and Lidcombe Public School was completed in April 2020.

The ASSISTANT SPEAKER ( Mr Jason Li ): Government members will come to order.

Mr RAY WILLIAMS: Canley Vale High School was completed in July 2020, Arthur Phillip High School in Parramatta was completed in late 2019, Parramatta Public School was completed in January 2020, Russell Lea Public School was completed in April 2019, Rosehill Public School was completed in 2019, Penrith Public School was completed in April 2019 and Merrylands Public School was completed in October 2019. Marie Bashir Public School—named after a fabulous former Governor of New South Wales—was completed in February 2016, Homebush West Public School was completed in January 2019, Claremont Meadows Public School was completed in April 2019, Cecil Hills Public School was completed in October 2019, Auburn North Public School was completed in September 2019, St Clair High School—and there is a list of schools in Penrith—was completed in October 2018.

There are more. The Glenmore Park school was completed in December 2016, Victoria Avenue Public School was completed in February 2015, Pendle Hill High School was completed in early 2023, Jordan Springs Public School was completed in March 2024, Epping West Public School was completed in January 2023, Seven Hills High School was completed in February 2024 and Wentworthville Public School was completed in October 2022. Samuel Gilbert Public School—which I formally represent—was completed in September 2022, Parramatta West Public School was completed in August 2021, Schofields Public School was completed in August 2020, and Riverstone High School—my fabulous old high school—was completed in April 2020. The list is endless. That is just a fraction of the 50 schools that the Liberal-Nationals delivered in government. [ Time expired. ]

The member for Albury spoke about teacher initiatives. Under those initiatives, teachers left the profession when the former Government suppressed their wages for 12 long years under a wages cap, and those members are still promising to bring back the cap. The former Government oversaw record teacher vacancies that exceeded more than 3,300, with resignations outstripping retirements, and 10,000 classes merged or cancelled every day. I am pleased that those days of the now Opposition's teacher incentives are behind us. The Minns Labor Government is determined to rebuild public education to restore confidence, deliver fairness and ensure that every child in New South Wales has access to world-class public education close to where they live.

We are not just making announcements; we are delivering results. Every community deserves schools that are modern, safe and properly equipped to give students the best start in life. Take Ulladulla High School on the South Coast. Members have probably never heard of it. It is a perfect example of what happens when governments talk about education but fail to act. For more than 10 years Ulladulla High School has been overcrowded, with teachers and students doing their very best in conditions that simply have not kept pace with demand. The previous Government did nothing—not one new building, not one additional classroom, not even a plan—despite years of pressure from the community. In Ulladulla and surrounding towns, families do not have the luxury of choice. Some 97 per cent of children attend public education. They do not walk past another school on their way to class. Public education is their only option. That is why it is so important that our public schools are properly funded, properly staffed and properly maintained. When we neglect them, we are not just failing schools; we are failing communities.

The Minns Labor Government is changing that. We are investing in the future of the South Coast with the largest investment in education the electorate has ever seen. We are delivering long overdue upgrades and new facilities where they are needed most. That includes at Ulladulla High School to relieve overcrowding and upgrade infrastructure that has been neglected for far too long; at Milton Public School, where upgrades will provide modern learning spaces for growing enrolments; at Ulladulla Public School to enhance facilities and improve accessibility; at Nowra East Public School to deliver a better environment for students and staff; and at Vincentia High School to remove all the demountables. There will be a new primary school for the growing Worrigee and South Nowra communities. We are also building three new public preschools for Greenwell Point, Nowra East and Sanctuary Point, giving our children and grandchildren the best start to their education.

We are cutting through the bureaucracy that stalled progress for years. We are turning plans into projects and promises into classrooms. We are listening to parents, teachers and communities. We know that the best education system is one built with local voices at its heart. Fixing the education system is not just about infrastructure; it is about fairness, opportunity and belief in our communities and children. It is the belief that every child, no matter where they live, deserves the best start in life. It is the belief that public education is at the heart of a fair and thriving society. It is the belief that government must never stop working to make that a reality. The Minns Labor Government is rebuilding public education, one teacher, one student and one community at a time. When we invest in the future of our children, we invest in the future of New South Wales.

… the department has decided to place Kambora Public School into recess from the beginning of Term 1 2026.

It goes on:

Placing a school in recess means that, while the school grounds and facilities will continue to be maintained, there will be no staff or students attending the school.

That is a school closure. It was reported in the media. I was shocked and heartbroken to learn that a school in my community in metropolitan Sydney is shutting down. The school is the heart of the community. The Sydney Morning Herald reported on the closure of Kambora in an article titled "Parents devastated as axe falls on northern beaches school". I told the Herald:

"Warning signs on enrolments were ignored. Enforcing the local enrolment area was ignored and the community was ignored …

"Closing a metropolitan school in Sydney is, as admitted by Department of Education officials in budget estimates in August 2025, quite a rare occurrence.

"That is the gravity of the situation."

A parent, Donna, also told the newspaper:

"Kambora had the stigma of being a small school, and parents became scared because student numbers kept falling. If we had more support from the department, we wouldn't be in this crisis …

She has now enrolled her daughter in a private school for next year. That is a loss for public school education. Another article by the Manly Observer , "Decision made: Kambora Public School to close", quotes from another parent, Lily:

"The handling of Kambora by the Department has been catastrophic …

"The school community has been left unsupported, families and children have suffered, and the stress inflicted is real and measurable …

Another article by Northside Living , "Kambora to close", states:

Year 4 parent Belinda Mason said there was a lot of anger, resentment and tears. "At the community meeting back in May, we were told we would not be out of pocket,"

…

"No one's taking accountability from the department which is deplorable … Someone needs to take responsibility … our children, families and amazing teachers. It's heartbreaking for us all. Our school is more than a place to learn. It is a place where our children feel safe, supported and respected."

Labor members have come into the Chamber and said they are fixing public education. But what are they doing? They are closing a metropolitan public school in the electorate of Davidson. It is completely heartbreaking and unacceptable. There are no words for it. Labor has form when it comes to closing schools. How many schools did it close when it was previously in government from 1995 to 2011? Was it 50? It was higher. Was it 60, 70, 80? Labor closed 83 schools when it was previously in government from 1995 to 2011. I will go through each year of school closures under Labor during that period. In 1995 eight schools closed; in 1996, four; in 1997, six; in 1998, eight; in 1999, two; in 2000, four; in 2001, five; in 2002, eight; in 2003, two; in 2004, three; in 2005, eight; in 2006, three; in 2007, four; and in 2008, one. In 2009—the year of shame—Labor closed 12 schools. And in 2010 it closed five. That is Labor's record in government. It is continuing that record by closing Kambora Public School in the electorate of Davidson.

That was followed up by the member for Davidson's effort, where he was slowly reading out a bar graph because he had no arguments to make. The member for Kellyville did bring up some work that the previous Government did when it came to public education. However, I will also mention two examples. The first is Denham Court Public School in my electorate, where the brains trust opposite decided to build a school on not one, not two but three gas lines. That means that that site is limited to a thousand persons. The school has reached its enrolment cap. When it has parent teacher nights or its annual presentation—

Mr Ray Williams: You're not allowed to smoke.

Mr NATHAN HAGARTY: You are not allowed to smoke, but half the school also has to leave the premises so that the mums and dads can see their kids get their awards. Then that half of the school has to leave so that the others can come back and get theirs. Now, I am not about just whinging in the Chamber about what those opposite did and their failures. I have solutions. That is why we are building Emerald Hills public school down the road. That is why we have cut the ribbon on Edmondson Park Public School and why we are upgrading Leppington Public School: to take some of the load off Denham Court.

The second example is Edmondson Park High School. The brains trust opposite were going to put that school in a multistorey commercial building opposite the shopping centre at Edmondson Park. The then education Minister, Sarah Mitchell, was asked at the time, "Can you guarantee that there won't be a McDonald's on the ground floor?" She said, "I can neither confirm nor deny whether there is going to be a McDonald's." That is just crazy stuff. But, again, we do not just have complaints; we have solutions. That is why we are building the school on the other side of the train track on a site with plenty of open space and next to the public school. We are thinking, delivering and fixing education in this State.
