That this House:

(1) Notes that the New South Wales Labor Government inherited a teacher shortage crisis from the former Liberal-Nationals Coalition, which saw up to 3,311 teacher vacancies in November 2022 and 10,000 merged and cancelled classes every day.

(2) Supports the removal of the wages cap, which allowed for an historic pay deal for teachers and has resulted in a 61 per cent drop in teacher vacancies from last year to this year in addition to halving the number of merged and cancelled classes.

(3) Supports the building of new and upgraded schools in fast-growing communities, including Emerald Hills, Grantham Farm, West Dapto, Wilton, Tallawong, Wentworthville, Calderwood, Jordan Springs and Leppington, after a decade of neglect by the former Liberal-Nationals Government, which left New South Wales with fewer schools than it started with.

Former Prime Minister Bob Hawke said:

The importance of education and the creation of equality of opportunity in education. These are, to me, the most fundamental things about a decent society.

Education is the great constant. It is where children build friendships, find purpose and begin to understand who they are as a person. As they grow, it becomes the foundation for the adults they will become, shaping how they think, contribute and engage with the wider world. I am a living example of what a strong public education system can do. My dad left school at 14 to become an apprentice carpet layer and help raise his siblings, while my mum left school at 15. In many parts of the world that would have been my path too, whether I liked it or not. But because I had access to a strong public education system, I had the chance to apply myself, go to university and eventually stand in this place.

This is a story shared by several generations across the State and the nation, where education has given families like mine the opportunity to build something better for future generations. However, under the previous Government, that opportunity became harder to reach. On any given day, public schools in this State were short by around 3,000 casual teachers, forcing thousands of classes to be merged, cancelled or left with minimal supervision. Nearly nine in 10 schools reported daily staff shortages, with principals pulled from their offices just to keep classrooms running. Public education funding was slashed, including a $148 million cut that left schools scrambling to meet basic needs; TAFE was gutted and hollowed out by a $196 million shortfall; and campuses were sold off, with hundreds of staff gone. The Liberals even closed schools. There were more public schools in New South Wales when they came to government than when they left. They walked away from their responsibility to provide every community with access to quality public education.

Those were not isolated incidents; they were deliberate choices to underfund, cut and walk away from public education. In doing so, too many students found it harder to access the one thing that could change their lives: a fair go in the classroom. The Minns Labor Government is rebuilding education from the ground up. We abolished the wages cap and delivered the biggest teacher pay rise in a generation, restoring respect, fairness and stability to the profession. We reduced teacher vacancies by 61 per cent, down from 2,460 under the previous Government to just 962 today. We halved the number of merged and cancelled classes, and teacher resignations are now at their lowest level in 13 years. The Government has also invested a record $9 billion in new and upgraded schools—more than at any time in the State's history—with 50 major projects already underway. We are also delivering 100 new public preschools, the biggest expansion of early learning this State has ever seen. The Liberals did not build a single public preschool in their 12 years in government.

I spoke about the number of schools that went down under the previous Government, but it gets worse. Two sites were earmarked as public schools in my electorate of Leppington, but both were relinquished by the former Government. In their place—surprise, surprise—three private schools have purchased those sites. So education will be provided there, but it will not be public education—because we know what the Opposition thinks about that. In 2024 the Government released the NSW Enrolment Growth Audit, which found that the Leppington‑Catherine Field area in my electorate ranked ninth in the entire State for student growth, with enrolments rising by 173 per cent between 2018 and 2023—which is 942 additional students in just five years—far outpacing the population forecasts. The same audit found that dwelling growth was up 98 per cent, nearly doubling from around 3,700 to 7,300. Those numbers tell a pretty obvious story to anyone who cares about public education: Rapid development and swelling enrolments meant that there was a clear need for more schools.

The previous Government failed to act, but this Government is getting on with the job. In Leppington, teacher vacancies are down by more than 55 per cent and six new public preschools are being built, at Eschol Park, Kearns, Robert Townson, Greenway Park, Leppington and Emerald Hills. The Government is also building the first public school for Austral, Leppington and Denham Court, where much of the growth in my electorate has been and at which I was very excited to recently do the sod turn. Thousands of houses have been built in that area over the past decade, and this Government is building its first high school. The Government is also investing in the existing public schools at Leppington, Austral, Greenway Park and Dalmeny as part of a broader statewide effort to match infrastructure with population growth.

I know that is a novel idea to those opposite, but it is something Labor members believe in. We know that education is not just a line item in a budget or a bunch of numbers in a spreadsheet. It is the foundation of opportunity, equality and growth. It lifts families, strengthens communities and builds a fairer State for everybody. Education changed my life, and I want it to change the lives of every child growing up in Leppington and across this great State. This Government is delivering on its mission to provide a stronger, fairer, better-resourced public education system for New South Wales.

Ms Liza Butler: What did you build?

Mr JUSTIN CLANCY: I am going to talk about that. In fact, let me go straight to it. Let us go to Labor's 2023-24 budget papers. This week the Government was out spruiking Western Sydney, where Labor claims to be delivering major projects for schools in Carlingford West, Cumberland High, Darcy Road, Girraween, Melrose Park, Parramatta East, Rydalmere, Telopea and Wentworth Point.

Mr Matt Cross: What does the budget say?

Mr JUSTIN CLANCY: This Government's first budget states, "Ongoing works—new and upgraded schools". Hang on a moment. Those were Coalition schools, weren't they? Some 106 of them were handed on to this Government. Labor members talk about rebuilding and fixing, but all they are good at is cutting the ribbons on projects already funded by the Coalition. They rebrand teacher initiatives as their own and pretend that the system is suddenly working better when they turn up for the photo. The Liberal-Nationals Government invested more than any government in New South Wales history, with a $17.7 billion pipeline, 213 new and upgraded schools delivered and, as I mentioned—as is in the Government's budget papers—106 were in progress when we left office. The Labor budget papers makes for great reading. They also say things like taxation revenue is up 26 per cent in the first two years of this Government; its deficit is up. These are great budget papers to read through in that regard.

This year Labor announced only 15 new or upgraded schools, while our last budget had 23. In our last budget, capital expenditure in education increased by 29 per cent; under Labor that is just 6.7 per cent, a fraction of what is needed to keep pace with enrolment growth. The Premier turned up to open Darcy Road Public School, which is another one in this budget paper listed under "Ongoing works—new and upgraded schools". That is a project entirely funded by the Liberal-Nationals Government, and it was claimed as a Labor success. All Labor members had to do was cut the ribbon. Having said that, there are schools like those in my own community—again announced in 2022, listed in the Labor budget papers—that are yet to see a shovel in the ground. That is again deeply concerning for my community and for a lot of communities across our State. We hear the talk, but we are yet to see the action.

I am pleased that the member for Leppington mentioned Bob Hawke when he talked about teachers. I mention another great Labor colleague in the Federal Government, Minister Jason Clare. As I have said before in this Chamber, he spoke about the post-COVID issue with teachers as being a nationwide crisis. Let us not pretend that it is unique to New South Wales; it is a national—in Victoria and Western Australia—and an international issue. Also, the issue is not just about wages. It is also about retention, workload, behaviour management and support. Our teachers in our electorates are telling us that. Remuneration matters. In fact, the Liberal-Nationals Government went to the last election with $152,000 salary for senior high-end teachers. Members can check this. As of August 2025, the website of those opposite says that same teacher can at the moment expect to be paid $144,000. Labor's problem is that they look for a headline, not a plan. I focus on something important in that regard. The member for Leppington touched on TAFE. I bring it back to early childhood. I ask the member, what is his Government doing for our community preschools?

Mr Warren Kirby: Public preschools in schools.

Mr JUSTIN CLANCY: Even when it is spoken about in the Chamber, those opposite do not hear it. They do not listen. They do not open their ears to the impact on community preschools.

Mr Warren Kirby: One hundred public preschools.

Mr JUSTIN CLANCY: I am happy for the member for Riverstone to talk about public preschools, because he continues to miss the point. He forgets about community preschools, and that is the problem we face. Those opposite sit there and forget everything about community preschools. The ones that are asked to do the heavy lifting should be supported. They are experiencing the pay gap and should be helped along. I move amendments, and I table those amendments— [ Time expired. ]

Looking at the population of The Ponds High School, this year it has 2,207 students enrolled. This year it has 330 students sitting for the HSC; next year that is expected to reach about 400. The neighbouring suburb on the other side of that area is Stanhope Gardens. Again, there was a proposed high school for Stanhope Gardens. Members would think that the previous Government would perhaps build a high school there to alleviate some of the pressure off The Ponds High School. But no, instead, again it relinquished that high school site and sold it off, again resulting in more houses.

It goes on and on with the previous Government. In the list of "Top 20 student enrolment growth areas in New South Wales government schools: 2018-2023", in terms of estimation compared with actual enrolments, Schofields - East was number one and Marsden Park was number two. A public school was opened in Marsden Park in 2021, with capacity for 1,000. But, of course, the school reached student enrolments of 2,000 by 2024. This Government built Melonba Public School and Melonba High School to meet the demand of an area that ranks second highest in New South Wales for student growth, which had increased by almost 1,000 per cent. In 2018 the Marsden Park area had 236 student enrolments. That number had ballooned to 2,493 by 2023, which is the year that those opposite left government.

This story goes on and on in north-west Sydney. Number six in the list was Box Hill-Nelson. The enrolments there had grown from 119 in 2018 to 1,445 in 2023. That is an increase of over 1,100 per cent. What did communities in that area get? They got zero schools. Not a single school was built. It is astonishing that members of the former Government are now running a campaign talking about how under-resourced that area is by our Government. But it was not our Government that let down the good people of Box Hill; it was the former Government and the council that runs that area. Over and over again, the record of the previous Government is deplorable. It can only be put into two baskets: either wilful neglect or gross mismanagement. Take your pick on those.

By contrast, this Government has built or is building nine new schools across north-west Sydney, across those three regions that I mentioned. A public primary school, with a co-located preschool, is almost completed at Nirimba Fields. A primary school in Tallawong is well and truly underway. We have a contract signed for Tallawong high school; that is soon to be built. Box Hill High School will open. In the case of Box Hill Public School, the situation was so acute that we had to build a temporary school to take care of the students while the permanent school is being built. Schools are being built in Marsden Park.

Grantham Farm is another area in the Riverstone electorate that has been exploding in population. Oddly enough, when the announcement was made for the new public school at Grantham Farm—one of my team managed to pull up a news article from 2017 when I was working in the business chamber—that site was also proposed to be sold off by the previous Government. Instead of building new schools, it was adamant that it would sell off the sites that were proposed for schools in the fastest growing area in New South Wales, with tens of thousands of young families moving there. Over and over again, those school sites were sold off. This Government is getting on with doing the job. But we are not just building schools. We have increased wages and given teacher numbers a massive boost in New South Wales. That is as a direct result of policies that we put in place.

Mr Nathan Hagarty: Point of order: I know those opposite had a problem delivering projects on time, but it appears they cannot deliver amendments on time as well. Can I have some clarity on whether the amendments of the member for Albury have been accepted?

Mr Ra y Williams: Just calm down, it's all right. There are two other speakers to come.

Mr Nathan Hagarty: He is the Assistant Speaker. I am seeking clarification as to whether the tabled amendments were accepted.

The ASSISTANT SPEAKER ( Mr Jason Li ): The amendments have not been moved yet.

Mr Nathan Hagarty: Thank you for the clarification. Two more strikes; I reckon those opposite can do it. All the best!

Public education is their only option. That is why it is so important that our public schools are properly funded, properly staffed and properly maintained. When we neglect them, we are not just failing schools; we are failing communities.

The Minns Labor Government is changing that. We are investing in the future of the South Coast with the largest investment in education the electorate has ever seen. We are delivering long overdue upgrades and new facilities where they are needed most. That includes at Ulladulla High School to relieve overcrowding and upgrade infrastructure that has been neglected for far too long; at Milton Public School, where upgrades will provide modern learning spaces for growing enrolments; at Ulladulla Public School to enhance facilities and improve accessibility; at Nowra East Public School to deliver a better environment for students and staff; and at Vincentia High School to remove all the demountables. There will be a new primary school for the growing Worrigee and South Nowra communities. We are also building three new public preschools for Greenwell Point, Nowra East and Sanctuary Point, giving our children and grandchildren the best start to their education.

We are cutting through the bureaucracy that stalled progress for years. We are turning plans into projects and promises into classrooms. We are listening to parents, teachers and communities. We know that the best education system is one built with local voices at its heart. Fixing the education system is not just about infrastructure; it is about fairness, opportunity and belief in our communities and children. It is the belief that every child, no matter where they live, deserves the best start in life. It is the belief that public education is at the heart of a fair and thriving society. It is the belief that government must never stop working to make that a reality. The Minns Labor Government is rebuilding public education, one teacher, one student and one community at a time. When we invest in the future of our children, we invest in the future of New South Wales.

… the department has decided to place Kambora Public School into recess from the beginning of Term 1 2026.

It goes on:

Placing a school in recess means that, while the school grounds and facilities will continue to be maintained, there will be no staff or students attending the school.

That is a school closure. It was reported in the media. I was shocked and heartbroken to learn that a school in my community in metropolitan Sydney is shutting down. The school is the heart of the community. The Sydney Morning Herald reported on the closure of Kambora in an article titled "Parents devastated as axe falls on northern beaches school". I told the Herald:

"Warning signs on enrolments were ignored. Enforcing the local enrolment area was ignored and the community was ignored …

"Closing a metropolitan school in Sydney is, as admitted by Department of Education officials in budget estimates in August 2025, quite a rare occurrence.

"That is the gravity of the situation."

A parent, Donna, also told the newspaper:

"Kambora had the stigma of being a small school, and parents became scared because student numbers kept falling. If we had more support from the department, we wouldn't be in this crisis …

She has now enrolled her daughter in a private school for next year. That is a loss for public school education. Another article by the Manly Observer , "Decision made: Kambora Public School to close", quotes from another parent, Lily:

"The handling of Kambora by the Department has been catastrophic …

"The school community has been left unsupported, families and children have suffered, and the stress inflicted is real and measurable …

Another article by Northside Living , "Kambora to close", states:

Year 4 parent Belinda Mason said there was a lot of anger, resentment and tears. "At the community meeting back in May, we were told we would not be out of pocket,"

…

"No one's taking accountability from the department which is deplorable … Someone needs to take responsibility … our children, families and amazing teachers. It's heartbreaking for us all. Our school is more than a place to learn. It is a place where our children feel safe, supported and respected."

Labor members have come into the Chamber and said they are fixing public education. But what are they doing? They are closing a metropolitan public school in the electorate of Davidson. It is completely heartbreaking and unacceptable. There are no words for it. Labor has form when it comes to closing schools. How many schools did it close when it was previously in government from 1995 to 2011? Was it 50? It was higher. Was it 60, 70, 80? Labor closed 83 schools when it was previously in government from 1995 to 2011. I will go through each year of school closures under Labor during that period. In 1995 eight schools closed; in 1996, four; in 1997, six; in 1998, eight; in 1999, two; in 2000, four; in 2001, five; in 2002, eight; in 2003, two; in 2004, three; in 2005, eight; in 2006, three; in 2007, four; and in 2008, one. In 2009—the year of shame—Labor closed 12 schools. And in 2010 it closed five. That is Labor's record in government. It is continuing that record by closing Kambora Public School in the electorate of Davidson.

That was followed up by the member for Davidson's effort, where he was slowly reading out a bar graph because he had no arguments to make. The member for Kellyville did bring up some work that the previous Government did when it came to public education. However, I will also mention two examples. The first is Denham Court Public School in my electorate, where the brains trust opposite decided to build a school on not one, not two but three gas lines. That means that that site is limited to a thousand persons. The school has reached its enrolment cap. When it has parent teacher nights or its annual presentation—

Mr Ray Williams: You're not allowed to smoke.

Mr NATHAN HAGARTY: You are not allowed to smoke, but half the school also has to leave the premises so that the mums and dads can see their kids get their awards. Then that half of the school has to leave so that the others can come back and get theirs. Now, I am not about just whinging in the Chamber about what those opposite did and their failures. I have solutions. That is why we are building Emerald Hills public school down the road. That is why we have cut the ribbon on Edmondson Park Public School and why we are upgrading Leppington Public School: to take some of the load off Denham Court.

The second example is Edmondson Park High School. The brains trust opposite were going to put that school in a multistorey commercial building opposite the shopping centre at Edmondson Park. The then education Minister, Sarah Mitchell, was asked at the time, "Can you guarantee that there won't be a McDonald's on the ground floor?" She said, "I can neither confirm nor deny whether there is going to be a McDonald's." That is just crazy stuff. But, again, we do not just have complaints; we have solutions. That is why we are building the school on the other side of the train track on a site with plenty of open space and next to the public school. We are thinking, delivering and fixing education in this State.

tree_branches.name: Mr JUSTIN CLANCY
tree_branches.path: Legislative Assembly (2025-10-14) > Public Interest Debate > Public Education > Mr JUSTIN CLANCY
tree_branches.text: Mr JUSTIN CLANCY ( Albury ) —I acknowledge Charles Sturt University as it celebrates 20 years of delivering nursing education at the Albury campus, a milestone that reflects dedication to strengthening our regional healthcare workforce. Since its first intake in 2005, the Bachelor of Nursing program has trained approximately 700 nurses locally, giving aspiring healthcare professionals in the twin cities the opportunity to study and serve close to home. Today, Charles Sturt University stands as the largest provider of registered nursing education in regional Australia, a remarkable achievement. Between 2020 and 2024, an estimated 2,000 students have graduated from the Bachelor of Nursing program, an average of 500 nursing graduates each year. This year alone, over 3,150 students are studying a Bachelor of Nursing through Charles Sturt, with 153 based in Albury-Wodonga. I thank Professor Kerryn Butler-Henderson, Head of Nursing, Paramedicine and Healthcare Sciences, and to the entire teaching and support team, for their role in this success. With 93% of undergraduate and 97 per cent of postgraduate nursing graduates securing full-time employment within four months, Charles Sturt University leads the nation in nursing graduate employability. Congratulations on 20 years of service to our region and beyond!

tree_branches.name: Mr WARREN KIRBY
tree_branches.path: Legislative Assembly (2025-10-14) > Public Interest Debate > Public Education > Mr WARREN KIRBY
tree_branches.text:
Mr WARREN KIRBY ( Riverstone ) ( 17:12 :48 ): The tale of public education failure from the previous Government is highlighted in no better way than in my electorate of Riverstone. I had the pleasure of attending The Ponds High School's tenth anniversary last year. It is interesting to note that it was the last high school built in my electorate. That is rather odd when put into context. In February 2024—the same year as the anniversary—a New South Wales enrolment growth audit handed down by School Infrastructure found that east Schofields, which is The Ponds' neighbouring suburb, had an enrolment growth of more than 210 per cent. In fact, the projected enrolment growth for 2023 was around about 1,500 students; the actual enrolment growth was 4,800 students. The population in the area had exploded. One would think a responsible government's response to that would be to look at the numbers and build new schools there. But what did the previous Government do with the high school site for Schofields high school? It sold the site, which now have houses.

Looking at the population of The Ponds High School, this year it has 2,207 students enrolled. This year it has 330 students sitting for the HSC; next year that is expected to reach about 400. The neighbouring suburb on the other side of that area is Stanhope Gardens. Again, there was a proposed high school for Stanhope Gardens. Members would think that the previous Government would perhaps build a high school there to alleviate some of the pressure off The Ponds High School. But no, instead, again it relinquished that high school site and sold it off, again resulting in more houses.

It goes on and on with the previous Government. In the list of "Top 20 student enrolment growth areas in New South Wales government schools: 2018-2023", in terms of estimation compared with actual enrolments, Schofields - East was number one and Marsden Park was number two. A public school was opened in Marsden Park in 2021, with capacity for 1,000. But, of course, the school reached student enrolments of 2,000 by 2024. This Government built Melonba Public School and Melonba High School to meet the demand of an area that ranks second highest in New South Wales for student growth, which had increased by almost 1,000 per cent. In 2018 the Marsden Park area had 236 student enrolments. That number had ballooned to 2,493 by 2023, which is the year that those opposite left government.

This story goes on and on in north-west Sydney. Number six in the list was Box Hill-Nelson. The enrolments there had grown from 119 in 2018 to 1,445 in 2023. That is an increase of over 1,100 per cent. What did communities in that area get? They got zero schools. Not a single school was built. It is astonishing that members of the former Government are now running a campaign talking about how under-resourced that area is by our Government. But it was not our Government that let down the good people of Box Hill; it was the former Government and the council that runs that area. Over and over again, the record of the previous Government is deplorable. It can only be put into two baskets: either wilful neglect or gross mismanagement. Take your pick on those.

By contrast, this Government has built or is building nine new schools across north-west Sydney, across those three regions that I mentioned. A public primary school, with a co-located preschool, is almost completed at Nirimba Fields. A primary school in Tallawong is well and truly underway. We have a contract signed for Tallawong high school; that is soon to be built. Box Hill High School will open. In the case of Box Hill Public School, the situation was so acute that we had to build a temporary school to take care of the students while the permanent school is being built. Schools are being built in Marsden Park.

Grantham Farm is another area in the Riverstone electorate that has been exploding in population. Oddly enough, when the announcement was made for the new public school at Grantham Farm—one of my team managed to pull up a news article from 2017 when I was working in the business chamber—that site was also proposed to be sold off by the previous Government. Instead of building new schools, it was adamant that it would sell off the sites that were proposed for schools in the fastest growing area in New South Wales, with tens of thousands of young families moving there. Over and over again, those school sites were sold off. This Government is getting on with doing the job. But we are not just building schools. We have increased wages and given teacher numbers a massive boost in New South Wales. That is as a direct result of policies that we put in place.

Mr Nathan Hagarty: Point of order: I know those opposite had a problem delivering projects on time, but it appears they cannot deliver amendments on time as well. Can I have some clarity on whether the amendments of the member for Albury have been accepted?

Mr Ra y Williams: Just calm down, it's all right. There are two other speakers to come.

Mr Nathan Hagarty: He is the Assistant Speaker. I am seeking clarification as to whether the tabled amendments were accepted.

The ASSISTANT SPEAKER ( Mr Jason Li ): The amendments have not been moved yet.

Mr Nathan Hagarty: Thank you for the clarification. Two more strikes; I reckon those opposite can do it. All the best!

tree_branches.text:
Mr RAY WILLIAMS ( Kellyville ) ( 17:19 :25 ): I move:

That the motion be amended by omitting all words after "House" and inserting instead:

(1) Notes the former Coalition Government delivered 213 new and upgraded schools between 2011 and 2023, with a further 106 planned for 2023-2027.

(2) Notes the Minns Labor Government's approach to education investment is to take credit for schools funded and approved by the Coalition, such as Darcy Road Public School, Carlingford West, Cumberland, Girraween, Melrose Park, Parramatta East, Rydalmere, Telopea, Wentworth Point and Westmead.

The one thing that members cannot question is what is in the budgets—current and previous. Budgets tell the tale of the legacy left by the Liberal-Nationals Government between 2011 and 2023. It will come as no surprise to most people across New South Wales that we made a multibillion investment in the upgrading or building of 213 schools. Fifty of those schools were built at a cost of $2 billion in Western Sydney. A $17 billion capital expenditure pipeline was increased by 30 per cent in the 2022-23 Liberal-Nationals budget. That is in contrast to the current 2025-26 budget, with capital expenditure by the Minns Labor Government at a mere 6 per cent. In the years to come there will be a rapid decline once schools are completed and the ribbons are cut on projects that we planned, funded and commenced construction on.

I put on record a few of those 50 schools. Nangamay Public School was completed in March 2023, Nepean Creative and Performing Arts High School was completed in October 2022, Mainsbridge School was completed in October 2022, Jamison High School was completed in April 2022, Greystanes Public School was upgraded and completed in March 2022, Glenmore Park High School was completed in October 2022, and Croydon Public School was upgraded and completed in January 2022. Cranebrook High School was completed in August 2022, Parramatta West Public School was completed in August 2021, Kingswood High School was completed in October 2021, William Stimson Public School was completed in February 2020, Westfields Sports High School—a wonderful school—was completed in August 2020, Pendle Hill Public School was completed in April 2020 and Lidcombe Public School was completed in April 2020.

The ASSISTANT SPEAKER ( Mr Jason Li ): Government members will come to order.

Mr RAY WILLIAMS: Canley Vale High School was completed in July 2020, Arthur Phillip High School in Parramatta was completed in late 2019, Parramatta Public School was completed in January 2020, Russell Lea Public School was completed in April 2019, Rosehill Public School was completed in 2019, Penrith Public School was completed in April 2019 and Merrylands Public School was completed in October 2019. Marie Bashir Public School—named after a fabulous former Governor of New South Wales—was completed in February 2016, Homebush West Public School was completed in January 2019, Claremont Meadows Public School was completed in April 2019, Cecil Hills Public School was completed in October 2019, Auburn North Public School was completed in September 2019, St Clair High School—and there is a list of schools in Penrith—was completed in October 2018.

There are more. The Glenmore Park school was completed in December 2016, Victoria Avenue Public School was completed in February 2015, Pendle Hill High School was completed in early 2023, Jordan Springs Public School was completed in March 2024, Epping West Public School was completed in January 2023, Seven Hills High School was completed in February 2024 and Wentworthville Public School was completed in October 2022. Samuel Gilbert Public School—which I formally represent—was completed in September 2022, Parramatta West Public School was completed in August 2021, Schofields Public School was completed in August 2020, and Riverstone High School—my fabulous old high school—was completed in April 2020. The list is endless. That is just a fraction of the 50 schools that the Liberal-Nationals delivered in government. [ Time expired. ]

tree_branches.name: Ms LIZA BUTLER
tree_branches.path: Legislative Assembly (2025-10-14) > Public Interest Debate > Public Education > Ms LIZA BUTLER
tree_branches.text: Ms LIZA BUTLER ( South Co ast ) —It was a true joy to celebrate Lyrebird Preschool's remarkable milestone - 50 years of nurturing, educating, and inspiring young minds in East Nowra. For half a century, Lyrebird Preschool has been a cornerstone of our community, giving generations of children the best possible start in life through quality early childhood education. This success story began under the leadership of Founding Director, Lola Wilson, whose 25 years of dedication set the standards of excellence that remain today. Lola's vision shaped the preschool's philosophy, from creating the first garden from bare ground to building deep and enduring connections with our local Aboriginal community. The celebration brought together past and present families at the pre-school for a wonderful gathering filled with joy, laughter, and fond memories. It was a heartwarming reflection of just how loved and valued this pre-school is within our community. Director Sharon O'Brien and her passionate team continue this proud legacy by fostering inclusion, creativity, and community spirit for every child and family who walks through their doors. Congratulations to everyone past and present on 50 wonderful years, and here's to the next 50 of learning, laughter, and belonging.

tree_branches.text: Mr MATT CROSS ( Davidson ) —I recognise the leadership of Melissa Brown as Principal of Covenant Christian School from 2020 to 2025. I have visited Covenant Christian School on several occasions and have seen firsthand the supportive and inclusive environment Mrs Brown has fostered. She is well respected from all aspects of our local community, including students, teachers, staff and volunteers. During her six years of service, Mrs Brown has guided the school with a vision underpinned by a Christ-centred educational framework that equips students academically and for lifelong success to help them become confident and well-rounded. We thank Mrs Brown for her faithful service and wish her every success as she continues her PhD studies and future endeavours. I am proud to recognise outstanding leaders like Melissa Brown who inspire the future of education. Thank you for your public service to our community.

tree_branches.text: Mr NATHAN HAGARTY ( Leppington ) ( 17:50 :35 ): I acknowledge CNA Multicultural Services' tenth anniversary. Marking a decade of tireless service to our community, CNA continues to lead with heart, this year dedicating its celebration, 3,000 Minds, to the nearly 3,000 Australians living with MND, and in memory of those lost, including CNA member and former editor of Allora! and my good mate Franco Baldi. tree_branches.text: Mr ROBERT DWYER ( Port Macquarie ) ( 17:51 :35 ): I recognise Jane Wright, who is a dedicated and compassionate First Nations member of the Supporting and Securing Tenancies program overseen by New Horizons Port Macquarie. Jane has helped numerous community members uphold and access tenancies in a challenging market. Her efforts as Aboriginal caseworker continue to strengthen our community and provide hope for many, particularly those experiencing or at risk of homelessness. Jane's commitment includes organising and overseeing her team at the biweekly Our Place hub and the annual Homelessness Week and NAIDOC Week activities. Whether organising activities, advocating on behalf of community members or simply offering a listening ear, Jane leads by example, with humility, kindness and a genuine desire to make a difference. Known for her tireless hard work and leadership, Jane brings warmth, integrity and a deep sense of service to everything she does. I commend Jane for her outstanding service and the positive impact she makes in our community.

tree_branches.text: Mr ROBERT DWYER ( Port Macquarie ) —I rise to recognise David Castleton, a driving force behind the growth and success of the Queens Lake Sailing Club for over two decades. Since joining as a junior sailor in 1997, David has demonstrated unwavering commitment to the sport and the community. His early advocacy saw sailing introduced as a school sport, personally providing boats and mentoring students. In 2013, David joined the committee, securing vital grants to upgrade safety equipment and improve accessibility for volunteers. He also championed junior development, enabling many young sailors to obtain their boat licences. As Commodore since 2015, David led the club through a period of remarkable growth, hosting state and national titles, expanding the fleet of club-owned boats, and launching inclusive 'Try Sailing' programs for all ages and abilities. His leadership saw the removal of hazardous debris from the lake, enhancing safety for all users. David's vision culminated in the successful extension of the clubhouse, providing essential boat storage and supporting family participation. His dedication is evident, from morning sailing sessions to competitive afternoon races, bridging generations with a 70-year age gap among sailors. David's legacy is one of inclusion, opportunity and enduring community spirit.

tree_branches.name: Lynette McFadden
tree_branches.path: Legislative Assembly (2025-10-14) > Community Recognition Statements > Lynette McFadden
tree_branches.text: Ms LIZA BUTLER ( South Coast ) ( 17:52 :40 ): I pay tribute to Lynette McFadden from Ulladulla, who has been named the inaugural emergency volunteer of the year. Lynette is an outstanding member of the Ulladulla unit of the State Emergency Service, where she helps lead, mentor and train her fellow volunteers, who are all dedicated individuals standing ready to protect our community during storms, floods and other emergencies. Now serving as the deputy unit commander of the Ulladulla SES, Lynette's leadership is matched by her depth of expertise, built over many years of committed service. Lynette has developed an impressive skill set that includes logistics, communications, mapping and navigation, land search and rescue, first aid and mental health awareness. Beyond her work with the SES, Lynette has also volunteered with Marine Rescue NSW, further demonstrating her dedication to community safety and service. Lynette McFadden exemplifies the very best of the South Coast's volunteer spirit: being selfless, skilled and always ready to lend a helping hand when it matters most.

tree_branches.name: Ms LIZA BUTLER
tree_branches.path: Legislative Assembly (2025-10-14) > Community Recognition Statements > Lynette McFadden > Ms LIZA BUTLER
tree_branches.text: Ms LIZA BUTLER ( South Co ast ) —It was a true joy to celebrate Lyrebird Preschool's remarkable milestone - 50 years of nurturing, educating, and inspiring young minds in East Nowra. For half a century, Lyrebird Preschool has been a cornerstone of our community, giving generations of children the best possible start in life through quality early childhood education. This success story began under the leadership of Founding Director, Lola Wilson, whose 25 years of dedication set the standards of excellence that remain today. Lola's vision shaped the preschool's philosophy, from creating the first garden from bare ground to building deep and enduring connections with our local Aboriginal community. The celebration brought together past and present families at the pre-school for a wonderful gathering filled with joy, laughter, and fond memories. It was a heartwarming reflection of just how loved and valued this pre-school is within our community. Director Sharon O'Brien and her passionate team continue this proud legacy by fostering inclusion, creativity, and community spirit for every child and family who walks through their doors. Congratulations to everyone past and present on 50 wonderful years, and here's to the next 50 of learning, laughter, and belonging.

tree_branches.name: Bellingen Hospital and Pink Auxiliary
tree_branches.path: Legislative Assembly (2025-10-14) > Community Recognition Statements > Bellingen Hospital and Pink Auxiliary
tree_branches.text: Mr MICHAEL KEMP ( Oxley ) ( 17:53 :41 ): Over the past year the Bellingen Hospital and Pink Auxiliary has gifted an incredible $28,436 worth of equipment and patients' comfort items to the Bellinger River District Hospital. From reclining treatment chairs and vital signs monitors to comfort throws, the donations make a tangible difference to patients' care. This remarkable achievement is made possible by the tireless efforts of the auxiliary's 46 volunteers, who keep Mary's Teahouse running five days a week, creating delicious food. Their creative fundraising and ready-made meals for families and the night staff reflect a dedication that goes far beyond a cafe. The Bellingen Valley is truly fortunate to have such passionate community groups coming together to support our hospitals and the people who really rely on them. I thank the Bellingen Hospital and Pink Auxiliary for everything it does to support our health services and for showing just how much of a difference its generosity makes in bringing comfort to every patient.

tree_branches.name: Mr MICHAEL KEMP
tree_branches.path: Legislative Assembly (2025-10-14) > Community Recognition Statements > Bellingen Hospital and Pink Auxiliary > Mr MICHAEL KEMP
tree_branches.text: Mr MICHAEL KEMP ( Oxley ) —Since the age of 12, Leyesha Campbell, a proud Dunghutti woman from Kempsey, has faced the realities of kidney disease. Diagnosed with end-stage renal failure as a child, she has undergone dialysis, treatment, and even a transplant - yet she has never let her illness define her. Instead, this extraordinary young woman has turned her experience into a mission to strengthen Aboriginal healthcare. I had the privilege of meeting Leyesha through the NSW Parliament's Young Aboriginal Leaders Program, where she delivered a powerful speech on the urgent need for better health outcomes for Aboriginal people living with kidney disease. Her courage, her determination, and her vision left a deep impression. Through her social platform, Leyesha's Journey, she shares advice, encouragement, and her lived experience. Beyond that, she contributes as a research assistant at the University of Sydney, helping to shape clinical guidelines that ensure care is culturally safe and accessible for Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander patients. Leyesha's story is a reminder that we must do more to deliver world-class healthcare in regional areas. She embodies resilience, leadership, and hope for young people across our communities.

tree_branches.name: Indian Crescent Society of Australia
tree_branches.path: Legislative Assembly (2025-10-14) > Community Recognition Statements > Indian Crescent Society of Australia
tree_branches.text: Mr JIHAD DIB ( Bankstown — Minister for Customer Service and Digital Government, Minister for Emergency Services, and Minister for Youth Justice ) ( 17:54 :38 ): I was proud to attend the Indian Cresent Society of Australia's eighth annual interfaith and social cohesion event, Interfaith Solidarity in Conflict—Building Peace through Shared Humanity. The event brought together faith leaders, political leaders, government agencies, community representatives and others to share in meaningful dialogue, cultural expression and connection. At a time when global conflict is rising, this gathering reminded us of the power of unity and compassion across faiths. Discussions throughout the event explored how shared human values can help build peace, even in times of deep social tension. With recent public commentary about Indian immigration as well as other migration to Australia and growing division around the world, it was heartening and important to see so many people coming together to focus on what unites us. The decline in global peace over the past decade and the economic and human cost of conflicts highlight just how important events like this are. Interfaith dialogue is part of the solution; it builds bridges, fosters respect and strengthens communities. I give huge thanks to President Abbas Alvi and the amazing organising committee for their tireless work. Their efforts are helping to build a more understanding, compassionate Australia.

tree_branches.name: Make-A-Wish Australia
tree_branches.path: Legislative Assembly (2025-10-14) > Community Recognition Statements > Make-A-Wish Australia
tree_branches.text: Mr MICHAEL REGAN ( Wakehurst ) ( 17:55 :46 ): I offer massive congratulations to Make-A-Wish Australia on reaching a remarkable milestone of 40 years of granting life-changing wishes to children with critical illness. Since its founding in 1985, the organisation has transformed the lives of over 11,000 children, bringing hope and joy to families across the nation during the toughest of times. Last month I was lucky enough to join its gala celebrations and hear heartwarming stories of wishes come true, from dream holidays to fairy tea parties and unforgettable meet-and-greets with sporting legends and many other celebrities. This incredible achievement would not have been possible without the unwavering dedication of the Wish Force team of volunteers, who work tirelessly to make wishes come true. I particularly thank the heroes of the Sydney North volunteer crew, who have made a huge impact on the lives of sick children in my community, including the family of one of my staff members. Here's to 40 years of pure magic. May the foundation continue to spark joy for the brave children battling critical illness across our country. The world is brighter because of them.

tree_branches.name: Aunty Lindy Lawler
tree_branches.path: Legislative Assembly (2025-10-14) > Community Recognition Statements > Aunty Lindy Lawler
tree_branches.text: Ms ANNA WATSON ( Shellharbour ) ( 17:56 :45 ): I acknowledge Aunty Lindy Lawler and congratulate her on receiving the Outstanding Contribution to Reconciliation (Aboriginal) award at the 2025 Local Government Regional NAIDOC Awards. Aunty Lindy's powerful voice and relentless advocacy for Indigenous people have been a driving force in building a more just, inclusive and culturally respectful community. Her work within the broader community reflects her deep care for others and her commitment to truth-telling, healing and change. Aunty Lindy creates safe spaces for young people to learn, speak and grow, always empowering them with pride in who they are and where they come from. On behalf of the Shellharbour electorate, I thank Aunty Lindy for her tireless work and congratulate her on being awarded the Outstanding Contribution to Reconciliation (Aboriginal) award at the 2025 Local Government Regional NAIDOC Awards.

tree_branches.name: Ms ANNA WATSON
tree_branches.path: Legislative Assembly (2025-10-14) > Community Recognition Statements > Aunty Lindy Lawler > Ms ANNA WATSON
tree_branches.text: Ms ANNA WATSON ( Shellharbour ) —I would like to acknowledge and congratulate Amanda Kowalczyk from Koonawarra Public School on receiving the Secretary's Award for Excellent Service. Amanda's tireless dedication and outstanding contributions to her school community have made a lasting impact on students, staff, and families alike. Her professionalism, compassion, and unwavering commitment to public education are truly commendable. This award is a reflection of her leadership and the care she brings to her role each day. On behalf of the Shellharbour electorate, I would congratulate Amanda on her amazing work and for being awarded the Secretary's Award for Excellent Service. The recognition is so well deserved, and I know the entire electorate joins me in celebrating her success.

tree_branches.name: Bella Power
tree_branches.path: Legislative Assembly (2025-10-14) > Community Recognition Statements > Bella Power
tree_branches.text: Mrs TANYA DAVIES ( Badgerys Creek ) ( 17:57 :42 ): I am pleased to commend and recognise St Clair High School Captain Bella Power for her outstanding leadership and compassion through many important initiatives. Last month Bella participated in Lifeline's Out of the Shadows walk, an important national initiative that raises funds and awareness for suicide prevention and mental health support, in which she walked 25 kilometres in one week and raised $762 for Lifeline. Bella's value of service and the strength of her character are evident from her consistent and long history of leadership, from serving on the student representative council in year 7 through to her position as school captain. Bella's outstanding commitment to service was recognised with her obtaining the Penrith Young Champions senior leadership award, presented by Rainbow Crossings. On behalf of my electorate of Badgerys Creek and the Parliament, I thank and commend Bella Power and wish her the very best in the future as she continues to work to secure a better life for those struggling with mental illness.

tree_branches.name: Mrs TANYA DAVIES
tree_branches.path: Legislative Assembly (2025-10-14) > Community Recognition Statements > Bella Power > Mrs TANYA DAVIES
tree_branches.text: Mrs TANYA DAVIES ( Badgerys Creek ) —I commend and congratulate Kris Hudswell on her retirement as the Principal of Blackwell Public School, after 25 years of distinguished service in this role. Her retirement coincided with her birthday of 25 August 2025. Mrs Hudswell's exceptional dedication to the education and development of her students leaves a lasting impact and her legacy will remain. One of her many initiatives included the Blackwell Buddies group, which is a precursor to kindergarten and is a 10-week program where local children who are scheduled to attend Blackwell Public School the following year for kindergarten can experience the school. On behalf of my electorate of Badgerys Creek, I thank Mrs Hudswell for her outstanding service to her students and the school community, and I wish her the very best in the next chapter of her life.

tree_branches.name: Sam Alidousti
tree_branches.path: Legislative Assembly (2025-10-14) > Community Recognition Statements > Sam Alidousti
tree_branches.text: Mr STEPHEN BALI ( Blacktown ) ( 17:58 :49 ): Congratulations to Sam Alidousti of Instant Solar on winning Business Person of the Year in the Blacktown City Local Business Awards. Sam has been operating since 2017, and this is his first nomination and first win. Sam's overnight success has been many years in the making and is the result of his hard work, dedication and professionalism, which is on display in our community. Sam is incredibly grateful to have been recognised in this way—it is no doubt a well-deserved boost to his recognition in the field. Sam humbly accredits his amazing career to his colleagues and employees, who pay meticulous attention to design preparation, installation, safety and handover to the satisfied customers. It is not about the speed of installation but the quality that lasts decades. I congratulate Sam Alidousti on his amazing accomplishment. May this award serve to motivate him to his next milestone and business success.

tree_branches.name: Mr STEPHEN BALI
tree_branches.path: Legislative Assembly (2025-10-14) > Community Recognition Statements > Sam Alidousti > Mr STEPHEN BALI
tree_branches.text:
Mr STEPHEN BALI ( Blacktown ) ( 20:19 :18 ): I speak about a new plan that has been tabled for consultation with the community called the Blacktown development control plan [DCP]. It is an opportunity to reset the policies for developers and future development, and let the public have their say in how they would like their CBD to look into the future. As the member for Riverstone is in the Chamber, I put on record that he has been advocating for the State Government to work with the council and the community in developing a DCP or master plan for the Riverstone area, which is a good way to progress.

Western Sydney has been developing at a fast pace and, unfortunately, the City of Blacktown—for whatever reason—has been left off, even though it is the fastest growing area. Everyone likes to give that title to themselves, but Blacktown is the fastest growing local government area in Australia. Some 12,000 people a year have consistently moved in over the past 10 years, according to the Australian Bureau of Statistics. Yet Liverpool, Campbelltown, Fairfield, Parramatta, Castle Hill and Penrith have all developed, and Blacktown has unfortunately been overlooked.

That, in itself, is probably an advantage. It is a disadvantage at the moment for people living in the area, but it is an advantage in that, given a brownfield site with a limited number of owners in certain areas, we have an opportunity to produce the city of the future. By 2035, Blacktown's population will exceed Tasmania's, but we do not have a Hobart or a Darwin to call home in the middle of Blacktown CBD. This is our opportunity to make a difference. Whether it is a night-time economy, live music or town squares, it is so important to get the people involved. What can make Blacktown different? Blacktown's 188 different nationalities and love for festivals are important aspects that should be incorporated, especially if we can wrap them into a CBD area.

I remember being on holidays in Bydgoszcz in Poland. There is a town square of about 100 metres by 110 metres. You can fit 10,000 to 12,000 people into the city centre for an exciting time. There is no CBD in the Sydney Basin that has that type of town square right in the middle of it. We could actually do that in Blacktown, with the major railway lines, bus routes et cetera that connect to it. Blacktown could be the festival capital of the Sydney Basin. Look at the success of the Ramadan festivals where, if people want to go anywhere near Lakemba, they need to park three suburbs away. Imagine building it in the Blacktown area, where there is plenty of potential parking onsite.

Unfortunately, council sold six acres—or 25,000 square metres—right in the middle of Blacktown to Walker Corporation, which wants to convert some of that area. It has put out a DCP that aims to convert Flushcombe Road, which is a major thoroughfare, into a pedestrian mall. They were exciting back in the 1980s. So many streets were converted into pedestrian malls right across Western Sydney, and most of them have been converted back into streets, including those in Blacktown and Penrith et cetera. But no traffic plan or supporting documents are supplied with the Blacktown City Council's DCP. It talks about parking that meets 25 per cent of the current needs.

Westpoint shopping centre, which covers 110,000 square metres—a pretty big shopping centre—currently has 4,600 car parking spaces. According to the proposed DCP, the maximum number of car parking spaces that an equivalent shopping centre will require is 1,400. The Walker proposal is $2.5 billion. It is about two to three times the size of the existing Westpoint, and yet it is going to have a quarter of the car parking spaces. The DCP actually talks about maximum car parking spaces. It does not have a minimum, so a new shopping centre could be brought into Blacktown with zero parking. This is the opportunity for the people of Blacktown to speak out. We want good, sustainable development. We need to have a proper thoroughfare. People have until Friday to put in their submissions. Let us get this deferred and have better public consultation.

The House adjourned, pursuant to standing and sessional orders, at 20:24 until Wednesday 15 October 2025 at 10:00.

tree_branches.name: Tribute to Dr William "Bill" Costello, OAM
tree_branches.path: Legislative Assembly (2025-10-14) > Community Recognition Statements > Tribute to Dr William "Bill" Costello, OAM
tree_branches.text: Mr RICHIE WILLIAMSON ( Clarence ) ( 17:59 :49 ): I acknowledge the passing of a true gentleman, the late Dr William Costello, OAM. Bill was one of the Clarence Valley's most distinguished citizens, with a long career as a surgeon at Grafton Base Hospital, where he left his mark on countless patients and families as well as the dedicated health professionals he worked with. Born in 1926, Dr Costello studied medicine before beginning a career that would span decades. Bill was an environmentalist, and a lover of beef cattle, his family and his patients. He was recognised for his service with the Medal of the Order of Australia in 1998 and the Centenary Medal in 2003, which honoured both his medical and his agricultural contributions. Dr Costello is survived by his wife, Margaret, their children and grandchildren, and a community that will long cherish his legacy in both medicine and agriculture. I thank Bill. May he rest in peace.

tree_branches.name: Mr RICHIE WILLIAMSON
tree_branches.path: Legislative Assembly (2025-10-14) > Community Recognition Statements > Tribute to Dr William "Bill" Costello, OAM > Mr RICHIE WILLIAMSON
tree_branches.text: Mr RICHIE WILLIAMSON ( Clarence ) —I acknowledge the incredible success of this year's Brooms to Bowlo Charity Day for Cystic Fibrosis, organised by Raine & Horne Maclean, Yamba and Iluka, together with the Yamba Bowling Club. On Sunday 3 August, the community once again rallied in a sea of red, walking from Brooms Head to Yamba and gathering at the Bowlo for a day of fundraising and fellowship. This year's event raised $22,292, bringing the total funds raised since 2008 to an extraordinary $133,000+ in support of Cystic Fibrosis Australia. The day was made possible thanks to the dedication of the organising team, the generosity of 67 local businesses and families, and the many volunteers who gave their time to ensure the event's smooth running. From the stunning 23-kilometre walk through Yuraygir National Park, to the family fun, raffles, auctions and entertainment, the Clarence Valley community showed once again what can be achieved when it walks together for a cause that touches so many lives. I congratulate Raine & Horne, Yamba Bowling Club, and everyone who took part in this remarkable day. Your efforts not only raised vital funds but showcased the true heart of our community.

tree_branches.name: Our Lady Queen of Peace Festa
tree_branches.path: Legislative Assembly (2025-10-14) > Community Recognition Statements > Our Lady Queen of Peace Festa
tree_branches.text: Dr HUGH McDERMOTT ( Prospect ) ( 18:00 :56 ): On 28 September I was delighted to join Our Lady Queen of Peace Parish, Greystanes, for the sixtieth anniversary of the OLQP Festa. The festa is a joyful celebration of Our Lady Queen of Peace. Originating in the historic Maltese community of Greystanes in 1965, it has become a truly multicultural festival, connecting our diverse community. At this year's festival, we were blessed to welcome His Excellency Most Reverend Father Anthony Teuma, Bishop of Gozo. I was pleased to join Bishop Teuma; reverend fathers; Anneliese Sammut, Consul-General of Malta in Sydney; and the OLQP Parish community for the procession of the statue of Our Lady. I even joined the strong, young parishioners carrying Our Lady's statue along the procession—albeit only for a short time, and I still carry the bruises. Festivities continued into the night, celebrating with delicious Maltese food, live music and fireworks. I congratulate parish priest Father Paul, festa chair Susanne Hatzis, treasurer Lisa Bright and our dedicated volunteers at OLQP Parish on a wonderful celebration of faith and community.

tree_branches.name: Dr HUGH McDERMOTT
tree_branches.path: Legislative Assembly (2025-10-14) > Community Recognition Statements > Our Lady Queen of Peace Festa > Dr HUGH McDERMOTT
tree_branches.text: Dr HUGH McDERMOTT ( Prospect ) —On Sunday 28th September, I was delighted to meet with volunteers and parishioners from Wentworthville Anglican Church and present them with a Community Building Partnership grant. Established more than a century ago in 1919, Wenty Anglican is an historic faith-based community located in the heart of our local Prospect Electorate. Today, the Church conducts English and Tamil language church services on Sundays and operate numerous community-focused services, including language classes for new migrants. Their community garden caters especially to refugees with a history of trauma and marginalised individuals from culturally diverse and disadvantaged backgrounds. This year, Wenty Anglican successfully applied for a Community Building Partnership grant of $42,562 to supply and install reverse cycle air conditioning units for their main auditorium. This grant will ensure that parishioners attending church services and community functions can operate comfortably through the colder and the warmer months. On the day, I joined the Wenty Anglican family during their Sunday service, to pray together and to connect afterwards for morning tea. Thank you David Misztal, Pastor, and all parishioners and volunteers at Wentworthville Anglican Church for your continued service and amazing community spirit.

tree_branches.name: Penny Mackay
tree_branches.path: Legislative Assembly (2025-10-14) > Community Recognition Statements > Penny Mackay
tree_branches.text: Dr JOE McGIRR ( Wagga Wagga ) ( 18:0 1 :01 ): If helping students into great careers is one mark of an excellent teacher, then Kildare Catholic College's Penny Mackay is at the top of the class. Ms Mackay, who began her working life in the hospitality sector, was recently named Vocational Education Teacher/Trainer of the Year in hospitality and business at the NSW Training Awards. It is fitting recognition for the talented teacher, who discovered a passion for training while working in hospitality and, as a teacher, has played a key role in helping students to explore vocational education training options while they complete their Higher School Certificate. It is a great way for students to make informed decisions when they leave school. Keen to end any separation of vocational education and training from the rest of the school, she is working on new courses that will create a more inclusive learning environment. Ms Mackay is now in the running for a national vocational education training award to be announced in Darwin, and our community is behind her as she continues to create the workforce of the future. I congratulate and thank Penny Mackay, an outstanding teacher.

tree_branches.name: Maitland Pickers Rugby League Club
tree_branches.path: Legislative Assembly (2025-10-14) > Community Recognition Statements > Maitland Pickers Rugby League Club
tree_branches.text: Ms JENNY AITCHISON ( Maitland — Minister for Regional Transport, and Minister for Roads ) ( 18:0 2 :08 ): It is not quite Halloween but it was a pumpkin picker's nightmare for the Cessnock Goannas. I acknowledge that the member for Cessnock is leaving the Chamber—just like we kicked them off the field. The Pickers first grade team made history, defeating the Cessnock Goannas 30-8 in the grand final and securing their fourth consecutive Newcastle Rugby League premiership—the first time any club has achieved that feat. I acknowledge the leadership of head coach Matt Lantry, whose vision, dedication and commitment to excellence have been central to the team's sustained success. But the day did not end there. The reserve grade team delivered a dominant performance to claim the premiership, while the women's tackle team made history of their own, winning the grand final and showcasing the incredible growth and talent in women's rugby league across our region. I thank every single player, coach, volunteer and supporter for their passion and hard work. I congratulate the mighty Maitland Pickers. The pumpkins are on us.

tree_branches.name: Ms JENNY AITCHISON
tree_branches.path: Legislative Assembly (2025-10-14) > Community Recognition Statements > Maitland Pickers Rugby League Club > Ms JENNY AITCHISON
tree_branches.text: Ms JENNY AITCHISON ( Maitland — Minister for Regional Transport, and Minister for Roads ) —VALE Judy Nicholson, a pivotal member of the Maitland Historical Society and past Local History Librarian, who passed away suddenly in August. Judy made a huge contribution to several local organisations, including Maitland's Australian Museum of Clothing and Textiles. Members of these organisations recently gathered to remember Judy's tireless work for her community. This includes her role as the editor of the Historical Society's quarterly bulletin. Judy made sure she left a detailed "template", making the job of those who will follow so much easier. Judy was also a valued volunteer with the Friends of Grossman and Brough Houses, where she generously shared her passion for history and community. Before Judy retired and started her volunteering career, she worked in the local history section of Maitland City Council library. She was always extremely helpful in answering questions and providing research material to curious community members. I join the Maitland community in remembering Judy's important contribution and mark her sad passing.

tree_branches.name: Middle Dural Rural Fire Brigade
tree_branches.path: Legislative Assembly (2025-10-14) > Community Recognition Statements > Middle Dural Rural Fire Brigade
tree_branches.text: Mr MARK HODGES ( Castle Hill ) ( 18:0 3 :15 ): I recently attended the Middle Dural Rural Fire Brigade eightieth anniversary event. The celebration and acknowledgement of the eightieth anniversary was held at Dural on 23 August 2025. To acknowledge the anniversary, long-term Middle Dural local Ian McArthur, who has two family members serving in the Middle Dural brigade, wrote a book. Titled The First 80 Y ears , the book tells the story of the much-loved community organisation. Former captains Jim Smith and Len Best spent many hours collating information for the wonderful book. It contains a collection of stories told from the perspectives of captains and firefighters, and shows how one brigade in the Hills district has made a positive difference to the lives of many people in our society. I acknowledge and thank every member who has served in the Middle Dural Rural Fire Brigade over the past 80 years.

tree_branches.name: Mr MARK HODGES
tree_branches.path: Legislative Assembly (2025-10-14) > Community Recognition Statements > Middle Dural Rural Fire Brigade > Mr MARK HODGES
tree_branches.text: Mr MARK HODGES ( Castle Hill ) —I congratulate the Australian Chinese Wushu (Kung Fu) Culture Association Inc. on the outstanding success of the Australia Kung Fu & Tai Chi Festival, held on 20 September 2025 in Castle Hill. It was a pleasure to attend this wonderful celebration, which brought together martial arts masters, families, and community in a spirit of friendship and mutual respect. The festival showcased the grace and discipline of traditional Chinese martial arts. It was inspiring to see so many people of all backgrounds participating, learning, and sharing in the joy of cultural exchange. I particularly wish to acknowledge Yunkuo Wang and Pablo Barreto, the President and Treasurer of the Australian Chinese Wushu (Kung Fu) Culture Association, as well as Vicky Jiang, Festival Host, whose leadership and enthusiasm were central to the event's success. Their dedication to promoting cultural understanding through the arts continues to strengthen community bonds within The Hills and beyond. The festival was a truly uplifting example of culture in action. The festival was a wonderful contribution to our community. The festival allowed our multicultural community to come together to enjoy and celebrate shared cultural, community and friendship.

tree_branches.name: Palm Grove Ourimbah Creek Landcare
tree_branches.path: Legislative Assembly (2025-10-14) > Community Recognition Statements > Palm Grove Ourimbah Creek Landcare
tree_branches.text: Mr DAVID MEHAN ( The Entrance ) ( 18:0 4 :07 ): I congratulate the Palm Grove Ourimbah Creek Landcare group, which celebrated its twenty-fifth birthday. The group was handed stewardship of a 24-hectare reserve situated on Ourimbah Creek Road next to the M1 motorway by Transport of NSW on 2 October 2000. The key focus of the group has been restoring the rainforest in that area, which was formerly farmland, to its original state, and it now has an abundance of wildlife that is enjoyed by all nature lovers, from birdwatchers to environment and conservation students, runners and walkers. Over the years, contributions by individuals and organisations such as council, Local Land Services, NSW Environmental Trust, Bangalow Bushland Management and WIRES have made the reserve an oasis of biodiversity. The four founding members—Eileen and Brian Paterson, Ray Galway and Ian Playford—were thanked recently at a special morning tea for their hard work and love over the past 25 years. On behalf of our community, I thank them for their work. I encourage members to become involved in their local Landcare group.

Mr DAVID MEHAN ( The Entrance ) ( 19:25 :55 ): On 10 October 1970, Fiji gained its independence, charting its own path as a sovereign nation and ending its status as a Crown colony of the British Empire. Each year since, Fijians across the globe have come together to honour that moment and to celebrate their culture, resilience and contribution to the world, and for the Fijian diaspora to remember their homeland. On Saturday 11 October, I was honoured to represent the Central Coast community and the New South Wales Government at celebrations held at Memorial Park in The Entrance to mark Fiji Independence Day. Celebrations were filled with colour, laughter, music and lots of wonderful food. It was wonderful to see so many families, young people and Elders coming together, united not only by their history but also by a shared hope for the future. It was wonderful to see so many people from my Central Coast community experience Fiji's culture and its history.

My position as an elected representative has provided several opportunities to engage with our Pacific family, including being involved in this Parliament's twin relationship with the Bougainville House of Representatives and serving as an election observer at the last election of the National Parliament of Solomon Islands. In the context of those experiences, it is important to reflect honestly on the journey of Australia's relationship with our Pacific family. During the Morrison Liberal-Nationals Government, relations between Australia and many Pacific nations became strained. Pacific leaders openly described Australia's approach as arrogant. They were frustrated by a perceived lack of respect and understanding, particularly around issues like climate change and regional partnership.

I recall the 2019 Pacific Islands Forum, when then Fijian Prime Minister Frank Bainimarama said, "After what we went through with Morrison, nothing can be worse than him." Those were difficult words to hear—especially for Scott Morrison, I am sure—but they were necessary ones. They remind us that true friendship requires listening, humility, action and a regard for your neighbour. The Pacific being "our backyard" was a term used by many members of the commentariat and the media—particularly the right-wing and Murdoch media— which I do not think helped Australia's relationship with the countries in that region.

Under the current Albanese Labor Government, we have seen a real shift and a reset in tone and substance. There is now a renewed focus on partnership rather than paternalism, on respect rather than rhetoric. Australia's re-engagement with the Pacific as part of our shared region has supported climate resilience, education, security and economic opportunity, all while listening to the priorities that Pacific nations have set. Renewed support for Pacific-led priorities like climate change is helping to rebuild trust and reaffirm Australia's place in the region as a respectful, reliable partner.

We face common challenges, and I feel there is more we can do as good neighbours to support our Pacific family. Almost 60 per cent of the roughly three million small island state peoples, including those of Fiji, Solomon Islands and Bougainville, live within one kilometre of the coastline and 90 per cent within five kilometres. Those people should be able to look to Australia as a refuge and for a helping hand should sea levels continue to rise at the current rate of three to five millimetres per year, as they are expected to do. Our response to the threats faced by our neighbours should be shaped by our common humanity, social solidarity and not only by considerations framed around national defence. The Pacific is not on the periphery of who we are; it is at the heart of our identity. I wish all members of the Central Coast Fijian community a very happy Fiji Independence Day. I thank John and President Va for their hospitality on the day. I look forward to working with all members of the Pacific family to strengthen our common humanity and build a better world.

tree_branches.name: Sapphire Speed Shear
tree_branches.path: Legislative Assembly (2025-10-14) > Community Recognition Statements > Sapphire Speed Shear
tree_branches.text: Mr BR ENDAN MOYLAN ( Northern Tablelands ) ( 18:0 5 :11 ): I recognise the Sapphire Speed Shear committee of Inverell for the great success of the first ever Sapphire Speed Shear, held at the Royal Hotel at Inverell. The day included a number of shearing categories, an auction, a raffle, a Calcutta and face-painting activities, and everyone had an absolutely cracking day. I congratulate all involved on using the event to raise awareness of mental health and on raising just under $12,000 on the day. I commend the committee for planning the speed shear in only three months, managing to secure 23 sponsors and drawing in over 45 entrants from across the Northern Tablelands. Special thanks to the committee members for staging the event, including Peter Handebo at the helm, Ty Glendinning, Steph Yarnold, Melanie Edwards, Matthew Edwards, Khloe Edwards, Clinton Materson and Daniel Bergantin. Each gave their time voluntarily and worked tirelessly to ensure that the shear ran smoothly. I thank everyone involved—it was a fantastic event.

tree_branches.name: Mr BRENDAN MOYLAN
tree_branches.path: Legislative Assembly (2025-10-14) > Community Recognition Statements > Sapphire Speed Shear > Mr BRENDAN MOYLAN
tree_branches.text: Mr BRENDAN MOYLAN ( Northern Tablelands ) —I recognise the many achievements of Inverell local Josh Cathie. Josh is an extraordinary young leader, whose achievements speak volumes about his integrity, drive and generosity. His leadership, initiative and dedication have made him a standout figure in the Inverell Shire and beyond. I congratulate Josh on his prestigious Minister's Award for Excellence in Student Achievement. Josh has been a vital member of the Inverell Youth Advisory Council for the past 3 years and was Chair for the last 12 months. Beyond this work, Josh is a committed member of the Inverell Toastmasters and has excelled in public speaking competitions. Honing his communication skills has allowed Josh to organise several charity events, which are reflective of his compassionate nature. Josh also serves as a corporal in the Australian Air Force Cadets, demonstrating his leadership skills, discipline, responsibility and a strong sense of service. I commend Josh on his achievements and the role model he presents for the youth in the region, and he is a shining example of what can be accomplished through hard work and dedication.

tree_branches.name: Paul Wilson
tree_branches.path: Legislative Assembly (2025-10-14) > Community Recognition Statements > Paul Wilson
tree_branches.text: Ms MARYANNE STUART ( Heathcote ) ( 18:0 6 :09 ): Paul Wilson is the director of M&G Truck Curtain Repairs, but his impact reaches far beyond his business. Paul utilises his position to engage with young people who have been suspended from school or are struggling to find employment, giving them the chance to learn practical skills like sewing curtain buckles and plastic welding. More than that, he is helping them build life skills, purpose and structure when they need it most. Paul is also a long-serving member of the Garie Surf Life Saving Club, dedicating 15 years to keeping the beaches of Garie and Wattamolla safe. His family has long been part of the Little Garie Cabin Community, where he plays an active role through the local Landcare group, tackling fire hazards, improving water quality, supporting bush regeneration and stabilising dunes. Beyond that—and symbolic of his energy, teamwork and being a firm foundation for those around him—Paul and his wife, Renee, are part of the Legacy cheerleading team that won gold at the State championships in September. Loyal, dependable and always there to help, Paul truly embodies a spirit of community worthy of recognition in this place.
