tree_branches.text:
Mr DAVID MEHAN ( The Entrance ) ( 19:25 :55 ): On 10 October 1970, Fiji gained its independence, charting its own path as a sovereign nation and ending its status as a Crown colony of the British Empire. Each year since, Fijians across the globe have come together to honour that moment and to celebrate their culture, resilience and contribution to the world, and for the Fijian diaspora to remember their homeland. On Saturday 11 October, I was honoured to represent the Central Coast community and the New South Wales Government at celebrations held at Memorial Park in The Entrance to mark Fiji Independence Day. Celebrations were filled with colour, laughter, music and lots of wonderful food. It was wonderful to see so many families, young people and Elders coming together, united not only by their history but also by a shared hope for the future. It was wonderful to see so many people from my Central Coast community experience Fiji's culture and its history.

My position as an elected representative has provided several opportunities to engage with our Pacific family, including being involved in this Parliament's twin relationship with the Bougainville House of Representatives and serving as an election observer at the last election of the National Parliament of Solomon Islands. In the context of those experiences, it is important to reflect honestly on the journey of Australia's relationship with our Pacific family. During the Morrison Liberal-Nationals Government, relations between Australia and many Pacific nations became strained. Pacific leaders openly described Australia's approach as arrogant. They were frustrated by a perceived lack of respect and understanding, particularly around issues like climate change and regional partnership.

I recall the 2019 Pacific Islands Forum, when then Fijian Prime Minister Frank Bainimarama said, "After what we went through with Morrison, nothing can be worse than him." Those were difficult words to hear—especially for Scott Morrison, I am sure—but they were necessary ones. They remind us that true friendship requires listening, humility, action and a regard for your neighbour. The Pacific being "our backyard" was a term used by many members of the commentariat and the media—particularly the right-wing and Murdoch media— which I do not think helped Australia's relationship with the countries in that region.

Under the current Albanese Labor Government, we have seen a real shift and a reset in tone and substance. There is now a renewed focus on partnership rather than paternalism, on respect rather than rhetoric. Australia's re-engagement with the Pacific as part of our shared region has supported climate resilience, education, security and economic opportunity, all while listening to the priorities that Pacific nations have set. Renewed support for Pacific-led priorities like climate change is helping to rebuild trust and reaffirm Australia's place in the region as a respectful, reliable partner.

We face common challenges, and I feel there is more we can do as good neighbours to support our Pacific family. Almost 60 per cent of the roughly three million small island state peoples, including those of Fiji, Solomon Islands and Bougainville, live within one kilometre of the coastline and 90 per cent within five kilometres. Those people should be able to look to Australia as a refuge and for a helping hand should sea levels continue to rise at the current rate of three to five millimetres per year, as they are expected to do. Our response to the threats faced by our neighbours should be shaped by our common humanity, social solidarity and not only by considerations framed around national defence. The Pacific is not on the periphery of who we are; it is at the heart of our identity. I wish all members of the Central Coast Fijian community a very happy Fiji Independence Day. I thank John and President Va for their hospitality on the day. I look forward to working with all members of the Pacific family to strengthen our common humanity and build a better world.

tree_branches.name: Maitland Riverlights Festival
tree_branches.path: Legislative Assembly (2025-10-14) > Private Members' Statements > Maitland Riverlights Festival
tree_branches.text:
Since those dark years, the festival has grown year on year and is now a week-long program that transforms the city into a vibrant global village, showcasing up to 50 cultures through live music, dance, food, art and interactive cultural experiences. Even though Riverlights goes for one week, preparations take place throughout the whole year. What makes the festival great is the community established by working together to prepare for the event. It was my privilege to attend the event on the weekend not only as a very proud local member but also on behalf of the Minister for Multiculturalism, the member for Rockdale. His agencies, Multicultural NSW and Destination NSW, both provided funding and support to the festival because such festivals bring everyone together as a community to celebrate in a spirit of curiosity, cooperation and joy.

Riverlights encapsulates the multicultural story of Maitland: the old meeting the new, welcoming each to the other, and valuing both our diversity of experience and our unique traditions and cultures. It is a beautiful expression of the understanding that can be found when we acknowledge the long history of multiculturalism in Maitland, the Hunter Valley and the wider area, and share and embrace our individual cultures and experiences. For millennia, the Wonnarua have traversed the hills around the Hunter Valley, with neighbouring nations like the Worimi, Awabakal, Gannilaroi and Darkinjung welcomed to join in local ceremonies as they passed through. Much more recently, European settlement has seen the region's population change. The 15 new citizens who officially became Australians at the event are part of the continuing story of Maitland's diversity.

We welcome everyone to Maitland and look forward to seeing how all of our new citizens will help shape our future. In the heart of the Hunter, we are used to working together and lending a hand during floods and natural disasters. This reliance on each other makes us a welcoming and resilient community. I first heard the many stories of refugees and migrant women when I started work at the then Department of Immigration and Ethnic Affairs nearly three decades ago. Their courage, resilience and persistence has continued to inspire me throughout my life in working for social justice and equality for all. As the MP for Maitland and Minister for Regional Transport, and Minister for Roads, I am committed to building a better New South Wales for all of us. Members are here because we want to be here. We are helping those in our communities build a life for each other that is diverse and different from that of their ancestors and brings a richness to every experience they have.

Every single person who comes to my community helps in some way. They build our experience and empathy, they help to build our homes, they help to educate our kids in our schools and they provide health care in our hospitals. They are part of us, and we are part of them. They contribute to the success of festivals like Maitland Riverlights by bringing many visitors into my community, including those who stay overnight to experience the city's wonderful hospitality. But most important for me was the curiosity of people walking along the Levee Riverbank when they saw cultures they may have only read about in books or visited for a few days and their joy at forming a connection with someone who grew up on the other side of the world who wanted to make Maitland their home.

tree_branches.path: Legislative Assembly (2025-10-14) > Private Members' Statements > Maitland Riverlights Festival > Ms JENNY AITCHISON
tree_branches.text: Ms JENNY AITCHISON ( Maitland — Minister for Regional Transport, and Minister for Roads ) —VALE Judy Nicholson, a pivotal member of the Maitland Historical Society and past Local History Librarian, who passed away suddenly in August. Judy made a huge contribution to several local organisations, including Maitland's Australian Museum of Clothing and Textiles. Members of these organisations recently gathered to remember Judy's tireless work for her community. This includes her role as the editor of the Historical Society's quarterly bulletin. Judy made sure she left a detailed "template", making the job of those who will follow so much easier. Judy was also a valued volunteer with the Friends of Grossman and Brough Houses, where she generously shared her passion for history and community. Before Judy retired and started her volunteering career, she worked in the local history section of Maitland City Council library. tree_branches.name: Central West Resilience and Recovery Package
tree_branches.path: Legislative Assembly (2025-10-14) > Private Members' Statements > Central West Resilience and Recovery Package
tree_branches.text:
In the immediate aftermath of the flood event, the State and Federal governments activated the Disaster Recovery Funding Arrangements, delivering relief grants, hardship support, and funding to repair essential services and infrastructure. Over time, several structured programs were developed to deliver a $100 million Recovery and Resilience Package, co-funded by the Federal and State governments. I will highlight some of the initiatives that are now underway and their impact in the Cabonne, Forbes and Parkes local government areas in the Central West. The Resilient Homes Program is a $40 million initiative that has offered eligible homeowners in flood-affected areas, including Cabonne, Forbes, Lachlan and Parkes, options such as voluntary buybacks, home raising, rebuilding and retrofitting resilience measures. This prolonged program has involved a lengthy assessment phase, but impacted locals are finally receiving this long-awaited assistance. The program is helping turn flood recovery from mere rebuilding into an opportunity for safer, longer-term housing outcomes.

As part of the $100 million funding package, the Community Assets Program funding stream has allocated nearly $24 million to restore and upgrade public infrastructure damaged by flooding, with a view to increasing resilience. Assets funded under this program in Cabonne in the Orange electorate include the restoration of lighting at Eugowra Showground, the refurbishment of the old Eugowra Preschool site, the refurbishment of Eugowra Swimming Pool and amenities, the activation of the Eugowra CBD, the activation of the Hunter Caldwell Sports Precinct at Molong, the restoration of Eugowra Historical Museum and Bushranger Centre, the relocation of the Manildra Multipurpose Courts, the restoration of Eugowra Memorial Park and the relocation of Molong hockey fields.

In Forbes shire, the assets funded include Forbes Netball Courts upgrades, the Lake Forbes Activation Plan for footpath resilience and betterment, and the Forbes Lake Activation Parks and Amenities Resilience and Betterment Project. For Parkes Shire Council, the program funded a new facility for the Parkes SES unit and flood damage repair of Berryman Oval at Trundle, Bushman's Dam and PAC Park. Those projects have not only repaired what was lost but also made these tight-knit country towns more resilient, renewing social vibrancy, instilling confidence and providing important gathering spaces for the impacted communities that are rebuilding and renewing.

Local roads and bridges and causeways are being rebuilt with resilience in mind through the Regional Transport Resilience Fund. Under the Disaster Recovery Funding Arrangements, $3.8 million has been allocated for floodway, culvert, drainage and bridge works, with a further $5.3 million dedicated to bridge upgrades. These works are underway across Cabonne, raising decks, improving drainage and strengthening crossings, so that when future flooding inevitably occurs, connectivity and safety are appropriately considered and not compromised. While repairing flood damage is critical, it is also important to support disaster-impacted communities to increase resilience and pivot to not just sustain residents but also grow these vibrant communities.

With that in mind, Cabonne Council has lodged a funding application under the Regional Economic Development and Community Investment Program. This $50 million fund supports regional initiatives that drive employment, infrastructure, services, industry and growth. Cabonne Council is seeking consideration from the New South Wales Government of $2 million in funding from this program to establish and release residential land in Eugowra that is located outside the mapped flood envelope in areas assessed and deemed low risk to support and sustain the existing population of residents relocating from properties for buybacks and providing housing opportunities for the future growth of the town.

I have thrown my weight behind the application in full support of the council's initiative and this funding. For Eugowra, it is vitally important that support is given to enable Cabonne Council's release of new residential land outside flood-prone zones to incentivise relocations so that the shire and the community have the chance to design and deliver a safer, more resilient future.

tree_branches.name: Mr PHILIP DONATO
tree_branches.path: Legislative Assembly (2025-10-14) > Private Members' Statements > Central West Resilience and Recovery Package > Mr PHILIP DONATO
tree_branches.text: Mr PHILIP DONATO ( Orange ) —Mr Speaker, I would like to acknowledge the wonderful achievement of Olsen Kennedy, who was awarded the Duke of Endinburgh's Gold award this year, the highest offered after securing the program's silver and bronze medals. Olsen is studying year 12 at St Stanislaus College in Bathurst where he has become the first student in the school's history to complete the Duke of Endinburgh three-level clean sweep. The award, which challenges its candidates to step outside their comfort zones and expand their horizons across community, fitness and skill development boundaries, has been running since 1956. Olsen took up the challenge in year nine and has been working steadily towards completion with an hour's work in each category a week. Olsen's gold medal achievement was highlighted by a trip to New Zealand on cricket tour while he has camped and hiked in a number of national parks in the region. He has learned the flute, worked with Stannies' St Vincent De Paul committee, played rugby, and assisted with college masses. I congratulate Olsen on his commitment to completing this arduous yet extremely worthwhile scheme. His dedication to its principles of personal growth will serve him well.

tree_branches.name: Fiji Independence Day
tree_branches.path: Legislative Assembly (2025-10-14) > Private Members' Statements > Fiji Independence Day
tree_branches.text:
My position as an elected representative has provided several opportunities to engage with our Pacific family, including being involved in this Parliament's twin relationship with the Bougainville House of Representatives and serving as an election observer at the last election of the National Parliament of Solomon Islands. In the context of those experiences, it is important to reflect honestly on the journey of Australia's relationship with our Pacific family. During the Morrison Liberal-Nationals Government, relations between Australia and many Pacific nations became strained. Pacific leaders openly described Australia's approach as arrogant. They were frustrated by a perceived lack of respect and understanding, particularly around issues like climate change and regional partnership.

I recall the 2019 Pacific Islands Forum, when then Fijian Prime Minister Frank Bainimarama said, "After what we went through with Morrison, nothing can be worse than him." Those were difficult words to hear—especially for Scott Morrison, I am sure—but they were necessary ones. They remind us that true friendship requires listening, humility, action and a regard for your neighbour. The Pacific being "our backyard" was a term used by many members of the commentariat and the media—particularly the right-wing and Murdoch media— which I do not think helped Australia's relationship with the countries in that region.

Under the current Albanese Labor Government, we have seen a real shift and a reset in tone and substance. There is now a renewed focus on partnership rather than paternalism, on respect rather than rhetoric. Australia's re-engagement with the Pacific as part of our shared region has supported climate resilience, education, security and economic opportunity, all while listening to the priorities that Pacific nations have set. Renewed support for Pacific-led priorities like climate change is helping to rebuild trust and reaffirm Australia's place in the region as a respectful, reliable partner.

We face common challenges, and I feel there is more we can do as good neighbours to support our Pacific family. Almost 60 per cent of the roughly three million small island state peoples, including those of Fiji, Solomon Islands and Bougainville, live within one kilometre of the coastline and 90 per cent within five kilometres. Those people should be able to look to Australia as a refuge and for a helping hand should sea levels continue to rise at the current rate of three to five millimetres per year, as they are expected to do. Our response to the threats faced by our neighbours should be shaped by our common humanity, social solidarity and not only by considerations framed around national defence. The Pacific is not on the periphery of who we are; it is at the heart of our identity. I wish all members of the Central Coast Fijian community a very happy Fiji Independence Day. I thank John and President Va for their hospitality on the day. I look forward to working with all members of the Pacific family to strengthen our common humanity and build a better world.

tree_branches.name: Non-Resident Nepali Association
tree_branches.path: Legislative Assembly (2025-10-14) > Private Members' Statements > Non-Resident Nepali Association
tree_branches.text:
Today more than 180,000 Nepalese-born individuals live in Australia, including over 65,000 in New South Wales. That makes the Nepalese community one of the fastest growing and most vibrant in our multicultural society. Many of those individuals and families have chosen to settle in the electorate of Oatley, calling suburbs like Mortdale, Penshurst, Riverwood and Peakhurst home. It is easy to see why. Our area is a wonderful place to live, work, study and raise a family. But for many new arrivals, the transition to life in Australia can be challenging, particularly when they are without a strong local network. That is where the NRNA plays such a vital role, offering guidance, friendship and practical support to help people settle and succeed. Over the past two years, the NRNA has distributed more than $72,000 through its Social Welfare Fund to individuals in need—many in my own electorate—while providing consular assistance to more than 3,000 community members.

Its generosity extends well beyond our borders. Following natural disasters in Nepal—most notably the 2015 earthquakes—the NRNA has played a central role in mobilising support and raising funds for schools, hospitals and essential infrastructure. Closer to home, it has been a lifeline for many Nepalese Australians in the electorate of Oatley, particularly during the COVID‑19 pandemic when international students and temporary workers faced significant hardship. Recently, the association achieved another major milestone with the establishment of its own office and community hub, a dedicated space that provides emergency support, social welfare assistance and a venue for community gatherings and events. The NRNA also serves as a powerful advocate, engaging with government agencies, diplomatic missions and local organisations on issues such as immigration, access to education, investment and recognition of overseas qualifications.

Through that hard work, the association ensures that the voices and aspirations of Nepalese Australians, especially those in the Oatley electorate and across New South Wales, are heard at every level. Equally inspiring is the NRNA's commitment to preserving and promoting Nepali culture, language and traditions. Over the past many years, it has hosted many Nepali festivals across Australia, attracting more than 120,000 attendees, including many from the Oatley and the St George communities. The festivals are joyful celebrations of culture, food and friendship. I confidently say that they are among the most vibrant events in our multicultural calendar.

The story of the NRNA is a testament to the power of multiculturalism and community spirit. Organisations like this remind us that while we may come from different places, we share a common purpose to contribute, belong and build a better future for everyone. I acknowledge Anil Pokhrel, the outgoing president of NRNA Australia, and his executive team for their tireless service and leadership. I also congratulate the incoming president, Santosh Kumar Bhai, and wish him every success in continuing to strengthen ties between Nepal and Australia, and with the Nepalese communities in the Oatley and St George areas. I look forward to continuing to work closely with the NRNA and the Nepalese community across New South Wales and in my electorate. Their story is one of compassion, unity and resilience. I thank them sincerely for the work that they do every day to make our State, and our local community, stronger and more inclusive for all.

tree_branches.name: Newcastle Electorate Live Music

tree_branches.text:
Newcastle post-punk band, Dust, was the first to grace the baths' stage. Dust is an up-and-coming band on the national and international stage, having performed at South by Southwest Sydney, the nationwide Laneway Festival and the Pitchfork Festival in London, and also supporting international acts like Slowdive and Bloc Party. The band has just released its debut album Sky Is Falling . I recommend that all members check it out or, as Molly used to say, "Do yourself a favour." Dust's set at the Newcastle Ocean Baths was momentous. Hundreds of people packed into the baths, and I have heard nothing but praise for the show. Spencer Scott, of the Hamilton Station Hotel, wrote to me following the gig saying:

Dust performing live at Newcastle Ocean Baths is the greatest show I have seen from a Newcastle artist. It might be one of the greatest concert experiences of my life, period ... The Newcastle Baths is one of the most beautiful places in the world, to see it utilised like this brings me so much joy.

The community really came out for these sets with massive turnouts at every SOAK set. I give a special thank you to New Annual festival director Tory Loudon for making SOAK happen, as well as curators Tim Levinson, Matt Field and Katerina Skoumbas. I am sure we will see SOAK on the 2026 New Annual program, and hopefully beyond the program as well. Lining up the final day of New Annual was the West Best Bloc Fest, which brought over 100 artists to 12 stages across the Midtown precinct. There was a palpable buzz on our streets. I often walked past people saying to their mates, "It is so great to see so many people out." And it really was. There were smiles all round as people of all ages and backgrounds enjoyed live music together. It demonstrated how music and art can unite our community.

That connectedness is why the New South Wales Government is supporting the Midtown precinct as part of the Uptown Accelerator program with $170,000 to support precinct‑wide events such as the West Best Bloc Fest. I thank its founder Dylan Oakes for putting on another fantastic festival. I also congratulate the whole West Best Bloc Fest and Midtown team on a great success. I also note five outstanding musical groups that performed on various West Best stages: Stomp, Bardvarkk, Trophy Wyfe, Citruss and Maple's Pet Dinosaur. Those five bands have two things in common: Their members are all still in high school and they are absolutely phenomenal. Those bands are the next generation of rockstars and the new sound of Newcastle.

I especially note that Maple's Pet Dinosaur, a hard rock band of students from Hunter School of the Performing Arts, has gone viral on social media. Its unique music video for anti‑bullying anthem lego has gained over 54 million views on Instagram, making it the most viewed reel by an Australian‑born artist in the world. I encourage members to have a look. It is awesome. The band has now secured a spot on the Good Things Festival line-up later this year, alongside rock A-listers like Tool and Weezer. It brings me so much hope and joy to see these young Novocastrians striking a chord with not only the local community but also the wider national and international audience. I cannot wait to see what is next and continue to support Newcastle artists, venues and events.

tree_branches.name: Regional Electricity Transmission Lines
tree_branches.path: Legislative Assembly (2025-10-14) > Private Members' Statements > Regional Electricity Transmission Lines
tree_branches.text:
That complete lack of consultation has galvanised the Walcha community. The community is fighting back, and I am fighting along with them. The path that the transmission lines are now proposed to take makes absolutely no sense. There is no logic behind it. The transmission line and the hub are not required, because there are no projects that I know of or that our community is aware of that will feed into this south‑central hub. The Government is looking to spend billions of dollars of taxpayer money building transmission lines that, quite frankly, are not required; nor is the hub required. Some 12 months ago this line was actually looked at by EnergyCo in an expensive investigation that was undertaken, again, using taxpayer money. Millions of dollars were spent. That report came back, and this particular route that EnergyCo has now adopted failed five out of six pillars of the Government's own thresholds. The route failed five out of six and yet this is the approach that the Government is taking to run the transmission lines into the New England.

Another reason this route is no good is that it is going to result in significant habitat damage. The Government was keen to announce the Great Koala National Park, but this transmission line will result in koalas losing habitat. There is a known population of koalas at Niangala. Right in the middle of that population is where that transmission line is going to go. Another reason this route is no good is bushfires. We have aerial application to fight bushfires in that country. It is quite steep country. The transmission line towers are as high as the Opera House. Even as an inexperienced, bad pilot I know that that makes fighting fires in that country all but impossible from the air. Those of us in the RFS do not want to go into that country to fight fires, because it is incredibly steep and difficult terrain. The transmission path cuts through airstrips on farmers' properties. It will decimate land value and carve through some of the very best grazing country that New South Wales has to offer. It will have a huge visual impact on the environment and on people's homes. That is the reality.

Yes, this is cutting through farming country. But that country is people's homes. People have lived there for generations. I have spoken with numerous farmers who have made infrastructure decisions, planning decisions and succession decisions based on the fact that this transmission route was dismissed and failed five out of the six pillars. And yet the Government has completely flipped the goalpost with no consultation or warning. It said, "Here you go, Walcha. Cop this. We've got to connect the New England Renewable Energy Zone." That is why people are completely losing faith in this rollout of renewables into the New England. No-one is taking into account the views and knowledge of locals. Those of us in regional communities who are facing this rollout feel like we are the speed humps. I urge the Government to work with regional communities and relook at the transmission line. This route is completely, utterly and fundamentally flawed.

tree_branches.text:
On our roads, long overdue improvements are finally underway. Stage 1A of the Henry Lawson Drive upgrade is now complete, delivered nine months ahead of schedule and on budget. That is a major win for the 43,000 vehicles that use this road every day. The completion of Stage 1A means smoother traffic flow, reduced congestion and safer conditions for commuters and local residents. Planning is already underway for the $220 million stage 1B upgrade, which will further improve traffic efficiency and safety along one of south‑west Sydney's most critical transport corridors. I was able to ensure that this upgrade retained all of our beloved Gordon Parker Reserve, a place that many of our community sports groups and locals enjoy. Saving this reserve while still delivering a major infrastructure upgrade shows what good planning and strong local advocacy can achieve.

The new $2 billion Bankstown Hospital is another transformative project that is now a reality under this Government. The hospital will include a larger emergency department and expanded maternity, mental health, surgical and intensive care services. That is the single largest health investment in the history of New South Wales and will ensure that families in our community and south-west Sydney can access world-class health care close to home. Those projects are proof that when it governs, Labor delivers not in promises but in progress that people can see, drive on and learn in every day. Rebuilding infrastructure in our community is not just about catching up on what was ignored; it is also about planning for the future. Our Government looks ahead, investing in infrastructure that meets today's needs and anticipates those of tomorrow.

Recently I met with Billie Sankovic, the new board chair of the South Western Sydney Local Health District, to discuss planning for the new Bankstown hospital and how we can continue building on the strong foundation of innovation that already exists in our local health system. Bankstown has pioneered a new model of mental health care—one that focuses on early intervention and integrated community support—and it is now being replicated across the city. Our discussions focused on how we can expand that model, plan for growth corridors and ensure that infrastructure in those areas keeps pace with population needs.

I also met with our local police commander to discuss innovative deployment models that are improving local response times and ensuring officers are better positioned to respond to incidents when they occur. Those improvements show how evidence-based planning and collaboration can deliver real results on the ground. In both health and policing, we are taking the best of what has been pioneered locally and growing it. We are not just delivering projects for today; we are futureproofing our community for tomorrow. This is what good government looks like: delivering long-promised upgrades, fixing what was neglected and building for the future. Whether it is new schools, safer roads, better hospitals or smarter service delivery, I am proud that my community is leading the way in what the Minns Labor Government can achieve when we put people first. Together, we are building stronger, safer and more connected communities for generations to come.

Mr STEPHEN BALI ( Blacktown ) ( 20:19 :18 ): I speak about a new plan that has been tabled for consultation with the community called the Blacktown development control plan [DCP]. It is an opportunity to reset the policies for developers and future development, and let the public have their say in how they would like their CBD to look into the future. As the member for Riverstone is in the Chamber, I put on record that he has been advocating for the State Government to work with the council and the community in developing a DCP or master plan for the Riverstone area, which is a good way to progress.

Western Sydney has been developing at a fast pace and, unfortunately, the City of Blacktown—for whatever reason—has been left off, even though it is the fastest growing area. Everyone likes to give that title to themselves, but Blacktown is the fastest growing local government area in Australia. Some 12,000 people a year have consistently moved in over the past 10 years, according to the Australian Bureau of Statistics. Yet Liverpool, Campbelltown, Fairfield, Parramatta, Castle Hill and Penrith have all developed, and Blacktown has unfortunately been overlooked.

That, in itself, is probably an advantage. It is a disadvantage at the moment for people living in the area, but it is an advantage in that, given a brownfield site with a limited number of owners in certain areas, we have an opportunity to produce the city of the future. By 2035, Blacktown's population will exceed Tasmania's, but we do not have a Hobart or a Darwin to call home in the middle of Blacktown CBD. This is our opportunity to make a difference. Whether it is a night-time economy, live music or town squares, it is so important to get the people involved. What can make Blacktown different? Blacktown's 188 different nationalities and love for festivals are important aspects that should be incorporated, especially if we can wrap them into a CBD area.

I remember being on holidays in Bydgoszcz in Poland. There is a town square of about 100 metres by 110 metres. You can fit 10,000 to 12,000 people into the city centre for an exciting time. There is no CBD in the Sydney Basin that has that type of town square right in the middle of it. We could actually do that in Blacktown, with the major railway lines, bus routes et cetera that connect to it. Blacktown could be the festival capital of the Sydney Basin. Look at the success of the Ramadan festivals where, if people want to go anywhere near Lakemba, they need to park three suburbs away. Imagine building it in the Blacktown area, where there is plenty of potential parking onsite.

Unfortunately, council sold six acres—or 25,000 square metres—right in the middle of Blacktown to Walker Corporation, which wants to convert some of that area. It has put out a DCP that aims to convert Flushcombe Road, which is a major thoroughfare, into a pedestrian mall. They were exciting back in the 1980s. So many streets were converted into pedestrian malls right across Western Sydney, and most of them have been converted back into streets, including those in Blacktown and Penrith et cetera. But no traffic plan or supporting documents are supplied with the Blacktown City Council's DCP. It talks about parking that meets 25 per cent of the current needs.

Westpoint shopping centre, which covers 110,000 square metres—a pretty big shopping centre—currently has 4,600 car parking spaces. According to the proposed DCP, the maximum number of car parking spaces that an equivalent shopping centre will require is 1,400. The Walker proposal is $2.5 billion. It is about two to three times the size of the existing Westpoint, and yet it is going to have a quarter of the car parking spaces. The DCP actually talks about maximum car parking spaces. It does not have a minimum, so a new shopping centre could be brought into Blacktown with zero parking. This is the opportunity for the people of Blacktown to speak out. We want good, sustainable development. We need to have a proper thoroughfare. People have until Friday to put in their submissions. Let us get this deferred and have better public consultation.

The House adjourned, pursuant to standing and sessional orders, at 20:24 until Wednesday 15 October 2025 at 10:00.

tree_branches.name: Midtown Macquarie Park
tree_branches.path: Legislative Assembly (2025-10-14) > Private Members' Statements > Midtown Macquarie Park
tree_branches.text:
However, what should have been a project to improve lives is, for some, devolving into disappointment. The challenges have largely emerged in the past year. I believe that, by tackling them now, we can prevent the compounding of problems for current and future tenants. My office and I have met with residents, both individually and in groups, to understand their concerns. Together, we have conducted a survey and created a petition calling for better management of maintenance claims, rental disputes and building defects, and clearer, more compassionate communication. We have called out the disgrace of embedded energy networks, especially in social and affordable housing, and we have tried to give a voice to the many individual complaints that have emerged from within Midtown.

The purpose of this speech is to once again place on record those challenges in the hope that the Government will take a closer, more forensic look at what is happening in my community. Standard responses, form letters and political pointscoring will no longer cut it for residents who are genuinely struggling. Almost daily I hear from tenants who have received unexplained rent increases in the middle of a housing crisis. That is bad enough when it comes from a private landlord, but it is particularly unsettling when it comes from the Government. Mission Australia, which manages Midtown, has rightly explained that rents are reviewed regularly and that tenants who do not opt in to automatic deductions through Centrepay may fall behind. That may be technically accurate, but accuracy alone is not good enough.

Many residents are facing financial hardship or mental health challenges, have experienced trauma or simply do not have the financial literacy to navigate the complexity of their leases. They are precisely the people who need a system that supports, not confuses, them. I am calling on the Government to work with interested MPs, residents, the sector and providers on a more transparent and streamlined approach to rental payments. If Commonwealth Rent Assistance is explicitly intended to cover rent, why not create a process where payments transfer directly to the provider? That would remove confusion, reduce administrative costs and prevent residents from falling into arrears through no fault of their own.

Turning to maintenance and building defects, I have spoken many times in this House about the unacceptable state of building defects in strata housing. When tenants are involved—and when those tenants are in social or affordable housing—the consequences are multiplied. Residents need a single source of truth: What can and can't they control? Who is responsible for what? Is it the provider, the builder or somebody else entirely? If they cannot get answers from the provider, where can they turn? As the member for Ryde I will always help, but it should not take the intervention of an MP to troubleshoot what should be people‑oriented government services. None of it is clear and I am not convinced that the Government fully understands the scale of the problem yet.

I was struck by an answer to a question I asked the Minister, which revealed that compliance assessments for some housing providers only occur every two years. While Mission Australia is assessed annually, many Midtown residents have lived there less than a year. That means the next assessment—and any meaningful change that follows—will dwarf their time living in Midtown. Some maintenance issues are small—mould, peeling plaster or broken fittings—but they are still unacceptable when they drag on. Larger defects, however, must be dealt with far more urgently. The Government wants to solve Sydney's housing crisis through more Midtowns. That strategy will fail if the apartments being built are not of high quality; taxpayers will foot the bill and residents will pay the price.

Finally, I speak about the human side of the issue: the relationships between tenants and providers. Those relationships can make or break whether someone is able to live a stable and fulfilling life in their home. I have heard too many stories of breakdowns in communication and trust at Midtown. I do not know every detail of every complaint, but I would bet that many staff are doing their best in an impossible system and are bearing the brunt of residents' legitimate frustrations. That is why I am raising the issue in Parliament today. The system needs close inspection and genuine reform, not to apportion blame but to protect staff, to identify where management is legitimately failing and, most importantly, to support vulnerable people who just want to live their lives with dignity—people like my constituents in Midtown. I will continue to defend and support them for as long as I am their local MP.

tree_branches.name: Castle Hill Electorate School Infrastructure
tree_branches.path: Legislative Assembly (2025-10-14) > Private Members' Statements > Castle Hill Electorate School Infrastructure
tree_branches.text:
Baulkham Hills North Public School was established in 1967 and for the past 58 years has expanded to meet the needs of the growing population. Over the years the school has increased the number of demountable buildings to meet that need. The school now has 18 demountable classrooms and two additional demountable buildings. On 11 July 2025 the Australian Financial Review published some comments on Baulkham Hills North Public School. They provide a staggering insight into the conditions at the school. The paper states:

At Baulkham Hills North Public School in Sydney's outer west, space is so tight teachers are forced to stand in the staff room and the students have to take turns using outdoor areas.

There are almost 900 children crammed into the school, almost double its intended student population. Half the classrooms are demountables, which former parents and citizens association president Alison Mackey says leak during bad weather, are prone to mould and have further shrunk the space otherwise available …

The school captain, Hannah Vijaykumar, sent an email to my office on 18 September 2025. She said:

I am Hannah, the school captain of a school built 60 years ago, for 500 students. We now have over 800. The government is going on multi-million-dollar upgrades to other schools, and the only thing that has happened to us is more demountable buildings.

No new toilets. There have been multiple years where I have been waiting for 5 minutes and I'm late to class, waiting for the toilet. My friend has not been to the toilet at school in years.

Our toilets are yucky, there is not enough, it isn't even decent. It's not good enough. More than half our classrooms are demountable classrooms [that] are cold in winter, hot in summer with NO insulation.

I learnt that at school. My sister, only a bit younger, hasn't. I know I leave my school this year, but I would never wish it on anyone to be in a demountable. Someone needs to fix this, and that someone is the government. All I can ask, is just please fix my school.

Hannah took interest in the petition debate in this House on the Hills Shire Council on 18 September 2025, and she also read the Government's written response to that petition. Hannah asked me to bring it to the attention of Parliament that Baulkham Hills North Public School has been "completely ignored in the result of the petition to Parliament". I have asked the education Minister and, subsequently, the acting education Minister to visit the Castle Hill electorate to view the development that is occurring and see the amount of apartments that are being built, but they have not taken up my request. The Castle Hill electorate is seeing more and more cranes building more and more apartment buildings. Where will the children who will live in those new apartments attend school?

In some cases, schools have double the student cap, such as Castle Hill High School, which has 51 demountable buildings. On behalf of parents and students in Castle Hill, I will continue to request that the Government funds new schools and upgrades existing schools. I agree with Hannah that it is not good enough. The Government must allocate funding to upgrade and build new primary and secondary schools within the Castle Hill electorate. I call on the Government to immediately allocate funding to upgrade Baulkham Hills North Public School, to acquire land and build a new primary school in the Castle Hill Showground precinct, and to acquire land and build a new secondary school in the Castle Hill precinct.

tree_branches.name: Preventative Health Care
tree_branches.path: Legislative Assembly (2025-10-14) > Private Members' Statements > Preventative Health Care
tree_branches.text:
We have a great hospital system in New South Wales. It is one of the best in the world, but it is focused primarily on fixing people and treating them rather than preventing illness in the first place. We are not unique in that regard. I want to talk about why we need a significant shift toward preventive health and what is at stake if we fail to act. New South Wales, like the rest of Australia, is ageing. By 2031 nearly one in five people in New South Wales will be 65 or older. The population aged 85 and over is projected to more than double in the next 20 years, from just over half a million now to 1.28 million in 2041—that is the tail end of the boomers hitting their eighties. We should celebrate that people are living longer. It is one of the greatest triumphs of modern medicine. But it also brings challenges, especially when those added years are not spent in good health.

The Australian Institute of Health and Welfare reported that older Australians account for about 40 per cent of all hospitalisations and more than half of all hospital patient days. A major study published in the Medical Journal of Australia estimated that the average hospital cost in the last year of a person's life is between $30,000 and $40,000. The average Australian can expect about 70.9 healthy years, but our life expectancy is just over 83. That means roughly 12 years lived with illness or disability. While our life span has been rising, our health span—the time we spend in good health—has not kept pace, and that has consequences. Our hospitals are under relentless strain.

In the June quarter there were over 785,000 emergency department attendances in New South Wales. Elective surgery wait lists are expanding, with over 100,000 in the last quarter. That has been reduced in the short term by a $200 million injection of funding by the Government, which is welcomed, but the cycle of boom and bust in emergency funding will continue. Behind each of those numbers is a person waiting, often in pain, anxious for answers. We are running a system that is trying to catch up with disease rather than get ahead of it. The Special Commission of Inquiry into Healthcare Funding put it bluntly:

A strong, coordinated focus on preventive health is essential to reduce future costs and improve population health outcomes.

In its submission to that inquiry the New South Wales primary health network also highlighted that investment in preventative health could deliver returns of up to $14 for every dollar spent. Sometimes people hear "prevention" and think it is about telling people to exercise more or eat better, but it is so much more than that. It includes primary prevention, which means stopping disease before it starts through smoking cessation, healthy weight programs, vaccination and reducing harmful alcohol use. It includes secondary prevention, which means finding diseases earlier, when they are easier and cheaper to treat, as well as better cancer screening programs or more regular health checks for people at risk, like skin checks, blood pressure checks, mammograms, Pap smears and diabetes checks. It also includes tertiary prevention, which means reducing the impact of established diseases and keeping people as healthy as possible so they avoid hospitalisation and maintain quality of life.

Let us not forget the social determinants of health, because health does not start in hospitals. It starts in our homes, schools and communities. Housing, education, employment and food security shape our health outcomes as powerfully as medical treatments. The choice is clear: We can keep pouring more money into treating disease after it happens, running faster on a treadmill that keeps getting steeper and steeper, or we can shift our focus and our resources to preventing disease before it happens. This is not a new problem; this has been happening for many years. But it is incumbent on all of us to look at the trends in our population and work to prevent disease rather than treat it when it is too late.

tree_branches.name: Out of the Shadows Walk
tree_branches.path: Legislative Assembly (2025-10-14) > Private Members' Statements > Out of the Shadows Walk
tree_branches.text:
The walk is more than a symbolic gesture; it is a powerful act of community healing. It is a space where survivors of suicide loss, first responders, support workers and families left behind can come together, share their grief and find strength in connection. It is truly a moment to say, "You are not alone." We remember those who have died by suicide: our sons and daughters, brothers and sisters, parents, friends and colleagues. Each life lost leaves behind a ripple of heartbreak. Families are forever changed, and communities carry the weight of unanswered questions and silent sorrow. The walk gives voice to that pain and transforms it into purpose.

I acknowledge the survivors, those who have faced the darkest moments and found the courage to keep going. Their resilience is extraordinary, and their presence at the walk is a testament to the strength of the human spirit and the importance of speaking openly about mental health. I honour the grief, memories and love of the families left behind. Suicide loss is a unique and devastating experience often compounded by stigma and isolation. Events like this help break that silence and create a safe space for remembrance and healing. I thank our first responders—police, paramedics and emergency service workers. They are often the first on the scene, bearing witness to unimaginable pain. Their role is critical, and their wellbeing matters. The support workers, counsellors and volunteers, especially those from Lifeline, are the backbone of suicide prevention. They answer calls at all hours, offer comfort in crisis and walk alongside those in distress. Every 24 seconds, someone in Australia calls Lifeline, which is over a million contacts a year. Their work is vital, and their compassion saves lives. I thank them.

The Out of the Shadows walk also serves to raise awareness and challenge stigma. Suicide is not a taboo subject; it is a public health issue that demands open conversation, education and community action. I commend CEO Catherine Vaara, Di Bannister, Kelly Saidey and their amazing team at Lifeline Mid Coast for their leadership in organising this event and for their ongoing commitment to suicide prevention. I thank also the many individuals and organisations who participated, donated and supported the walk. Their involvement makes a difference. Let us continue to build a community where mental health is prioritised, where help is accessible and where no-one feels they have to face their darkest moments alone. Let us walk together, not just on one morning in September but every day, in support, in remembrance and in hope. The Out of the Shadows walk is a reminder that, even in our deepest grief, there is light, connection, healing and always hope.

tree_branches.name: Mr ROBERT DWYER
tree_branches.path: Legislative Assembly (2025-10-14) > Private Members' Statements > Out of the Shadows Walk > Mr ROBERT DWYER
tree_branches.text: Mr ROBERT DWYER ( Port Macquarie ) —I rise to recognise David Castleton, a driving force behind the growth and success of the Queens Lake Sailing Club for over two decades. Since joining as a junior sailor in 1997, David has demonstrated unwavering commitment to the sport and the community. His early advocacy saw sailing introduced as a school sport, personally providing boats and mentoring students. In 2013, David joined the committee, securing vital grants to upgrade safety equipment and improve accessibility for volunteers. He also championed junior development, enabling many young sailors to obtain their boat licences. As Commodore since 2015, David led the club through a period of remarkable growth, hosting state and national titles, expanding the fleet of club-owned boats, and launching inclusive 'Try Sailing' programs for all ages and abilities. His leadership saw the removal of hazardous debris from the lake, enhancing safety for all users. David's vision culminated in the successful extension of the clubhouse, providing essential boat storage and supporting family participation. His dedication is evident, from morning sailing sessions to competitive afternoon races, bridging generations with a 70-year age gap among sailors. David's legacy is one of inclusion, opportunity and enduring community spirit.

tree_branches.text: Mrs JUDY HANNAN ( Wollondilly ) —Veronica has been nominated for the Wollondilly Australia Day Awards in the category of Local Hero, for her outstanding contributions as the Event Coordinator at the Silverdale Probus Club. Veronica's dedication to organising engaging activities and events has significantly enriched the lives of retirees in our community. Her tireless efforts have created a space where seniors feel connected, supported, and valued. Through her leadership at the Silverdale Probus Club, Veronica has cultivated an environment that encourages friendship, purpose, and joy. She understands the challenges that can come with retirement, especially the risk of isolation, and works passionately to ensure no one feels left out or alone. Veronica's approach is warm and inclusive, taking the time to listen, to welcome new members and to create opportunities for meaningful interaction. Her events are thoughtfully planned to foster laughter, learning, and companionship, helping retirees stay active and engaged. Beyond her role in the club, Veronica's impact is felt throughout the Wollondilly community. She is a shining example of how one person's dedication can transform lives and build a stronger, more connected community.

tree_branches.text: Mrs JUDY HANNAN ( Wollondilly ) —It is with respect that I honour the life and legacy of Mrs. Marion Palmer of Bargo. Marion, born 1st May 1943, was a woman of grace, strength, and unwavering devotion to her family and her passing on 10th July 2025 was felt by all who knew her. She was the beloved wife of William, whose partnership she cherished throughout their years together. Marion was a devoted mother to Peter, Robyne, and David, and a supportive mother-in-law to Dave. Her nurturing spirit and steadfast love were the foundation of her family. Marion's memory lives on through her grandchildren—Kara, Grant, Luke, Ryan, and Aaron—each of whom she adored deeply. Her joy was further multiplied by her great-grandchildren: Charlotte, Liam, Atticus, Pixiella, Harriet, Hamish, Finn, and Hudson, who brought her immense pride and happiness. Her presence enriched the lives of all who knew her. Marion will be remembered for her kindness, wisdom, and enduring love.

tree_branches.name: Vivian Allen
tree_branches.path: Legislative Assembly (2025-10-14) > Written Community Recognition Statements > Vivian Allen
tree_branches.text: Mrs JUDY HANNAN ( Wollondilly ) —Mrs Vivian Allen has been recognised for her contributions to Wollondilly, through her nominations in the 2025 Wollondilly Australia Day Awards, in the category of Senior Citizen of the Year. Vivian is a charter member of The Oaks Historical Society Incorporated, which was established on 1st May 1979. Since its inception, she has remained a dedicated and active contributor, taking on numerous roles including inaugural treasurer, secretary, public officer, librarian, photographic archivist, family historian, newsletter team member, and regular weekend volunteer. Vivian's willingness to step into any role needed has greatly benefited the Wollondilly Heritage Centre and Museum. Her extensive knowledge of museum operations and historical research has made her a valuable mentor to others within the society. Over the past year, Vivian has continued her weekend volunteer duties while undertaking the significant task of digitising the library's resources to improve accessibility for researchers. She has also played a key role in developing historical content for the society's newsletter, helping to preserve and share the rich heritage of the Wollondilly Shire. Vivian is a humble and respected member of the society, and a true pillar of the local historical community.

tree_branches.path: Legislative Assembly (2025-10-14) > Written Community Recognition Statements > Bloomfield Hospital Auxiliary
tree_branches.text: Mr PHILIP DONATO ( Orange ) —I would like to take this opportunity to acknowledge the work of the Bloomfield Hospital Auxiliary which, for more than 40 years, has provided support to Orange's mental health campus and its patients. I would also like to recognise the work of president Tania O'Donahue, vice-president Luke O'Donahue and treasurer Harry Smith, the last three members of the auxiliary before its wind-up in September this year. During its 43 years of service the Bloomfield Hospital Auxiliary has raised money to assist with the purchase of items which can help with a patient's treatment or manage their illness. Sensory blankets, soft toys, Easter eggs and other items that helped patients' wellbeing have been purchased by the Auxiliary. At Christmas time, the Auxiliary gave each patient a $50 gift voucher. Funds raised came from raffles, supported with items donated by the community but run by the volunteers, including long-serving secretary Sr Mary Trainor. Unfortunately, the amount of people now volunteering in our communities is dwindling, and the Bloomfield Hospital Auxiliary is a victim of the shortage. I thank the all volunteers who have contributed to this group during its 43-year history.

tree_branches.name: Mr PHILIP DONATO
tree_branches.path: Legislative Assembly (2025-10-14) > Written Community Recognition Statements > Bloomfield Hospital Auxiliary > Mr PHILIP DONATO
tree_branches.text: Mr PHILIP DONATO ( Orange ) —Mr Speaker, I would like to acknowledge the wonderful achievement of Olsen Kennedy, who was awarded the Duke of Endinburgh's Gold award this year, the highest offered after securing the program's silver and bronze medals. Olsen is studying year 12 at St Stanislaus College in Bathurst where he has become the first student in the school's history to complete the Duke of Endinburgh three-level clean sweep. The award, which challenges its candidates to step outside their comfort zones and expand their horizons across community, fitness and skill development boundaries, has been running since 1956. Olsen took up the challenge in year nine and has been working steadily towards completion with an hour's work in each category a week. tree_branches.name: Jason Lewis
tree_branches.path: Legislative Assembly (2025-10-14) > Written Community Recognition Statements > Jason Lewis
tree_branches.text: Mr PHILIP DONATO ( Orange ) —Mr Speaker, an extraordinary commitment to enabling young swimmers to realise their potential has earned Orange coach Jason Lewis an honour at the Swimming NSW 2025 Awards for Excellence. Nominated in the Leaders in Community and Club Excellence category, Mr Lewis was awarded Volunteer of the Year for his contributions to the Orange Aquatic Club. As a co-founder and head coach, Jason donates more than 20 hours a week to support his swimmers, developing programs and researching the sports development while balancing a full-time job. Always cheerful, funny, intelligent, positive and passionate about the sport, Mr Lewis fosters a trusting rapport with his swimmers. He has put in many hours' work on his own development as a coach and regularly makes himself available for swimming carnivals of any level. He doesn't shy at using his annual leave to give young swimmers the support they need to compete at their best. The result? Orange Aquatic Club is one of regional NSW's strongest teams. I congratulate Mr Lewis on this well‑deserved accolade and thank him for his dedication to our young swimmers.

tree_branches.name: Margaret Clarke
tree_branches.path: Legislative Assembly (2025-10-14) > Written Community Recognition Statements > Margaret Clarke
tree_branches.text: Mr MARK SPEAKMAN ( Cronulla ) —Recently retired Margaret Clarke's extraordinary teaching career was recognised last month with the award of the NSW Service Medallion at NSW Parliament House for 50 years of service to the Department of Education. The medallion is awarded for meritorious service of over 40 years in the NSW Public Service, a fitting acknowledgment of her dedication and impact. Margaret, of Cronulla, first taught at Canley Vale and Banksia Road public schools, before beginning her teaching in inclusive education at Carinya School for Specific Purposes. She later taught at Minerva Schools for 20 years and at Endeavour Sports High School for over 20 years, where she established the Special Education Support Class. Margaret's commitment to professional development is also noteworthy – she has been instrumental in mentoring new educators, fostering a culture of continuous learning and advocating for the rights and needs of students with disabilities. Whether through creating work experience programs enabling students to gain employment, launching RUOK? Packs to her students during COVID-19, taking students to the doctors or assisting in filling out Centrelink forms, her work has left an indelible mark on the field, influencing policies and practices which prioritise inclusion and accessibility.

tree_branches.name: Mr MARK SPEAKMAN
tree_branches.path: Legislative Assembly (2025-10-14) > Written Community Recognition Statements > Margaret Clarke > Mr MARK SPEAKMAN
tree_branches.text: Mr MARK SPEAKMAN ( Cronulla ) —I was delighted to join the Cronulla Public School community last month to mark 100 years on the school's Burraneer Bay Road site. It was an opportunity for past and present students, families and staff to celebrate public education at the beautiful location where its iconic building has been a focal point since the school – now 115-years-old - moved from what is now Monro Park. More important than the bricks and mortar, of course, is the legacy of knowledge and skills imparted, and character built, over many generations - and the continuing commitment to knowledge, skills and the character for future generations. The school's rich history was on display through photos and records, before everyone came together for a special school assembly. I acknowledge principal Trent Bridgland and his wonderful team for the fitting celebration and what they do every day. A special mention to student leaders Summer Ransom, Dallas Towers, Will Green and Boston Highland for hosting the assembly and doing their school proud. Thousands of families are thankful for the learning, fun times and friendships built on the site and vision to locate the school in its idyllic spot.

tree_branches.name: A Fond Farewell After 30 Years of Service – Pharmacist Jeff Nelson
tree_branches.path: Legislative Assembly (2025-10-14) > Written Community Recognition Statements > A Fond Farewell After 30 Years of Service – Pharmacist Jeff Nelson
tree_branches.text: Mr JUSTIN CLANCY ( Albury ) —I congratulate Jeff Nelson (Pharmacist), who officially retired on September 10, marking the end of an extraordinary 30-year career at Lavington Square, Terry White Chemmart Pharmacy. Mr Nelson began his journey at the pharmacy in 1994, became a partner in 2000, and has long been a respected and familiar presence within our community. From Sydney to London, Canberra to Albury, Mr Nelson's career took him far and wide, but it was in Lavington that he truly found his professional home. Forming lasting bonds with generations of families, becoming not just a pharmacist, but a trusted friend and confidant to many. A standout moment in his career was his involvement with Terry White Chemmart's Advisory Group, contributing to the broader pharmacy network and proudly celebrating the 2013 national award for Best Pharmacy in Australia. Mr Nelson's final days were filled with emotional goodbyes from the community he served so faithfully. His retirement will begin with a volunteer trip to Cambodia, where he will help build homes for those in need. Thank you, Jeff, for your service, heart, and humanity.

tree_branches.name: Mr JUSTIN CLANCY
tree_branches.path: Legislative Assembly (2025-10-14) > Written Community Recognition Statements > A Fond Farewell After 30 Years of Service – Pharmacist Jeff Nelson > Mr JUSTIN CLANCY
tree_branches.text: Mr JUSTIN CLANCY ( Albury ) —I acknowledge Charles Sturt University as it celebrates 20 years of delivering nursing education at the Albury campus, a milestone that reflects dedication to strengthening our regional healthcare workforce. Since its first intake in 2005, the Bachelor of Nursing program has trained approximately 700 nurses locally, giving aspiring healthcare professionals in the twin cities the opportunity to study and serve close to home. Today, Charles Sturt University stands as the largest provider of registered nursing education in regional Australia, a remarkable achievement. Between 2020 and 2024, an estimated 2,000 students have graduated from the Bachelor of Nursing program, an average of 500 nursing graduates each year. This year alone, over 3,150 students are studying a Bachelor of Nursing through Charles Sturt, with 153 based in Albury-Wodonga. I thank Professor Kerryn Butler-Henderson, Head of Nursing, Paramedicine and Healthcare Sciences, and to the entire teaching and support team, for their role in this success. With 93% of undergraduate and 97 per cent of postgraduate nursing graduates securing full-time employment within four months, Charles Sturt University leads the nation in nursing graduate employability. Congratulations on 20 years of service to our region and beyond!

tree_branches.name: Lachie Wheatley – Xavier College Albury
tree_branches.path: Legislative Assembly (2025-10-14) > Written Community Recognition Statements > Lachie Wheatley – Xavier College Albury
tree_branches.text: Mr JUSTIN CLANCY ( Albury ) —I would like to extend my congratulations to Lachie Wheatley, a year 11 student from Xavier College Albury, on his outstanding achievement in representing NSW Combined Catholic Colleges [NSWCCC], in the 18 years and under division, at the Australian Schools Water Polo Exchange held this August. Earning selection in the NSW team requires tremendous commitment, perseverance and dedication. Lachie and his NSW teammates can take pride in their achievements and in the outstanding way they displayed their talent, teamwork, and sportsmanship on the national stage. Well done Lachie and Team NSW.

tree_branches.path: Legislative Assembly (2025-10-14) > Written Community Recognition Statements > Nourished Australia
tree_branches.text: Mr GREG PIPER ( Lake Macquarie ) —I congratulate the dedicated team of volunteers behind NourishEd Australia on reaching a significant milestone, namely the first anniversary since opening their doors in Toronto. Under the leadership of Directors, Nicholas Cade and Jeremy Eastham, NourishEd has secured it's standing as an essential service in the Lake Macquarie area. Nick and Jeremy volunteer full time to keep the grass roots organisation up, running and growing. Through their open-access pantry, free meal service, community cafe, and library, the NourishEd team have provided food relief, community connection, and dignity to hundreds, if not thousands of people across the region over the past 12 months. NourishEd has not only provided food to fill hungry tummies, but also solace for the lonely, a safe space for the vulnerable and a compassionate ear for anyone doing it tough. Following this amazing progress, their plans for Recovery Groups and Education are destined for success. The success and growth of this service is testament to the passion and dedication of the volunteers. I wish NourishEd a very happy first birthday and look forward to many more years of this hub of help making a real difference in our community.

tree_branches.name: 25 Years of Settlement Services International [SSI]
tree_branches.path: Legislative Assembly (2025-10-14) > Written Community Recognition Statements > 25 Years of Settlement Services International [SSI]
tree_branches.text: Ms JULIA FINN ( Granville ) —I would like to acknowledge the 25th anniversary of Settlement Services International [SSI], an organisation that has transformed the lives of thousands of people across Australia. From its humble beginnings in 2000, with no staff and just one program, SSI has grown into a national organisation employing over 1,100 people and delivering more than 50 programs that support migrants, refugees, people with disability, and vulnerable families. At the heart of SSI's story is empathy and community. Under the leadership of CEO Violet Roumeliotis AM, SSI has stayed true to its founding principle — that settlement and social services must be led by lived experience and rooted in compassion. For 25 years, SSI has championed inclusion, diversity and opportunity, proving that good policy and humanity can go hand in hand. I congratulate SSI's staff, member organisations and partners on this remarkable milestone and thank them for their enduring contribution to building a fairer, more inclusive Australia.

tree_branches.text: Ms JULIA FINN ( Granville ) —I acknowledge the unveiling of the NAEOTOM Alpha Pro photon-counting CT scanner at Medscan Merrylands on World Heart Day, 29 September 2025 — a major milestone for healthcare innovation in Western Sydney. Developed by Siemens Healthineers and introduced through Quantum Medscan and Heartscan Australia, this world-leading imaging technology delivers unprecedented clarity in cardiac diagnostics, reduces radiation exposure, and allows for earlier, safer, and more accurate diagnosis of heart disease. It is only the second installation of its kind in NSW, and it will be bulk billed to ensure local patients have equitable access to cutting-edge healthcare. This technology represents a leap forward for preventive medicine and will directly benefit communities in Western Sydney, where rates of heart disease remain among the highest in the state. I commend Dr John O'Rourke, Chris Munday, and the Medscan team for their vision, collaboration, and commitment to improving cardiac health outcomes for all. This is an extraordinary achievement for our local area — bringing world-class innovation home to Western Sydney.

tree_branches.name: Opening of Wentworthville House – Women's Community Shelters
tree_branches.path: Legislative Assembly (2025-10-14) > Written Community Recognition Statements > Opening of Wentworthville House – Women's Community Shelters
tree_branches.text: Ms JULIA FINN ( Granville ) —I welcome the opening of Wentworthville House, a remarkable new development providing ten new homes for women and children escaping domestic and family violence. Wentworthville House represents a vital partnership between the NSW Government and Women's Community Shelters, co-funded through the Community Housing Innovation Fund – DFV alongside generous community donors including the George and Mary Beswick Fund and Lendlease FutureSteps. These ten homes – five social and five affordable – are safe, stable, and welcoming spaces that offer a pathway to independence and dignity for families rebuilding their lives after trauma. This project showcases how government, community, and philanthropy can come together to deliver long-term, compassionate solutions to the housing and domestic violence crises. I thank Annabelle Daniel OAM, CEO of Women's Community Shelters and the entire WCS team for their leadership and collaboration. Wentworthville House stands as a symbol of what's possible when we combine empathy, expertise, and shared purpose and as a proud step forward for women and children across Western Sydney.

tree_branches.text: Mr MARK SPEAKMAN ( Cronulla ) —I join with my old club in celebrating the remarkable 40 year contribution of life member Giulio Di Stefano to the Caringbah Redbacks Football Club. Giulio is the enthusiast every local sports club needs. He first pulled on a Redbacks shirt as a player in 1985 and in the four decades since he's gone on to also be a coach, leader, mentor, committee man and a driving force behind the growth of local football. Giulio is a very familiar face at North Caringbah Oval where I've seen him full of enthusiasm on a cool winter evening sharing his love of the game with the Redbacks' youngest players. Alongside his tireless work for the Redbacks he also found the time to serve as Sutherland Shire Football Association treasurer for more than 20 years. The club says of Giulio's 40 years with the Redbacks: "Along the way he's collected premierships, lifelong friendships, and a reputation as one of the most respected figures in the Shire's football family. His contribution is measured not only in matches coached and played, but in the players he's guided, the initiatives he's pushed forward, and the standards he's set." Congratulations Giulio!

tree_branches.name: Kempsey Cannonballs 50 Year Reunion
tree_branches.path: Legislative Assembly (2025-10-14) > Written Community Recognition Statements > Kempsey Cannonballs 50 Year Reunion
tree_branches.text: Mr MICHAEL KEMP ( Oxl ey ) —For half a century, the Kempsey Cannonballs have been more than just a rugby team, they've been a family and a source of pride for Kempsey. Generations have worn the Cannonballs colours with passion, building a legacy of mateship, resilience, and community spirit. This past weekend, our community came together to honour an incredible milestone -the 50th Reunion of the Kempsey Cannonballs Rugby Club. The celebrations were filled with laughter, memories, and camaraderie as past and present members reunited to honour five decades of Cannonballs history. From the Welcome Drinks at the Kempsey Macleay Sports & Bowling Club to the 50th Year Reunion Dinner at the Kempsey Showground, the weekend was a heartfelt reflection of what makes this club so special. The festivities also included the popular 300 Club raffle and the chance to pick up some Cannonballs merchandise, adding extra fun and nostalgia to the event. Congratulations to everyone who has been part of the Cannonballs' journey - players, coaches, volunteers, and loyal fans alike. Your dedication and passion have shaped a proud legacy that continues to unite and inspire the Kempsey community.

tree_branches.name: Mr MICHAEL KEMP
tree_branches.path: Legislative Assembly (2025-10-14) > Written Community Recognition Statements > Kempsey Cannonballs 50 Year Reunion > Mr MICHAEL KEMP
tree_branches.text: Mr MICHAEL KEMP ( Oxley ) —Since the age of 12, Leyesha Campbell, a proud Dunghutti woman from Kempsey, has faced the realities of kidney disease. Diagnosed with end-stage renal failure as a child, she has undergone dialysis, treatment, and even a transplant - yet she has never let her illness define her. Instead, this extraordinary young woman has turned her experience into a mission to strengthen Aboriginal healthcare. I had the privilege of meeting Leyesha through the NSW Parliament's Young Aboriginal Leaders Program, where she delivered a powerful speech on the urgent need for better health outcomes for Aboriginal people living with kidney disease. Her courage, her determination, and her vision left a deep impression. Through her social platform, Leyesha's Journey, she shares advice, encouragement, and her lived experience. Beyond that, she contributes as a research assistant at the University of Sydney, helping to shape clinical guidelines that ensure care is culturally safe and accessible for Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander patients. Leyesha's story is a reminder that we must do more to deliver world-class healthcare in regional areas. She embodies resilience, leadership, and hope for young people across our communities.

tree_branches.name: Dennis Hughes Honoured by Wauchope Golf Club
tree_branches.path: Legislative Assembly (2025-10-14) > Written Community Recognition Statements > Dennis Hughes Honoured by Wauchope Golf Club
tree_branches.text: Mr MICHAEL KEMP ( Oxley ) —Community clubs thrive because of people like Dennis Hughes. For 13 years, Dennis has given his heart and soul to the Wauchope Golf Club, serving as Captain and helping guide the club through good times and challenges alike. Since taking on the position in 2012, Dennis has been a driving force behind the growth and success of the club. From overseeing computer system upgrades, to supporting major events like the Top Gun competition, to introducing the Player of the Year Trophy, Dennis has always sought ways to keep the club modern and inclusive. Dennis' leadership was particularly evident during the challenging Covid years. While many clubs struggled, Dennis worked hard to ensure the club remained active and connected. The Junior Development fund is thriving today because Dennis personally collected cans and bottles from the golf course bins, turning recycling into opportunity for young players. Dennis has left an undeniable mark on Wauchope Golf Club, helping shape it into one of the most welcoming clubs in our region. In recognition of this remarkable contribution, members unanimously awarded him life membership. Congratulations Dennis on this well-deserved honour.

tree_branches.text: Mr MICHAEL KEMP ( Oxley ) —Since the age of 12, Leyesha Campbell, a proud Dunghutti woman from Kempsey, has faced the realities of kidney disease. Diagnosed with end-stage renal failure as a child, she has undergone dialysis, treatment, and even a transplant - yet she has never let her illness define her. Instead, this extraordinary young woman has turned her experience into a mission to strengthen Aboriginal healthcare. I had the privilege of meeting Leyesha through the NSW Parliament's Young Aboriginal Leaders Program, where she delivered a powerful speech on the urgent need for better health outcomes for Aboriginal people living with kidney disease. Her courage, her determination, and her vision left a deep impression. Through her social platform, Leyesha's Journey, she shares advice, encouragement, and her lived experience. Beyond that, she contributes as a research assistant at the University of Sydney, helping to shape clinical guidelines that ensure care is culturally safe and accessible for Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander patients. Leyesha's story is a reminder that we must do more to deliver world-class healthcare in regional areas. She embodies resilience, leadership, and hope for young people across our communities.
